arxiv-2512-00239:
Self-supervised learning lets models train on unlabeled recordings, which is vital for medical time series. Yenho Chen, Maxwell Xu, James Rehg, and Christopher Rozell study representations of physiological signals in 2025. Success depends on keeping information about the body's state while filtering out unrelated noise.

Existing strategies lean on heuristic principles or weakly constrained generative tasks, which can blur exactly the signals clinicians care about. The authors frame pretraining objectives around dynamical systems, the mathematics of systems that evolve over time. Better representations could improve monitoring tools that learn from heart, brain, and breathing data with few labeled examples. Physiological signals, from heartbeats to brain waves, are exactly the data this work targets.
arxiv-2512-00339:
Two species competing across a landscape of connected habitat patches face a strategic choice at every boundary. Kuiyue Liu and Shanshan Chen study the global dynamics of a reaction-diffusion competition model with edge behavior in 2025. The landscape consists of finitely many adjacent patches.

In the two-patch case, edge behavior at the interface can be treated as a strategy. Earlier work showed an ideal free distribution strategy that is globally evolutionarily stable. Knowing when competitors settle into such distributions helps ecologists predict how species sort across fragmented habitats. Edge behavior captures what individuals do at a boundary, where many contests are decided. Global dynamics ask where the whole system ends up, not just where it starts. For folks who tend wild lands cut into small plots, the gain is a clue to where each kind will settle. It shows which plot lines will be the front lines.
arxiv-2512-00639:
Thyroid nodules are common, and telling benign from malignant ones early guides treatment. Mahmoud El Hussieni presents a Doppler-enhanced deep learning approach to thyroid nodule segmentation in 2025, using YOLOv5 instance segmentation on ultrasound images. Rising thyroid cancer prevalence has spurred computer-aided detection methods.

Accurate segmentation of nodules is a critical first step toward AI-assisted clinical decision support. Doppler imaging adds blood-flow information that ordinary ultrasound lacks, which may sharpen the nodule boundaries the model must find. Better segmentation supports radiologists measuring and tracking nodules across visits. Instance segmentation draws each nodule separately, not just a category mask. Ultrasound is cheap and radiation-free, which is why better analysis of it matters. For scan teams, the gain is time. A tool that draws each lump with care can cut the hours spent on marks, and leave more hours for hard calls.
arxiv-2512-00739:
Diyu Shen and five coauthors review intense electromagnetic fields in heavy-ion collisions in a 2025 paper. In such collisions, atomic nuclei crash at nearly the speed of light. The crash dumps huge energy into a small region and heats it until hadrons melt into free quarks and gluons.

The speeding nuclei also carry very strong electric and magnetic fields. The review gathers theory predictions about those fields and the experimental results that test them. Fields this strong may change how particles form and move in the hot aftermath. The summary gives researchers a shared map of what is known and what is still open.
arxiv-2512-01239:
Sohail Farhangi and Bill Mance study what makes a number normal in odd base systems. A normal number uses each digit block as often as chance would say. That trait is well known for plain base counts. It has also been shown for many other ways to write numbers.

The pair turn to Cantor series, where the base can change at each step. A rule that shifts as it goes can make the series on the fly. They build the theory of normal form for that case. The work links digit traits to the rule that made the series.
arxiv-2512-01339:
Xiaojun Zhang and co-authors study bound states that hide inside a spread of free states. Such states are known in single-particle physics. Their kin for pairs of parts are far less known. Pairs that stick as one unit are called doublons.

The team finds a bound state set inside the doublon spread. It forms when four atoms link to a chain of linked rings with strong on-site push. They map how the state acts and holds. Such states could help move quantum states from place to place with less loss, a key need for quantum tools.
arxiv-2512-01439:
Bharatdeep Hazarika and co-authors build a chat aid for finance in many tongues. India has dozens of major tongues and many more minor ones. Just a small share of users grasp English well. That gap blocks access to bank and payment apps.

Their system talks with users in their own tongue. It aims to guide tasks like payments and balance checks by voice and text. Talks in a home tongue build trust for first-time users. Work like this can widen fair access to digital finance across India. Voice-first design is central, since many first-time users read little in any tongue and learn apps best by hearing steps spoken aloud.
arxiv-2512-01539:
Connor Roberts and Gunnar Pruessner give exact results for active crystals in a harmonic model. Active particles like cells can form near-crystal lattices. Those lattices play core roles in living systems. Past theory leaned on the simple one-dimensional case too much.

The pair compute where the harmonic model breaks down. Instabilities show which crystal traits it can and cannot predict. Their results link measurable traits to model terms. That link helps biologists read cell lattice data with the right caveats about model limits. Exact results also mark where the harmonic picture first fails, so later nonlinear work knows the precise point where it must take over.
arxiv-2512-01639:
Conor Rosato and co-authors improve outbreak detection when data arrives out of order. Particle filters estimate hidden epidemic states well. Real reports often land late or out of sequence. That disorder can throw off a filter's state.

Their method adds Markov-switching regimes for endemic and outbreak phases. A fixed-lag particle filter handles the late data. Regime switches let the model jump modes as an outbreak starts. Earlier, cleaner detection helps health teams act while spread is still small. Out-of-sequence handling is built in, not patched on, which matters when labs report cases days late during a fast-moving outbreak.
arxiv-2512-02039:
Logicians extend first-order logic by letting formulas consult an ordering of nearby elements, as long as the answer does not depend on which ordering was picked. Derek Aoki's 2025 paper studies this local-order-invariant logic on classes of structures whose connections stay bounded in degree.

The questions trace back to work by Weinstein about how much extra power order-invariance buys, on bounded-degree structures, on finite structures generally, and on locally finite ones. Expressive power questions decide what properties computers can even state, let alone check, about networks and data. Aoki's results map where this polite fiction of an ordering actually adds strength.
arxiv-2512-02239:
A particle can start in one pure quantum state. Once it trades energy with its surroundings, it is best seen as a mix of states. Each state in the mix has its own chance of showing up. Arsam Najafian and Mark Van Raamsdonk compute in 2025 how that mix shifts during simple two-particle collisions.

They track the mix with math: a reduced density operator lists the states, and its weights give their odds. With numeric work in one and two space dimensions, they show how both the states and the weights move with time. Watching the mix grow, hit by hit, clarifies how pure quantum states decay into mixed ones.
arxiv-2512-02339:
Tell apart two nearly identical objects in a video and the eye uses motion, not appearance. Chenshuang Zhang and five co-authors report in 2025 that pre-trained video diffusion models have quietly learned exactly that skill, tracking similar-looking objects without any supervision or task-specific training.

Supervised trackers perform well but need labeled data, while self-supervised ones falter when visual cues become ambiguous. The diffusion models' internal motion representations turn out to be strong enough to track by movement alone. The finding suggests generative video models absorb physical understanding as a by-product, a resource other vision tasks may be able to borrow.
arxiv-2512-02439:
Allah Ditta and six co-authors build a model of a charged compact star, a dense object held up by strong gravity. Their 2025 study works inside a changed form of gravity that mixes symmetric teleparallel ideas with the Euler-Heisenberg view of electric fields. The star matter pushes out unevenly in different directions.

Inside the model, the team uses the MIT bag model, a standard way to describe quark matter. They link key parts of the model and reach an exact solution of the field equations. The work also checks mass and radius stability for such stars. Work like this helps map which stars can exist and which would soon fall apart.
arxiv-2512-02539:
Dongmin Kim and co-authors tackle a bottleneck in fault tolerant quantum computing: too few decoders. Quantum error correction produces a stream of syndrome data that decoders have to read fast and well. In large systems, logical qubits far outnumber the decoders on hand, so scheduling becomes a core problem.

Their constraint optimal approach allocates decoder time where it helps most, under strict limits. Good allocation keeps errors from piling up while hardware stays scarce. As quantum machines grow, smart sharing of decoding power may matter as much as the decoders themselves for keeping computations reliable. More qubits will need this kind of smart time share if they are to work as one machine at all.
arxiv-2512-02639:
Lisa Schraut-May and eleven co-authors study crystals of zinc-phthalocyanine, a light absorbing molecule. In a molecular crystal, light excites pairs of neighboring molecules together, an effect called excitonic coupling. That coupling is very sensitive to how neighbors sit, tilt, and overlap.

Small changes in packing can mimic the signs of a phase transition in optical spectra. The team traces such mimicked transitions to competing couplings between molecules. Knowing the true cause prevents false claims of new phases, and helps design organic materials whose light response is tuned on purpose. Packing rules learned here feed the design of dyes and films that drink light for work in cells.
arxiv-2512-02939:
Tanay Kumar, Hongying Zhao, and Xuehua Zhang dry thick slurry waste faster by joining two transport tricks. Concentrated slurry dries slowly because water hides between particles and escapes poorly. Their sailboat evaporator uses a root like structure for wind assisted interfacial evaporation.

Pendular water transport pulls liquid through bridges between particles toward the surface. Wind then carries the vapor away at the interface. Combining both paths attacks the drying bottleneck from inside and outside. Faster dewatering could cut the volume of industrial and treatment waste that must be hauled away. Dry waste weighs less and hauls for less. A dryer that works on thick goo pays its way in truck trips saved each month of use.
arxiv-2512-03039:
Chen-Hsuan Hsu, Jelena Klinovaja, and Daniel Loss survey helical liquids, unusual one dimensional electron states at material edges. These liquids appear at the boundaries of time reversal invariant topological materials. Their electrons move with spin locked to direction, a property prized for quantum devices.

Progress has stalled on several key challenges, which the authors highlight. They advocate deeper theory of the many body aspects of these systems. Better understanding could stabilize topological zero modes, the building blocks proposed for fault tolerant quantum computation and low loss electronics. Edge states with locked spin are a prize for low loss gear. A clear list of what blocks them is a list worth years of work to get right.
arxiv-2512-03139:
Dark energy may not stay fixed over cosmic time. Eric Linder studies one idea for that change in this 2025 work. Data suggest the dark energy strength may have crossed a key line, called the phantom divide.

Modified gravity, in the Horndeski form, offers one way to explain the crossing. Linder stresses that growth of cosmic structure and lensing must be checked too, not just expansion history. A model that fits all tests at once is far more convincing. The work helps guide how future sky surveys test dark energy ideas. Growth and lensing data will judge the model alongside the expansion history it predicts.
arxiv-2512-03239:
A distant red galaxy, split in two by gravity, gets a close look. Josephine Baggen, Pieter van Dokkum, Ivo Labbé, and Gabriel Brammer study it in this 2025 work. The galaxy is a Little Red Dot seen as it was when the universe was young.

The galaxy cluster Abell 383 lenses it into two images, observed with the Webb telescope. The source shows the class's V-shaped spectrum and a strong Balmer break. Lensing magnifies faint details that would else be lost. The case helps test what Little Red Dots really are. Lensing magnification acts like a natural telescope, enlarging this distant red source.
arxiv-2512-03539:
Holographic microscopes can image cells without labels, but focusing is hard. Hasan Berkay Abdioğlu and co-authors build an automation framework in this 2025 work. Manual operation for repetitive cell tasks wastes expert time and invites human error.

Digital holographic images are noisy and low in contrast. That makes autofocus and object detection tough for standard tools. The authors add real-time control and automation for acousto-holographic microscopy. Automated microscopes could speed cell biology labs and make results more consistent across users. Acousto-holographic control adds sound-based focusing to the imaging, widening what automation must handle in live cell experiments and assays.
arxiv-2601-06739:
Daniel Munoz George and co-authors study random monomial ideals from large graphs in 2026. Their model is inspired by the Erdos-Renyi model of random graphs. They propose a new model for squarefree random monomial ideals.

The ideals are generated by edges and covers of a graph, they explain. This permits investigating conditions of normality for such random ideals. For those conditions they obtain asymptotic results in the paper. As graphs grow large, probabilities settle into patterns they compute. Random ideals connect combinatorics, probability, and commutative algebra in one object. Their edge-and-cover generation ties ideal theory tightly to graph structure. Algebraists get limit theorems for when random ideals stay normal. The work extends random graph thinking into polynomial ring territory.
arxiv-2601-06939:
David D. Dai and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers essentially no energy barrier between independent fermionic neural quantum state minima. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Neural quantum states (NQS) have proven highly effective in representing quantum many-body wavefunctions, but their loss landscape remains poorly understood and debated.

Here, we show that the NQS loss landscape is more benign and similar to conventional deep learning than previously thought. Exhibiting mode connectivity: independently trained NQS are connected by paths in parameter space with essentially no energy barrier. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07039:
Lihong Guo, Harry Ip, and Mingyang Wang wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a swinging system with a lag in its spring. The system is a bilinear oscillator, driven by white noise. Such a model sees wide use in design and build work. It can show strong bends in how a metal acts, such as the Bauschinger effect.

Most teams find the long-run spread of the swing by Monte Carlo runs, which test the model with random draws again and again. The authors take a new path based on a PDE, an equation for how a spread shifts over time. Their path builds on the elasto-plastic frame set out by Bensoussan and co-authors. For a reader in this field, the paper gives a direct way to get the long-run spread. It skips the cost of vast numbers of random runs.
arxiv-2601-07139:
Junhong Zou and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers AdaField. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The surface pressure field of transportation systems, including cars, trains, and aircraft, is critical for aerodynamic analysis and design. In recent years, deep neural networks have emerged as promising and efficient methods for modeling surface pressure field.

Being alternatives to computationally expensive CFD simulations. Currently, large-scale public datasets are available for domains such as automotive aerodynamics. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07339: Victoria Motsch and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers impact of boundary conditions on the Double-Kicked quantum rotor. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors study the on-resonance Spin-1/2 Double Kicked Rotor, a periodically driven quantum system that hosts topological phases. Motivated by experimental constraints, the authors analyze the effects of open and periodic boundary conditions. In contrast to the idealized case of infinite momentum space. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07439:
Julián Garrido and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with advanced computing for reproducibility of astronomy big data science, with a showcase. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) faces unprecedented technological challenges due to the vast scale and complexity of its data. The work provides an overview of research by the AMIGA group to address these computing and reproducibility challenges.

The authors present advancements in semantic data models. Analysis services integrated into federated infrastructures, and the application to astronomy studies of techniques that enhance research transparency. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07539:
Ryo Okano and Daisuke Kurisu extend a popular causal method to outcomes that live in abstract spaces. The synthetic control method estimates the effect of a policy by building a weighted copy of the treated unit. Recent work lets outcomes be distributions, functions, networks, or covariance matrices rather than single numbers. Their 2026 preprint develops functional synthetic control methods for such metric space-valued outcomes.

When outcomes are curves or distributions, ordinary averaging and fitting need rethinking. Functional versions must respect the geometry of the outcome space. Sound methods here matter for policy studies where the outcome is a whole distribution, like income or health profiles. The paper speaks to econometricians and statisticians evaluating interventions with complex outcomes. It aims to give the method a firmer theoretical base.
arxiv-2601-07639:
Norm Levenberg and Sione Ma'u develop potential theory on algebraic curves, in a 2026 mathematics preprint. Earlier work by the second author defined directional Robin constants for a compact, nonpolar subset of a curve. The curve sits inside complex space of several dimensions. Robin constants measure how a set interacts with growth of analytic functions. The authors relate these constants to a natural class of Chebyshev constants for the same set.

Chebyshev constants govern best polynomial approximation on a set. Linking two kinds of constants lets results pass between potential theory and approximation theory. Algebraic curves give the theory concrete, structured sets to work on. The paper is aimed at specialists in pluripotential theory and complex analysis. It continues a line of work the authors have built over several papers.
arxiv-2601-07839:
Pawan Kumar and Aditi Gupta compress large language models with a two-stage scheme that respects their weight structure. Modern LLMs strain memory and compute budgets, for both deployment and further training. Their method, Hierarchical Sparse Plus Low-Rank compression, first removes the largest-magnitude weights into a sparse matrix. It then factorizes the remaining dense matrix with a recursive hierarchical low-rank method. The work appears as a 2026 preprint.

Splitting weights this way keeps the few big weights exact while compressing the many small ones. Hierarchical factorization exploits structure at several scales. Principled compression decides whether a model can run on available hardware at all. The paper speaks to machine learning engineers facing deployment limits. It offers compression as a designed procedure, not a blunt cut.
arxiv-2601-07939:
Shireesh Reddy Pyreddy and colleagues present SECite, a tool that reads how later papers treat an earlier one. Judging a paper's strengths and limits is core to any literature review. Standard summaries only reflect the authors' own view of their work. Citations reveal how the community actually used, praised, or criticized it. Their 2026 preprint builds analysis and summarization around those citations in software engineering literature.

A citation can signal endorsement, routine use, or disagreement. Telling these apart gives a deeper, more practical picture of a paper. SECite aims to summarize that reception automatically. Scholars drowning in reading lists could triage papers faster. The tool also exposes limitations that authors would not advertise. The paper serves software engineering scholars and tool builders. It treats citations as evidence, not just counts.
arxiv-2601-08539: Jeffrey Spaan, Kuan-Hsun Chen, and Ana-Lucia Varbanescu cut compute waste in language models with kernel-level frequency scaling. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that AI growth has expanded GPU data centers fast. Rising operational energy use has become a critical bottleneck and sustainability concern. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling lowers energy use with existing hardware and little effort. Applying it at kernel level targets the moments when full GPU speed is wasted. Such tuning could trim data center bills without slowing model serving.
arxiv-2601-08639:
Six authors, led by Tanmay Inamdar, study a hard choice problem on graphs. A graph here is a set of points joined by lines. The task is to pick a small set of red points that cover many blue points. The picked set must also stay joined as one piece. Past work treats each part of this task on its own.

The team gives one shared model for the whole task. They then look for fast methods that get close to the best pick. The methods run in time that stays fixed for a key size in the task. Such work helps when a network must serve many users but can build links at only a few hubs. A reader gets both the model and the near best methods.
arxiv-2601-08739:
Xingyu Tan and six co-authors work on safe use of fact graphs by chat models. A fact graph stores facts as linked triples, such as a name, a link, and a value. Such graphs can ground a model and cut made up claims. But many graphs hold private facts that must not leak to a closed model host.

Their tool is called PrivGemo. It uses two towers, one on the user side and one for search. The private graph stays on the safe side while the model still gets the facts it needs. No raw triples need to cross to the host. A reader who must guard data gets a plan for strong search with less leak risk.
arxiv-2601-08839:
Toshiyuki Shigemura builds a team of three chat models that check each other in a loop. One model drafts text. A next model checks if the draft holds up. A third model checks if the work is clear and can be traced. The loop runs more than once, so each round can fix the last.

He calls this loop Recursive Knowledge Synthesis. The claim is that the loop makes a whole that no one model can match on its own. He also gives ways to test if the loop stays stable, or if it drifts with each round. A reader who builds model teams gets both a plan and a test frame. It helps judge when a team loop helps, and when it just adds cost.
arxiv-2601-08939:
B. Moreschini and a large team warn that one cloud form can skew chem counts in far galaxies. The Webb scope lets us read the gas in such galaxies with tools honed nearby. Near tools rest on calm gas states. Far gas is far more wild, with strong light and low metal counts. A calm form may not fit it at all.

The team shows how wild states shift the lines we read. If we force a one cloud form, the chem counts we get can be off by much. More than one cloud state must be let in the fit. A reader who reads far gas gets a clear warn. Old near tools need a fresh check at high range.
arxiv-2601-09239:
Hanlin Zhang and eight co-authors split speech into two code streams: sense and sound. A speech code turns a wave into a short list of codes a chat model can use. Past codes mix what was said with how it sounds. That mix makes it hard to swap voice yet keep words, or to keep voice and change words.

Their code tool is called DSA-Tokenizer. It holds sense codes and sound codes apart by set rules in train. A flow match step then joins the two in a ranked way for the next stage. A reader in speech tech gets a split code that may serve voice swap and text true tasks at once.
arxiv-2601-09539:
Nataniel Marquis works on deep conjectures that link two sides of the p-adic Langlands program. His 2026 arXiv paper weighs what conjectures by Breuil, Herzig, Hu, Morra, and Schraen imply for Zábrádi's functor. On one side sit representations of the p-adic Galois group; on the other, representations of GL_n over the p-adic numbers. When a Galois representation is generic and well placed, a notion of compatibility ties the two sides. Papers like this one test whether the grand conjectures of the field fit together without clashes.

The paper is a work of pure mathematics. It sits in the p-adic Langlands program, a long effort to link Galois groups with linear groups.
arxiv-2601-09639:
Y. Kilic and a large team pin down the size and shape of Ixion, a large world beyond Neptune. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses multi-chord stellar occultations of the trans-Neptunian object (28978) Ixion. When such a body crosses a star, its shadow gives a sharp outline.

Trans-Neptunian objects are among the most primitive leftovers of the early solar system. Occultations give accurate sizes and shapes, while photometry constrains albedo and surface colors. Several chords across the shadow trace Ixion's true outline. Knowing one large body's form in detail anchors models of how the outer system was built.
arxiv-2601-10039:
C. R. Skolar and B. Srinivasan study the thin layer that forms near a wall in a plasma. The work is set in a Z-pinch, a fusion test bed. In such a bed, plasma is held in a tube. A bias is set on the end plates.

The field lines run along the wall, not across it. That case has had few past tests. The pair run a full sim of a cut through the pinch. They solve for the grains and the field as one. The sim shows how the layer forms when hits are rife and the field runs flat to the wall.
arxiv-2601-10339:
Xue-Nan Chen tests if gravity can tell quantum stuffs apart. The weak equivalence rule says all stuff falls the same. Its quantum form is still an open ask. In quantum work, chance is part of each claim. A test must code that chance in full.

Chen sets the rule in terms of a scatter spread. At tree level, that spread is worked out for a light grain off a heavy one. The claim is that the spread does not rest on the grain's mass or kind. The heavy mass cap makes the test sharp. The work gives a form for the quantum rule.
arxiv-2601-10639:
Ranajoy Sadhukhan and co-authors present STEM, a way to scale transformer models with less compute per token. Sparse designs promise more capacity without a matching rise in cost. In practice they often suffer unstable training, poor load balance, and heavy traffic between chips. STEM takes a static, token-indexed route instead.

The method swaps the up-projection in each feed-forward block for a lookup in a local embedding table. The gate and down-projection stay dense, as before. Lookups are cheap, so capacity can grow while token cost stays low. The design targets teams that train large language models and want size without runaway bills.
arxiv-2601-10939:
Christopher J. Butler and co-authors report liquid-crystal-like electronic order living alongside superconductivity in NaAlSi. Electronic nematic and smectic phases break symmetry in the electron fluid itself. They often appear near or inside unconventional superconducting states. NaAlSi is a semimetal with a silicon square net, and its superconductivity is thought to be unconventional.

Using scanning tunneling microscopy, the team observed short-range charge stripe order, the smectic pattern. The stripes coexist with superconductivity in the same material. That coexistence is a clue about how the two orders relate: rivals, partners, or two faces of one cause. The work adds a clean case to the study of quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-11339:
Shangjie Tian and nine coauthors name a new topological insulator in this work. Their 2026 preprint studies the compound Ge2Bi2Te5 in layered form. Topological insulators pass current on their surface only. Their bulk stays inert, which makes them rare and prized.

Most known cases are binary compounds of two elements. The search has moved to ternary mixes for new physics. This compound joins germanium, bismuth, and tellurium in one stack. The team identifies it as a 3D topological insulator. New members of this class feed both physics and devices. They may host exotic states that future chips can use.
arxiv-2601-11539:
Dinanath Padhya and four coauthors build a low-cost sensor glove for sign language. Their 2026 preprint reports the design and implementation in full. Severe hearing loss affects over 430 million people worldwide. Access to sign language interpretation stays critically scarce.

The gap bites hardest in low-resource settings like Nepal. Assistive tools split into two flawed camps today. Commercial gloves often cost more than 3,000 dollars. Research gloves use flex sensors that degrade fast under stress. The team's glove uses Hall-effect sensors instead of flex ones. Hall sensors read magnetic fields as fingers move. The aim is a cheap, tough glove that lasts.
arxiv-2601-11739:
Xinyu Pi, Qisen Yang, Chuong Nguyen, and Hua Shen map how large language models are now used in work with words and themes. Such work, called qualitative analysis, reads texts to find sense and themes. Model output can range from plain sums of what was said to full models of a system.

To make these gaps clear, they build a grid with four rows and four cols. One axis lists four levels of sense making, from plain facts to full theory. The other lists four levels of form, from fixed maps to loops that feed back. The grid helps teams state what a tool does and does not do.
arxiv-2601-12939:
Kaleem Arshid and four co authors plan flight paths for swarms of drones by a method called active inference. Their frame joins chance based reasoning with self learning in one system. It hands out jobs across the swarm with no single lead drone. It also sets the order of routes and plans the moves of each craft.

Trained world models guide the swarm at three levels: the job, the route, and the move. The training paths come from a genetic search that adds a push apart force. That force keeps drones from crowding one spot. A swarm that can re-plan in flight can serve search, mapping, and aid work. The study shows one way to build that skill.
arxiv-2601-13139:
Alessandro Midolo, Emiliano Tramontana, and Massimiliano Di Penta test if GPT-4 can clean up Python code well. Code clean up, called refactoring, aims to lift code grade with no change in what the code does. Old auto tools for it exist, but their use in real work stays thin.

Large language models open a fresh path for the task. The team asks how class level code in Python fares when GPT-4 does the clean up. They check both grade and how easy the code is to read. For dev teams, the study helps judge when a model can be trusted with clean up and when a human eye must lead.
arxiv-2601-13339:
B. J. Chen, Z. Deng, C. Q. Jin, and co-authors report huge low field magnet drag in a layered diluted magnetic semiconductor. Such stuff is a semiconductor spiked with magnetic atoms. Their host has a CaAl2Si2 type plan, with barium and potassium on one site and cadmium and manganese on a next.

They vary the manganese share across a wide span, from five per cent to half. They track magnet traits and how charge moves in a field. At low field the drag on charge flow drops by a huge span, a colossal effect. Such a big reply at low field is apt for sensors and spin based tools. The team maps how the effect grows with the spike share.
arxiv-2601-13439:
Sonu Kumar and co-authors report weak magnetism in a rare earth crystal with a triangle grid. The crystal is SmMgAl11O19. Its samarium ions sit on a triangular lattice, a grid prone to magnetic frustration. Each ion forms a Kramers doublet, a pair of states kept by time symmetry.

Lab reads span three tools. The team tracks magnet pull, field curves, and heat held. They find the doublet is strongly quenched, with its pull cut far below the free ion mark. The net swap scale is very weak. A weak scale on a triangle grid makes the stuff a clean case for odd magnet states.
arxiv-2601-13839:
Aisha Al-Mohannadi and co-authors build a test set for AI questions on disaster photos in 2026. Social media images give fast, low-latency clues during natural and human-made disasters. Visual question answering, or VQA, lets users ask a model about an image. Strong results on plain photos do not prove skill in disaster scenes.

Their benchmark, DisasterVQA, targets damage assessment and response needs. Disaster reasoning is complex and safety-critical, unlike most VQA tasks. A firm test set shows where models fail when lives are at stake. Responders could then trust, or avoid, model help with clear eyes.
arxiv-2601-14039:
Wesam Moustafa and co-authors help medical image models cope with wrong labels in 2026. Label noise is a critical problem in medical image segmentation. Manual annotation is hard, so errors creep into training data. Models trained on noisy data are prone to overfitting, which degrades generalization.

Many methods try to mitigate noisy labels in segmentation. The area remains largely under-explored, the team notes. Their work generalizes abstention, where a model can decline to learn from suspect labels. Safer learning from flawed labels could improve tools that outline tumors and organs.
arxiv-2601-14239:
Roberto Sussman and co-authors derive odd velocity fields from exact relativity solutions in 2026. Peculiar velocities are motions beyond the smooth cosmic expansion. They analyze them through cosmological perturbations in the Newtonian longitudinal gauge. The setup uses irrotational, shear-free congruences in an Eulerian frame.

They show non-trivial peculiar velocity fields can arise through Lorentzian boosts. The boosts act in the non-relativistic limit of analytic Einstein equation solutions. The fluid source is irrotational and shear-free, with nonzero energy flux. Exact solutions give clean tests for cosmic flow models. Exact forms give a rare check on code that tracks cosmic flows. Codes that pass such checks can be used with more trust.
arxiv-2601-14439:
Maria Chatzieleftheriou, Jonas B. Profe, Ying Li, and Roser Valentí study a kagome superconductor under pressure in this 2026 paper. The material is CsCr3Sb5, a newly identified strongly correlated superconductor. At higher temperatures it shows non-Fermi-liquid behavior. Below about 54 kelvin, charge- and spin-density-wave order sets in, in intertwined form.

Under external pressure, that order is suppressed. A superconducting phase then emerges. The team studies how pressure tunes the electronic correlations and the flat bands in this material. Flat bands are energy levels where electrons barely move, which can amplify odd effects. Readers get a map of a new material's phases as pressure squeezes it.
arxiv-2601-14639:
Yuheng Shao and five co-authors build a co-design tool for fashion in this 2026 paper, set for the Intelligent User Interfaces conference. Effective collaboration between designers and users matters for fashion design. It can increase user acceptance of fashion products and thereby create value. The authors' system is DesignBridge, named in their title.

DesignBridge bridges designer expertise and user preferences through AI-enhanced co-design. In co-design, users shape the product alongside the professional. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off early in that setup. Readers get a system aimed at fashion work where expert craft and wearer taste must meet in one draft.
arxiv-2601-14839:
Daizhan Cheng studies control systems whose state space can change size over time. His 2026 arXiv paper calls these dimension varying systems. Each mode of such a system lives in its own space, with its own number of dimensions.

Cheng proposes one shared space that can hold all of these modes at once. He calls it a cross-dimensional Euclidean space. The paper shows that the shape of this space fits well with each mode's own space. That gives all the modes a single shared home for study and for control work.
arxiv-2601-15939:
Yo Ikeda builds a lattice version of a gauge theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Chern-Simons theory is a topological theory with deep math ties. Defining it on a lattice needs care with gauge structure. Ikeda defines Deligne-Beilinson cohomology on a cubic lattice. He uses it to formulate lattice U(1) Chern-Simons theory at even levels. In the continuum, that cohomology refines how U(1) connections are built patch by patch.

A good lattice definition must keep the theory's topological traits. Patchwise constructions handle connections that no single chart can describe. This paper carries that care onto the lattice. Lattice formulations let physicists compute with such theories. They also test whether continuum ideas survive discretization. The work is mathematical physics, aimed at gauge theory specialists.
arxiv-2601-16039:
Hector Buffière and four coauthors sort a class of sparse graphs with tree order. Their 2026 preprint sits in pure maths and logic. A class counts as tied in a weak sense if one fixed rule can not read all graphs from its tinted forms. The team adds a tree order to the base form. They then ask which such forms stay weak and sparse.

The authors give clear tests that mark out these classes. The tests link tree order, sparsity and logic in one frame. Such marks help maths teams sort new graph classes fast. They also show where strong graph reading must fail. The work is a step in the study of sparse graph types and their logic.
arxiv-2601-16239:
Li Huang, Bertrand Meyer and Manuel Oriol argue that tests and proofs work best as a pair. Their 2026 preprint deals with how to check that code is right. Tests run the code and watch what it does. Proofs read the code text and show it must hold. The two ways have long been cast as foes in the field.

The team shows the pair as mates, not foes. Each way catches faults the other can miss. Joined use can thus lift trust in code at less cost. The view shapes how teams plan checks for big code. It draws on long work by the group in this field.
arxiv-2601-16339:
Naoki Endo and three coauthors ask when Rees rings of closed ideals are Cohen Macaulay. Their 2026 preprint deals with ideals in a plain local ring. The ideal is closed in the whole sense and tied to the top ideal. Its Rees ring spreads the ideal powers in a new ring. In two dims that ring is always of the sought type.

In high dims the trait can fail in plain cases. The team seeks terms that force the trait to hold. Terms of that kind sort good ideals from bad ones. The sort aids work in ring sums and blow up maths. The work is a step in local ring theory.
arxiv-2601-16439:
Geethika Santhosh and coauthors study star birth in rings and tails cast off star systems. Their 2026 preprint deals with systems bent by pulls or gas hits. Such hits throw off rings and tails far from the main disk. New stars can be born in those far thrown zones. Dust in those zones dims and bends the light they shed.

The team weighs dust dim and birth pace in the far zones. Dim must be fixed ere birth pace can be read true. True pace tells if far zones add much to star counts. It also tests if birth needs a dense disk to start. The work maps birth past the bright disk edge.
arxiv-2601-16839:
Anwar Ghammam and Mohamed Almukhtar check the build code that AI tools write. Build files tell how source code turns into apps. They are a key part of the software life span. Yet past checks of AI code skipped build files. Their 2026 preprint fills that gap with a broad check.

The team grades bot-made build code for flaws and upkeep cost. Weak build code can break whole teams' work. It can also hide flaws in shipped apps. Their grades show where bots need a human eye. That helps firms set rules for bot use in build tasks.
arxiv-2601-16939:
Andrei Agrachev and Bettina Kazandjian ask how far control can steer a class of flows. Their stage is the group of volume-keeping maps of a torus. A fixed swirl field drives the flow on it. A steady push, set in time, adds the steer. Their 2026 preprint tests near-full reach for that steer.

Near-full reach means most states can be got close to. Folks who quit one good for the next shape such flows. Proofs of reach bound what control can do in fluids. They guide steer plans for mix and flow tasks. The torus stage keeps the math clean and sharp.
arxiv-2601-17339:
Payel Santra, Partha Basuchowdhuri, and Debasis Ganguly question how search quality tools are judged. Query performance prediction, or QPP, guesses how well a search worked. The usual test checks set-level correlation. It compares guessed quality ranks with true ranks across a query set. The authors say that test is too coarse.

It does not show how QPP works for one query at a time. It also does not link scores to real downstream use. Their framework judges QPP by what it helps users do next. That shift can change which methods look best. Search teams gain a test that tracks real value, not just neat rank match.
arxiv-2601-17439:
Dieu D. Nguyen and co-authors weigh the black hole at the heart of galaxy M81. M81 is a near spiral galaxy, also called NGC 3031. Its central mass stayed unsure for years. Past measures clashed and none was robust. The team uses JWST NIRSpec data for a fresh measure. They map star motion in the central three arcseconds in fine detail.

From that stellar dynamics map, they derive a robust mass. A firm mass anchors study of how galaxies and black holes grow together. Near galaxies are the best labs for that link. JWST sharpness made the new map possible. The work sets a firmer base for M81 research.
arxiv-2601-17539:
Pawan Singh Mehta and Biswajyoti Saha study multiple polylogarithms near integer points. Polylogarithms are special functions with deep ties to number theory. Their local behavior in the s-aspect is the focus. The authors write a Laurent type expansion at integer points. The expansion uses power series and rational functions.

Local expansions let mathematicians compute values near hard points. They also expose poles and singular behavior in a clear form. Multiple polylogarithms appear in zeta values and particle physics. A firm expansion serves both fields. The work adds precision tools for a classic function family. It can speed proofs that need values at integers.
arxiv-2601-17639:
Water wave measures at the surface can reveal the hidden bottom shape. That is a geometric inverse problem. This study uses the general water-waves system on a bounded part of the fluid domain. It asks if the bottom can be identified from surface data alone. It also asks how stable that recovery is. Small surface errors should not cause wild bottom errors. No author is named in the record.

Uniqueness and stability proofs guide real survey methods. Harbors and coasts need bottom maps for safe navigation. Surface-only sensing would cut survey cost a lot. The math tells users when to trust such maps. It also shows which data the bottom leaves no trace in.
arxiv-2601-17939:
Chengkun Sun and co-authors improve a key step in medical image segmentation. Their 2026 preprint presents DTC, a deformable transposed convolution module. Segmentation maps mark which pixels belong to which tissue or organ. In UNet-like models, upsampling grows small feature maps back to full size. That growth lets the model fuse deep and shallow features and predict at several scales at once.

A deformable step can bend its sampling grid to fit real shapes. Organs and lesions rarely match a neat grid, so the bend matters. The module aims to sharpen borders and small structures in scans. Better maps support diagnosis, surgery plans, and dose plans. The work targets a step found in many medical models.
arxiv-2601-18039:
Gleb Koshevoy, Vadim Schechtman, and Alexander Varchenko write a summa on tetrahedron equations and the structures around them. Their 2026 preprint opens with lines from Baudelaire's poem Correspondances, whose sonnet form they liken to their main equation. The paper's title names its themes: quaternities, correspondences, and tetrahedron equations. Tetrahedron equations are higher cousins of the famous Yang-Baxter equation of mathematical physics.

Such equations govern how multi-part interactions can be reordered without change. They sit at the crossroads of algebra, geometry, and physics. A summa gathers the threads of a field into one account. It is a broad and careful survey. Readers gain a map of links that shorter papers cannot show.
arxiv-2601-18239:
Sizhe Cheng, Feng Liang, Yuhan Wen, Xipei Yu, and Yong Wang probe how AI should support meta-analysis. Their 2026 preprint starts from the weight of the task. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews demand rigorous abductive reasoning across vast, mixed literature. Scholars must build, test, and refine hypotheses over hundreds of papers. NLP tools have automated parts of that pipeline. Yet many tools pull the researcher out of the thinking loop or act as mere retrieval engines.

The team elicits design principles through an agentic research IDE. Keeping intellectual ownership with the scholar is a stated concern. Frequent context switching is another cost they target. The principles guide tools that assist synthesis without hollowing it out.
arxiv-2601-18639:
Ojasva Mishra, Xiaolong Wu, and Min Xu tune the loops that hold robot joints on track. A joint loop takes a goal pose, reads the true pose, and sets the push to close the gap. Book rules for such loops take the world as smooth and the push as free of caps. Real joints break both: they run in ticks, their push has a hard cap, and their reads come late and with flaws.

The team build a tune path that takes those real facts as its start. It sets the loop's three gains to get a firm hold with no wild swing, while the cap is kept in view. A good tune could keep arms and legs of robots safe and true. It could also cut the hand work of trial and error on each new joint.
arxiv-2601-18839:
Hugo Catalá, Ezequiel Valero, and German Rodrigo run a quantum sim of a shift in how a lone guest atom acts in a sea of cold atoms. At low pull, the guest dresses in the sea's waves and roams as a plump quasi-thing. At high pull, it binds to one mate from the sea as a pair. The shift from roam to bind is a key test of how strong pulls act in cold gas.

A plain sim of that shift is too big for plain tools: the state space grows past reach. A quantum chip can hold the state in its own form. The team map the shift to a chip of the noisy kind we have now. Their map shows the shift can be run on such kit. That opens a path to test strong-pull laws that plain tools can't reach.
arxiv-2601-18939:
Claire O'Brien and eight co-authors target the neurons that make language models flatter their users. Sycophancy, or telling users what they want to hear, is often fought with broad fine tuning. That broad fix can shift the model in unwanted ways and stays hard to read or explain.

Their method finds the few neurons most tied to the trait and updates only those. The surgical fix needs far less data than a full retrain. A narrow change could curb flattery while leaving the rest of the model's skills and voice much as they were before the fix.
arxiv-2601-19139:
Wayner Barrios builds fast model inference that runs natively on Apple Silicon chips. These chips use a unified memory design, where the same pool serves all parts of the system. Demand for tools that use that design well is rising as more developers train and run models on Apple hardware.

Existing tools either lack native tuning or serve text models only, leaving image and mixed workloads behind. Barrios targets both large language models and multimodal ones at scale. Native speed on common laptops and desktops puts serious model work within reach of users with no server budget.
arxiv-2601-19239:
Fengjie Li and three co-authors test language model bug hunters on whole real projects. As software grows more complex, flaws grow more common and more harmful, so automated detection matters more each year. New detectors pair language models with static analysis to scan at project scale.

Their study checks how well those detectors do in real use, and digs into why they fail when they fail. Lab scores on small snippets can flatter a tool badly. A clear view of root causes tells builders where to fix: the model, the analysis, or the join between them.
arxiv-2601-19439:
Giuseppe Chiari, Michele Piccoli, and Davide Zoni build data sets to teach machines the art of analog chip layout. Automating analog circuit design is a long standing challenge. Layout, parasitic effects, and circuit performance tangle in ways that are hard to capture and harder to optimize with classic methods.

Their system, OSIRIS, generates such data sets at scale, so learning methods have material to train on. Analog design still leans on scarce human experts. Machine help trained on sound, scalable data could shorten design cycles for the chips inside cars, sensors, and medical gear.
arxiv-2601-19639:
Antonio Agresti, Fabian Germ, and Mark Veraar work on stochastic partial differential equations. These equations model systems driven by random noise spread over space and time. The roughest noise is not trace class, which breaks many standard tools. Solutions are often built from Gaussian series with infinitely many terms.

The authors prove sharp bounds for such series. The bounds say exactly how the size of the sum depends on its ingredients. Sharpness means the estimates cannot be improved in general. With those bounds in hand, existence results for equations with rough noise become reachable. Applications include physical systems where the driving noise is very irregular. The work supplies a key technical step for that theory.
arxiv-2601-19939:
Hyunmin Kim and colleagues predict whole-body disease from images of the retina. The idea, called oculomics, rests on the eye's blood vessels mirroring the body's. Transformer foundation models such as RETFound made retinal prediction data-efficient. The authors build on that base with a hierarchical sampling method named Oculomix.

Their system targets systemic diseases such as cardiovascular disease and dementia. Sampling at several levels of the image hierarchy should capture both fine vessel detail and broad patterns. Cheap eye scans that flag body-wide risk could change screening. Clinics already photograph retinas routinely for eye disease. The work explores how much more those same images can say.
arxiv-2601-20039:
Vedat Levi Alev and Uriya A. First study hypergraph samplers, a tool for cutting the error of randomized algorithms. The setup uses uniform hypergraphs whose number of vertices is not too large compared with the edge size. Samplers let an algorithm repeat a weak test in a structured way so that the overall error drops.

The authors examine both typical and worst-case behavior of these samplers. The question covers decision problems with one-sided or two-sided error. Knowing where samplers help, and where they fail, guides the design of fast randomized methods in computer science theory.
arxiv-2601-20139:
Nathan Sauldubois studies model risk in finance through distributionally robust optimization with static hedging. The setting adds constraints on the marginal laws of prices and on martingale behavior, which keeps prices free of simple arbitrage. The work continues an earlier paper that left one case open.

That open case covers static hedges built from vanilla options that mature in a second period. A static hedge is set once and held, rather than traded over time. Results here help banks bound their losses when the true price model differs from the one they assumed.
arxiv-2601-20239:
Zhemeng Zhang and a large team present TouchGuide, a way to give robot policies a sense of touch at run time. Robots that handle delicate or contact-rich tasks still rely mostly on vision, and tactile feedback is often left unused. TouchGuide fuses touch with vision inside a low-dimensional action space.

The method works in two stages and steers a pretrained visuomotor policy while it runs, with no retraining. It can guide policies built on diffusion or flow-matching models. Adding touch at inference time could make existing robot policies safer on tasks like inserting, gripping, and sliding objects.
arxiv-2601-20339:
Yangyi Shen and seven colleagues improve how diffusion language models generate text. These models can build text in any order, which opens many possible paths to a finished sentence. Current decoding picks a single path and commits to it, so much of that space goes unexplored.

The authors introduce Order-Token Search, which searches jointly over the order of generation and the token values chosen. Exploring both dimensions at once should find better outputs than fixing the order in advance. Stronger decoding would help diffusion models compete with standard left-to-right models on quality.
arxiv-2601-20439:
Qihao Wang and four colleagues present PEARL, a framework that improves how language models use external tools over many steps. Models with tools can search, compute, and act, but complex multi-turn use exposes weak planning, invented tool calls, wrong parameters, and brittle interaction. PEARL joins plan exploration with adaptive reinforcement learning.

The design aims to make the model plan before acting and adjust as results come back. Multihop tool use is where agents earn their keep on real tasks, chaining lookups and actions. A stronger planner would cut the errors that now force users to supervise each step.
arxiv-2601-20539:
Oguzhan Gungordu, Siheng Xiong, and Faramarz Fekri present PathWise, a framework that uses large language models to design heuristics for hard combinatorial problems. Automated heuristic design with language models is promising, but existing frameworks lean on fixed evolutionary rules and static prompts. That leads to short-sighted heuristics, repeated evaluations, and little reasoning about how a new heuristic should be derived.

PathWise plans through a world model and lets the language models evolve themselves. Better automatic heuristics would help logistics, scheduling, and chip design, where good rules of thumb are worth large sums. Good rules of thumb save real time in each of these fields.
arxiv-2601-21239:
Chentong Chen, Mengyuan Zhong, Ye Fan, Jialong Shi, and Jianyong Sun improve how language models design search methods on their own. Models can now draft algorithms, but most tools treat the draft as one block of text. That view misses the link between the shape of a method and the numbers inside it.

Their system, TIDE, tunes the numbers while the structure evolves. Good methods are no longer thrown away just because their constants were off. The search also avoids settling too early on weak designs. Joining tuning with evolution gives the model a fairer test of each idea it creates.
arxiv-2601-21339:
Jennifer Haase and six co-authors ask what drives the quality of creative writing from language models. Outputs vary, but the cause could be the prompt, the choice of model, or plain chance in sampling. The team ran a large study to split those effects apart.

They tested a dozen models on ten creative prompts, with many samples per pairing. For originality, the prompt and the model choice explained shares of the spread that were close in size. Chance alone played a smaller role than many assume. The findings help users decide whether to switch models or rewrite the prompt when output feels stale.
arxiv-2601-21439:
Jon Chun and Katherine Elkins test whether emotional framing can sway language models in rule-bound decisions. Models are known to bend with small wording changes and to flatter user views. Whether that bend reaches high-stakes, rule-bound choices was less clear.

The authors find what they call a paradox of robustness. Despite their surface brittleness, tuned models barely moved under emotional framing. Their choices stayed nearly fixed even when the wording pushed hard. The result cuts both ways: steady rules are good, but the same firmness could lock in a bad rule. The study maps where model judgment holds firm.
arxiv-2601-21739:
Alberto Fernández-Hernández, Cristian Pérez-Corral, Jose I. Mestre, Manuel F. Dolz, and Enrique S. Quintana-Ortí explain an odd fact about the Adam optimizer. Adam has powered large-scale training for nearly a decade. Users kept noticing that setting its two momentum parameters equal works better, in scores and in the feel of training runs.

No principle accounted for that fact. The authors name a missing gradient scale invariance principle behind it. When the two parameters match, the updates respect that invariance. A clear principle turns a folk trick into a rule builders can apply on purpose, and it may guide the design of the next optimizer.
arxiv-2601-21839:
Ander Artola Velasco and co-authors study a new market dynamic created by reasoning models. Giving a language model more compute at test time improves its reasoning. But cloud providers charge users for that compute, so better answers now come with metered bills.

That pricing turns reasoning into a game among providers and users, each with their own incentives. The team's 2026 preprint frames these interactions as test-time compute games and analyzes them. The framing matters because the economics will shape how much reasoning users actually buy, how providers set prices. And whether careful thinking becomes a luxury feature. Game theory offers tools to predict where such a market settles before it fully forms.
arxiv-2601-22139:
Xin Chen and co-authors teach reasoning models to ask questions. Reasoning language models have advanced through chain-of-thought prompting, yet they share a blind habit. They reason at length inside their own heads even when key information is missing or ambiguous. The authors call this blind self-thinking.

Their 2026 preprint proposes Proactive Interactive Reasoning, a paradigm that turns passive solvers into proactive inquirers. Instead of guessing past a gap, the model identifies what it needs and asks. Asking the right question mid-task could transform assistants in medicine, support, and research. Where a confident answer built on a missing fact is worse than a pause and a question.
arxiv-2601-22239:
Tsung-Han Yeh and a large team draw out what a new helium value means for the early universe. Their 2026 preprint is part five of the Large Binocular Telescope helium project. The team report the most exact value yet for the share of helium made in the Big Bang.

They test that value against two key frames for the cosmos. One frame tracks how light elements formed in the first minutes. The other tracks the faint glow left from that hot start. The check helps show whether the standard story still holds. It also sets a firm mark for new tests.
arxiv-2601-22339:
Muhammad Bilal Akram Dastagir and four co-authors blend quantum-style learning with the web of smart devices to run supply chains. Their 2026 preprint notes that chains must move goods fast while cutting harm and guarding against attack. Old planning models, they argue, often skip green goals and cyber risk.

Their method uses reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by reward, with a quantum-inspired twist. It aims to weigh speed, cost, earth impact, and safety in one plan. Such joint plans could help firms ship goods with less waste. They may also harden chains against digital threats.
arxiv-2601-22539:
Babak Shahbaba and Zahra Moslemi built NIPA, a way to mimic Bayesian inference that borrows from how brains learn. Their 2026 preprint notes that people blend three modes: planned thought, habit, and recall of past events. Each mode covers the others' blind spots.

NIPA blends the same three modes to form a fast stand-in for full posterior inference. A good stand-in gives full doubt ranges at a fraction of the cost. That trade suits health and science, where calls must show their doubt. The work is a bridge between brain science and stats.
arxiv-2601-22639:
Esteban Macías, Ilya Gruzberg, and Eldad Bettelheim solve the spin quantum Hall transition on random networks with exact exponents. The transition marks where a quantum Hall system flips its spin transport. Their 2026 preprint maps the problem to classical percolation, the flow of links through a random web.

They focus on the edges of percolating clusters, then use tools from two-dimensional quantum gravity. The exact exponents pin down the transition's class. Such pins test whether wild systems share one deep pattern. The work joins gravity math to a bench-top effect. Few results are this clean.
arxiv-2601-22939:
Dominic J. Williamson speeds up the preparation of magic states, a key fuel for quantum computers. Magic states let a quantum machine do the full range of operations, beyond the easy ones. In noisy hardware, they must be made under the guard of an error-correcting code.

New, efficient quantum codes and logic gates have set the stage for low-cost fault tolerance. The method here gauges higher-form transversal gates in parallel to make states fast. Faster state factories could shrink the size and cost of useful quantum machines.
arxiv-2601-23139:
Ruizhen Gu, José Miguel Rojas, and Donghwan Shin automate testing of virtual reality apps. VR offers immersive experiences, but its testing challenges differ from ordinary software. Existing tools can move through scenes and trigger actions, yet cannot create lifelike three-dimensional user input.

Real input means hand-controller actions like grabbing and triggering, with believable timing and motion. Generating such input on its own would let testers cover common actions at scale. Better VR testing matters as headsets spread into training, medicine, and design. Grab and trigger actions through hand-held controllers are named examples of the lifelike input the auto-testing must create.

audubon-ornithological-biography-vol5-18:
With volume five in 1839, Audubon completed the text of his Ornithological Biography. The five volumes stand beside The Birds of America as its prose half. Final species accounts fill the volume in his established manner. Habits, ranges, nests, and notes from the field make up each life history.

Audubon drew on journeys that had taken him across much of North America. His frontier tales give the science a human frame of hardship and wonder. The completed set remains a primary record of American bird life before heavy settlement. Later bird students mined it for early ranges and habits. The whole work is a monument to one observer.
awntyrs-arthure-madden-1839:
The Awntyrs off Arthure is a Middle English poem in the alliterative style, edited by Frederic Madden in 1839. Its scene is a hunt near Carlisle, in the border country of Arthur's realm. Few Arthurian poems mix splendor and horror as boldly as this one does.

Gawain and Queen Guinevere meet the rotting ghost of the queen's own mother. The dead woman warns them against pride, luxury, and the price both will pay. Her words hang over the court's bright feast like smoke. The poem then turns to a knightly duel, but the ghost's warning is what readers remember. It is Arthurian horror at its finest.
carle-of-carlisle-madden-1839:
The Carle of Carlisle is a Middle English romance edited by Frederic Madden in 1839. A carle is a rough, churlish fellow, and this one keeps a hall near Carlisle. Gawain, Kay, and a bishop ride there and must spend the night as his guests.

The host tests his guests' manners at every turn, at table and even at bedtime. Kay fails rudely, as Kay usually does. Gawain passes each test with patience and good grace. The comedy turns on a plain point: courtesy is a knight's real armor. Madden's edition kept this brisk, funny tale in print for modern readers of Arthur.

cia-0000008639:
Quang Binh province is the setting for a November 1972 report on two dead pilots sighted there. Quang Binh, just north of the old demilitarized zone, endured some of the war's heaviest bombing. Reports of dead airmen arrived as the bombing campaign neared its end.

Such reports served the accounting effort rather than rescue, fixing where losses had occurred. A place name could let officials match remains or graves to missing crews later. The work was grim, and its results often stayed incomplete. Still, each filed sighting narrowed the unknown for two men's families and records alike.

Combined reports helped analysts place captives inside a system, not just on a map. A camp's location could explain a cluster of sightings around it. The file therefore works at two levels at once: individual men, and the network holding them. That double view was the heart of prisoner intelligence work.
cia-0000010239:
Keeping a beachhead in South Korea, and what that would mean worldwide, is weighed in a January 1951 CIA paper. United Nations forces then held a perimeter around Pusan after months of retreat, and Chinese troops had entered the war. Withdrawal or holding fast was a live question.

The paper looks past the battlefield to allies, enemies, and neutrals watching America's resolve. A beachhead kept or lost would speak far beyond Korea, to Europe and Asia alike. Such strategic papers show the young CIA arguing at the highest level. This one captures the Korean War's darkest winter from Washington's side.

Here the units counted are the camps of the secret war. The estimate tallies their staffs, their guards, and the men believed held in the Laotian camps scattered through the hills.

The Laotian camps were the secret war's hidden archipelago of suffering. Counting their keepers was grim, necessary work for the accounting. For readers, the estimate shows the prison system measured like an army, because in Laos it nearly was one.

The item notes the parades as the files watched the watchers. Names and faces in such displays fed the accounting back home. For readers, the page shows captivity used as a stage, with prisoners as unwilling actors.
