The brief record is a service activities file from the first day of 1946.
cia-0000119739: A September 1956 CIA report covers military activity linked to the Hungarian crisis. Troop movements gave hard backing to the political rumors then flying around Budapest. The report tracks the forces gathering near a country weeks away from open revolt. Analysts treated such movements as the firmest evidence available, harder to fake than speeches and more telling than official denials from either capital.
cia-0000124339: A July 1950 CIA document titled simply 'Military.' Filed in the first weeks of the Korean War, the single word covered everything. The document preserves the file as labeled — the contents will have to speak for themselves.
cia-0000132239: Situation report 556, from January 1991, covers political developments including a European trip by Iran's foreign minister Velayati, the heading breaking off. Iran played its own diplomatic game at the war's edges that winter. The report follows the tour. A European tour by Tehran's foreign minister signaled Iran bidding for a role in the settlement, a thread the daily watch followed from capital to capital.
cia-0000132339:
The Caribbean situation fills a CIA briefing prepared for the National Security Council. The briefing is dated June 3, 1959. It came five months after Fidel Castro's victory in Cuba had shaken the whole region and its governments.

Inside, analysts survey unrest and political change across the island chain. Cuba's example was encouraging rebels and worrying friendly governments at the same time. The Caribbean had become Washington's most unsettled neighborhood almost overnight. For readers, the briefing shows how widely American officials were looking for the next crisis. It dates from the months when Castro's win was still new and its effects were still spreading.
cia-0000132639:
A planned visit by Khrushchev to Cuba fills a CIA document dated May 6, 1960. A Soviet premier landing in Havana would have been the boldest Cold War gesture yet seen in the hemisphere. No Soviet leader had ever made such a trip.

The document tracks the plan and the reports behind it. In the end Khrushchev never made the journey to the island. Even so, the plan itself was major news in Washington. For readers, the entry shows how seriously a rumored visit was taken. It also marks how close Moscow and Havana already seemed by the spring of 1960.
cia-0000132739: Three fronts share a CIA item on Cuba dated March 4, 1961. The item covers anti-Castro work at home, hard times in the economy, and Cuba at the United Nations. Its headline misspells difficulties as difficluties, a slip kept from the original. The roundup form shows the Cuba watch running at full pace. The short item takes each front in turn.
cia-0000135839: Document in the declassified files, dated 4 September 1952, covers the Central American situation as a whole, surveyed before the Guatemala coup. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000135939: The record dated 3 January 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about a request for an employment deception plan, fake jobs to serve as cover for real agents. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136139: Dated 2 April 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records shipping information for ONTRICH and Lugton, seaborne supplies tracked for two readers at once. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136239: One CIA cable dated 4 May 1954 handles topics for broadcast about the liberation movement attack, talking points for the radio war. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136639: The catalog dates this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade files to 3 February 1961, marked as an estimated date. The brigade was in its final training phase under CIA supervision. No subject appears in the record for this document. Preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, it belongs to the cluster of brigade items from the first days of February 1961, its timing set by estimate.
cia-0000136939: A large dossier has been built on a man called GRUSON. This April 1954 cable reports it to the Guatemala City station. The file covers his past acts and associations. It also covers his unreliability. His activities are called extremely harmful. The station does not rule out using the material. It asks to hear of any big developments. The regime might use him to probe the American position. Reports on Fortuny's removal from office are handled too.
cia-0000139039: Greek Prime Minister Stefanopoulos worries about Soviet shipbuilding negotiations with a private Greek shipowner, this 1966 memorandum signed by Deputy Director for Plans Desmond FitzGerald reports. The arrangement could give the Soviets 60-percent ownership in a fleet of 70 Greek merchant ships. His situation is worsened because Greece finds it hard to dispose of large tobacco stocks, one item the Soviets are willing to accept as barter for the ships. The file's titled subject, Soviet control of a numbered asset, is partly redacted.
cia-06552139: CI INTERMEDIATE INTERROGATION REPORT (CI-IIR) NO. 57, a CIA document. The interrogation report. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-06587139: IRAN: COMMANDER SAYS US NAVY'S 'IRRESPONSIBLE' MOVEMENTS IN GULF COULD HAVE LE, a CIA document. The Gulf warning. This file preserves that declassified paper. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
cia-06752239: THE SITUATION IN VIETNAM - 28 DECEMBER 1967, a CIA assessment. The next day's briefing. The archive keeps it. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
cia-06786639: THE SITUATION IN SOUTH VIETNAM NO. 28, a CIA assessment. The Vietnam update. It stays in the collection. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
crania-americana-or-a-comparative-view-o: Crania Americana of 1839 compared skulls of native peoples. The American crania. The comparative anatomy. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care for all readers. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
dreams-pg1439: Olive Schreiner's 1890 book of allegories: dream-visions about life, death, labor, and women's lot, written in biblical, poetic prose. "The Hunter" and other parables made her a prophet to a generation of reformers. Strange, beautiful, and fiercely moral.
europmc-pmc10163139:
Kautzky-Willer, Leutner, and Harreiter review sex differences in type 2 diabetes in a 2023 paper. Diabetes is rising in both sexes, but men tend to be diagnosed younger and at lower body fat than women. Worldwide, millions more men than women live with the disease, while women often carry a heavier load of risk factors at diagnosis.

The review compares causes, complications, and treatment responses in men and women. It argues that care and prevention should account for these differences. The paper is a compact guide to a topic long treated as one-size-fits-all.
europmc-pmc10180739:
Fusco and colleagues review gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids in a 2023 paper. These fatty acids are made when gut microbes ferment fiber from food. They feed the gut lining, calm inflammation, and help control metabolism, and their shortage is linked to bowel disease, colon cancer, and heart and metabolic disorders.

The review names the key bacterial producers and the foods that feed them. It explains what the acids do in the gut and the wider body. It also weighs probiotic and diet strategies to raise their levels.
europmc-pmc10273039:
Abd-Alrazaq and co-authors review large language models in medical education in a 2023 paper, covering opportunities, challenges, and future directions. Models in the GPT family can answer questions, explain concepts, and draft text in a natural style. Medical schools are weighing how such tools change the way students learn and are tested.

Drawing on past reviews, the authors set out the gains schools might see, from personal tutoring to faster feedback. They also face the risks: wrong answers, bias, and threats to honest assessment. The paper offers a balanced guide for educators.
europmc-pmc10353939:
Bellaver and a large team asked in 2023 why some brains with amyloid do not go on to form tau tangles. Amyloid and tau are the two hallmark proteins of Alzheimer's disease. Some people carry amyloid yet stay sharp and show no tau harm. Astrocytes are star-shaped support cells in the brain that can switch to an active state.

Bellaver studied 1,016 people across three groups who had no memory loss. Amyloid linked to raised tau in blood only in people whose astrocytes were active. Brain scans showed the same split for tau growth over time. The finding puts active astrocytes early in the chain of the disease. It may help pick the right people for early drug trials.
europmc-pmc10390339:
The GBD 2021 Sickle Cell Disease Collaborators tracked the global toll of sickle cell disease from 2000 to 2021. The disease warps red blood cells into a stiff sickle shape. It passes from parents to children through genes. The study spans 204 nations and areas and counts births, cases, and deaths.

Births of babies with the disease rose 13.7%, to 515,000 in 2021. Growth was driven by population gains in the Caribbean and sub-Saharan Africa. People living with the disease rose 41.4%, to 7.74 million. Death records alone put deaths at 34,400 in 2021. The team warns that this count misses many deaths and understates the true burden.
europmc-pmc10502239:
Muzellec and colleagues built PyDESeq2 in 2023, a Python version of a key gene analysis flow. The flow tests which genes change between two sample groups in bulk RNA data. The original tool, DESeq2, lives in the R language. Many labs now work in Python, and no native tool fit this task.

Their rebuild gives near-matching results with a better fit score, Muzellec reports. It also runs faster on large data sets, as shown on cancer atlas data. The code is free under the MIT licence on GitHub. It joins the scverse family of Python tools for cell data. Users gain clean links to modern data science stacks.
europmc-pmc1238739:
Zamarin and colleagues traced how a flu protein kills cells in 2005. The protein, PB1-F2, is a small part of influenza virus. It settles in mitochondria, the energy hubs of cells. Earlier work showed it triggers cell death, but the route was unclear.

Cells with the protein reacted more strongly to death signals. Tests on mouse liver mitochondria showed a key protein leaking out. The viral protein bound two gate proteins in mitochondrial walls. Those gates control what passes between cell compartments. Zamarin links those contacts to the death effect.
europmc-pmc1240439:
Eriksson, Jakobsson, and Fredriksson asked if flame retardants harm the developing brain in 2001. These chemicals spread through goods like electronics and textiles. They persist and build up, much like older banned pollutants. Levels in breast milk were rising at the time.

Newborn mice got single doses of two common PBDE types. A third flame retardant was tested the same way. Doses were given at day ten, a key brain growth stage. Later behavior tests checked for lasting harm. Eriksson raises concern that these chemicals act as developmental neurotoxicants. Behavior was checked in the adult mice later on.
europmc-pmc1288039:
Fowler and co-authors discovered a working amyloid inside mammal tissue in 2006. Amyloid fibers are protein clumps tied to Alzheimer and Parkinson disease. They were assumed to be purely harmful accidents. A pigment cell protein changed that picture.

The protein Pmel17 forms amyloid that templates melanin production. Melanin protects against ultraviolet light and oxidative damage. The amyloid also traps toxic melanin building blocks safely. Cells orchestrate its formation through membrane and cutting steps. Fowler proves amyloid is a normal fold used from bacteria to humans. Sequestration inside the organelle guards the host cell meanwhile.
europmc-pmc1395339:
Yuan, Reed, Chen, and Stewart compared statistics for real-time PCR data in 2006. Real-time PCR is used across biomedical science. Sound statistical treatment for its data was lacking. Confidence intervals and significance were often left implicit.

Four analysis approaches were built and compared head to head. One uses multiple regression to derive the standard fold-change measure. A second uses covariance analysis for the same quantity. Two simpler routes apply group tests after a first calculation step. SAS programs were written for all four models. A data quality control model was added.
europmc-pmc1779539:
Ekman and colleagues asked in 2006 what sets hub proteins apart in baker's yeast. In the protein interaction network, most proteins touch only a few partners. Hubs are the rare proteins with very many partners. The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae has about 6,000 proteins and tens of thousands of links.

The team compared hubs with non-hubs across the known network. Hubs turned out to be enriched for proteins built from many domains, which are reusable folding units within a protein. Hubs also often carried the same domain repeated several times. Earlier work had shown hub proteins are roughly three times as likely to be vital for survival. The domain pattern gives a concrete trait that marks these highly connected proteins.
europmc-pmc1802739:
Pahel, Rozier and Slade developed in 2007 a short scale that measures how tooth problems affect preschool children and their families. Dental disease and its treatment can lower daily quality of life, yet no tested tool existed for very young children. Their scale is called ECOHIS, short for Early Childhood Oral Health Impact Scale.

Experts first judged a pool of 45 candidate items, and parents then rated which mattered for preschoolers. The final scale kept 13 items, nine about the child and four about the family. It was tested on 295 parents of five-year-olds, plus 46 parents for repeat testing. Scores were worse when parents rated the child's health as fair or poor, or when dental disease was present. Consistency scores were high, at 0.91 for the child section and 0.95 for the family section.
europmc-pmc1847839:
Dunbar, Moran and co-authors pinned an aphid's heat tolerance in 2007 on a single DNA letter change in the bacteria living inside it. Pea aphids depend on the bacterium Buchnera, which feeds them essential nutrients. The change sits in a promoter, the switch region, for a small heat-shock protein gene named ibpA.

The deletion shortens a run of repeated letters and nearly wipes out the gene's heat response. It also lowers expression at cool and mild temperatures. After brief heat exposure as juveniles, aphids with the short form produced few or no offspring and held almost no Buchnera. In constant cool conditions those same aphids bred earlier and kept higher fertility. The mutation recurs in lab lines and occurs in field populations, trading heat safety for cool-weather gain.
europmc-pmc2008239:
Tannock studied in 1968 how cell growth in a mouse tumour relates to its blood vessels. Tissues need vessels for nutrients, so cells near vessels may divide faster. Most tumours are too tangled for this test. The transplanted mammary tumour used here grew in cords of living tissue around fairly straight vessels, with dead tissue beyond.

Most cords had radii between 60 and 120 micrometres. The central vessels averaged about 9.5 micrometres in radius, and cord size did not change with tumour weight. Cells near vessels showed high protein making and rapid proliferation. Growth fell with distance from the vessel. Tannock concluded that oxygen likely controls growth mainly through the growth fraction, the share of cells actively dividing.
europmc-pmc2034139:
Thomsen and colleagues measured nitric oxide production in human breast tumours in 1995. Nitric oxide is a small signalling molecule made by enzymes called nitric oxide synthases. The team had already found these enzymes in gynaecological cancers. Here they assessed enzyme activity and nitric oxide output in breast tumours and in normal breast tissue, and located the enzymes by staining.

Both calcium-dependent and calcium-independent enzyme activity ran high in invasive tumours. Nitric oxide output was also higher than in benign or normal tissue. For invasive ductal cancers, output was significantly greater in grade III tumours than grade II, linking it to tumour grade. Staining placed the inducible enzyme mainly in macrophages, immune cells gathered around the tumour. Other staining appeared in blood vessel and muscle-like cells.
europmc-pmc2124739: A medical paper with experimental studies on pneumococcus infections. The pneumonia germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2125139: A medical paper with further observations on goitre, so-called thyroid carcinoma. The swollen neck. This article preserves that oncology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128339: A medical paper on the influence of glands with internal secretion on respiratory exchange. The breathing glands. This article preserves that endocrinology. Later readers can locate it. It retains its place in time. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2130939: Both radiation and dry heat knock down antibody production, and this paper set the two side by side. Researchers compared the immune damage from each treatment. The weakened defenses, measured head to head. The article preserves that immunology research for modern readers.
europmc-pmc2131239: Another medical paper with studies on the foot-and-mouth disease virus properties. The cattle virus again. This article preserves that virology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2131439: A medical paper on udder infection with streptococci of the scarlet fever type, the influence. The cow udder. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes.
europmc-pmc2140739: A biology paper with a test for diffusible ions, the ionic nature of pepsin. The charged enzyme. This article preserves that biochemistry. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2180239: A medical paper with studies on agglutination with the aid of the centrifuge, the influence of temperature. The spun clumping. This article preserves that serology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2194739:
Larsen and co-workers benchmarked five computer methods in 2007 for predicting cytotoxic T-lymphocyte epitopes. Epitopes are the protein fragments immune killer cells recognise, and predicting them can cut the lab work of vaccine design. Their tool, NetCTL, combines predictions of protein cutting, fragment transport and immune receptor binding. Four rival methods make similar attempts, but no shared benchmark existed to compare them fairly.

The team built standard performance measures and two test sets of known HIV epitopes. In head-to-head ranking, the updated NetCTL-1.2 beat all four rivals on every measure, though not always significantly. On 216 HIV epitopes spanning all twelve HLA supertypes, it placed over 72 percent of true epitopes in its top five percent of scores. The best rival reached 64 percent.
europmc-pmc2362439:
Peto and colleagues forecast Europe's mesothelioma epidemic in 1999. Mesothelioma is a usually fatal cancer of the lining of the lung, caused almost always by asbestos dust breathed in decades earlier. Western Europe used asbestos heavily until about 1980, so deaths were still rising.

The team fitted a model to male pleural cancer deaths from 1970 to 1989 in six countries, then checked it against 1990 to 1994 deaths. They projected yearly deaths would almost double, from five thousand in 1998 to roughly nine thousand near 2018, then fall. The total came to roughly 250,000 deaths across the 35 years covered. Men born around 1945 to 1950 faced the highest risk, with about 1 in 150 of them expected to die of the disease.
europmc-pmc2377339:
Boyko and a large team estimated how harmful new gene mutations are in humans in 2008. They used data from 35 people, 20 of European and 15 of African ancestry, covering 47,576 spelling changes in protein-coding genes. Their method separated the effects of population history from natural selection, a step earlier work often missed.

The data showed an ancient population expansion in the African-ancestry sample and a recent squeeze in the European one. After allowing for that history, they predicted 27% to 29% of protein-changing mutations are harmless or nearly so. Another 30% to 42% are mildly harmful, and almost all the rest are strongly harmful or lethal. Between humans and chimpanzees, they estimated 10% to 20% of protein differences were favoured by selection. They also warned that gene hunts for disease may miss harmful variants.
europmc-pmc2422839:
Chow and Chang reviewed adaptive trial designs for drug testing in 2008. An adaptive design lets researchers change a running trial, its dose, its patient mix, or its statistics, using data gathered so far. The promise is faster, leaner trials, and the approach had grown popular in drug development.

They sorted adaptive designs into three kinds: planned in advance, improvised mid-trial, and applied backwards to finished data. Each carries risks. Changes can shift the patient group away from the one the trial meant to study. Poorly controlled changes can also inflate the false-positive rate, claiming a useless drug works. The authors discuss rare diseases, where small patient pools make flexibility precious, and give examples from the cancer drug Velcade's development. Practical pitfalls in running such trials round out their survey.
europmc-pmc2440739:
Hatch and colleagues looked for links between plastic chemicals and body size in US survey data in 2008. Phthalates are chemicals that soften plastics and appear in many consumer products. Lab work suggested they can disrupt hormones and may promote obesity, so the team used the national NHANES survey from 1999 to 2002.

They measured six phthalate breakdown products in urine from 4,369 people aged 6 to 80, and compared them with body mass index and waist size. In men aged 20 to 59, both measures rose steadily across intake levels of one metabolite, MBzP, from a body mass index of 26.7 to 29.0 across the four groups. Teenage girls showed rising size with another metabolite, MEP, but falling size with MEHP. Children showed no clear pattern, and older adults showed some reverse links. The authors called it exploratory.
europmc-pmc2475539:
Strimmer unified the statistics of false discoveries in genome-scale testing in 2008. When scientists run thousands of tests at once, some hits are pure chance. The false discovery rate estimates that share, but two versions existed, tail-area and local, each with its own scattered algorithms.

His method estimates both versions in one pass. It works from many kinds of test output: p-values, correlations, and z or t scores alike. A modified density estimator, based on Grenander's method, shapes the underlying distribution, and the fitting uses a truncated maximum-likelihood step. For non-p-value statistics it models the null behaviour from the data itself, which lets it absorb dependencies between tests. In comparisons it matched the best specialised tools. The algorithm ships in a free R package named fdrtool.
europmc-pmc2495039:
Rumpler and co-authors examined in 2008 how physical shape steers the growth of new tissue. Cells respond to chemical signals, but the authors asked whether the geometry around them also matters. Their test system was bone-forming cells called osteoblasts growing inside an artificial three-dimensional matrix pierced by tiny channels.

The team found that the local growth rate of the tissue depended strongly on channel shape. Tissue grew fastest where surfaces curved, and cells reacted to curves with radii far larger than the cells themselves. Computer simulations matched the growth patterns seen under a confocal microscope, pointing to curvature and mechanical forces inside the tissue as the drivers. The findings bear on bone healing and on designing scaffolds for tissue engineering.
europmc-pmc2543039:
Dehghan and Merchant assessed in 2008 whether bioelectrical impedance can measure body fat reliably in large population studies. The technique passes a weak electric current through the body and infers fat from resistance, since fat and muscle conduct differently. It is quick and non-invasive, and it performs well under controlled clinic conditions, but field results have been uneven.

The authors reviewed newer foot-to-foot and hand-to-foot systems and the factors that sway readings, including surroundings, ethnic background, menstrual cycle phase, and illness. They conclude the method measures body fat accurately only in the specific groups it was calibrated for. For large studies spanning diverse populations, they advise against it unless separate calibration equations are built for each group taking part.
europmc-pmc2584039:
Eid and colleagues tested in 2008 whether blocking a pain sensor called TRPA1 could ease chronic inflammatory and nerve pain. Safe treatments for such pain remain an unmet need, and TRPA1, a channel opened by irritants like mustard oil, had been implicated in short-lived pain models. The team characterised a selective blocker, HC-030031, in cells and then in rats.

The compound blocked TRPA1 activation in the micromolar range. Given by mouth at 100 milligrams per kilogram, it reduced the pain behaviour triggered by mustard oil. More importantly, the same dose significantly reversed mechanical hypersensitivity, pain from light touch, in a long-running inflammation model and in a spinal nerve injury model of neuropathic pain. The authors propose TRPA1 blockade as a route to new painkillers for both pain types.
europmc-pmc2588639:
Prince, Adamo, Hamel, Hardt, Connor Gorber, and Tremblay systematically reviewed in 2008 how well self-reported physical activity agrees with directly measured activity in adults. Surveys are cheap, but devices such as accelerometers and doubly labelled water measure movement objectively. The team searched eight databases and abstracted data from 187 studies comparing the two approaches.

Correlations between self-report and direct measures ranged wildly, from minus 0.71 to 0.96, and were generally low to moderate overall. No consistent pattern emerged in the average gap: self-reports came out both higher and lower than device readings. Trends shifted with the activity measure used, the intensity studied, and participants' sex. Over a third of studies scored poorly on quality. The authors warn that measurement method alone can change the activity levels a study reports.
europmc-pmc2647739:
Kitzbichler and colleagues tested in 2009 whether the resting human brain sits in a special state called criticality. In such a state, a system hovers between order and chaos. It shows bursts of activity at every size, long-range links in space and time, and fast shifts when pushed.

The team first checked two computer models known to pass through this state. Only when the models sat at the critical point did their timing measures follow a power law, a pattern where big events are rare but never absent. Brain scans and magnetic recordings from resting volunteers then showed the same pattern. Pairs of brain areas stayed in step for stretches of every length, and whole-brain sync flipped in sudden jumps. The pattern held at all signal speeds tested, from slow waves to fast ones.
europmc-pmc2680339:
Greer and Brunet tested in 2009 whether all forms of eating less extend life through the same genes, using the roundworm C. elegans. Cutting food is famous for lengthening life from yeast to mammals, but diets differ: steady dilution, fasting cycles, and feeding mutants that eat slowly. The pathways behind each were unclear.

Two energy sensors, the kinase AMPK and the factor FoxO, proved necessary for the team's own diet method and for one other. Two further methods did not need them at all. A red wine compound, resveratrol, which mimics some diet effects, did need AMPK. Five other genes famed from diet studies each proved dispensable for the team's method, bar one. Combining two diets added their benefits together, as expected if they work through mostly separate wiring. One diet drug, the results warn, will not capture them all.
europmc-pmc2688939:
Rody and co-authors mined gene data from 1,781 breast tumors in 2009 to read the immune cells inside them from gene signatures alone. Tumors are often infiltrated by immune cells, but whether that helps or harms was disputed. Earlier gene signatures had stamped all hormone-insensitive tumors with a bad outlook, immune cells or not.

From a cluster of nearly 600 immune genes, the team distilled seven metagenes, signature sets that stand in for specific immune cell types. A B-cell signature carried no survival signal. A T-cell signature, marked by the gene LCK, carried a strong good one, but only in hormone receptor-negative tumors and in hormone-positive ones overproducing HER2. Tumors high in both B-cell and T-cell signatures also answered pre-surgery chemotherapy better. The immune mix, read precisely, splits seemingly doomed groups apart.
europmc-pmc2726439:
Sarris and co-authors showed in 2008 that neuropilin-1, a protein on regulatory T cells, lengthens their contact with dendritic cells and sharpens their response to antigen. Regulatory T cells hold immunity in check, while dendritic cells present antigen, the target signal, and decide whether a response starts. How long the two cells stay joined helps set that outcome.

Regulatory cells stuck to immature dendritic cells far longer than naive helper T cells did without danger signals present. Neuropilin-1, made by most regulatory cells but not naive helpers, drove that prolonged contact. Longer contact let regulatory cells sense very small antigen amounts, which gives them an edge that defaults to suppression when no danger is present.
europmc-pmc2755039:
Kinali and co-authors tested in 2009 local injection of AVI-4658, a splice-switching drug, in seven boys and men with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a fatal muscle-wasting disease. Mutations break the reading frame of the dystrophin gene, so no working dystrophin protein is made. The drug skips exon fifty-one in the gene message, which can restore the frame and yield a shorter but functional protein.

One foot muscle received the drug and the other received saline, with biopsy weeks later. No related adverse events occurred. At the higher dose, all treated muscles showed increased dystrophin, with staining intensity averaging about a quarter of healthy muscle and significantly above the saline side. Fibers near the injection track showed the strongest restoration.
europmc-pmc2760139:
Samsa and co-authors found in 2009 that dengue virus capsid protein, the shell protein that packages the viral genome, gathers on lipid droplets inside infected cells. Dengue causes the highest disease and death rates among flaviviruses, yet how the capsid recruits the genome for packaging was little known. Lipid droplets are fat storage organelles derived from the cell's internal membranes.

Mutating two hydrophobic amino acids at the capsid center broke its targeting to lipid droplets and impaired formation of new viral particles. Infection also increased the number of lipid droplets per cell. Changing droplet amounts with drugs altered viral replication, and misplaced capsid protein also reduced viral RNA amplification. Droplets may thus store capsid early and scaffold genome packaging later.
europmc-pmc2770639:
Homer, Merriman, and Nelson introduced in 2009 BFAST, a tool for aligning billions of short DNA reads to a reference genome. New sequencing machines made whole-genome resequencing practical, but they produce short reads, twenty-five to one hundred bases, laced with errors and true variants. Aligning them fast without losing accuracy, especially around insertions and deletions, was the bottleneck.

BFAST builds flexible whole-genome indexes to map reads to candidate spots, allowing several indexes for robustness against errors. A Smith-Waterman step then aligns locally with gaps, catching small indels. Against BLAT, MAQ, SHRiMP, and SOAP on simulated and real data, it gained clear sensitivity while keeping adequate speed and cutting false mappings. It aligned a billion reads, a full human resequencing run, in under a day on a modest cluster.
europmc-pmc2781139:
Mishra and Palanivelu overviewed in 2008 the effect of curcumin, the active compound in the spice turmeric, on Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's is a progressive brain disease that erodes memory and daily function, and its pathology involves beta-amyloid plaques, oxidative stress, metal toxicity, and inflammation. Curcumin, long used in Indian medicine, acts as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory and has been tried for many conditions.

They review how curcumin might act on each strand of the disease. Reported effects include fewer beta-amyloid plaques, slower neuron breakdown, binding of harmful metals, calmer inflammation, and less growth of microglia, the brain's immune cells. Together these actions have improved overall memory in patients in the studies surveyed. The paper gathers the proposed mechanisms and the pathology they target, as a case for curcumin's potential in prevention and treatment.
europmc-pmc2860339:
Schulz, Altman, Moher, and the CONSORT Group issued in 2010 an updated rulebook for reporting randomized trials, the studies that randomly assign patients to treatments. Poor reporting hides flaws and wastes research, so the CONSORT checklist tells authors exactly what a trial report must state. The 2010 version updates the 2001 rules using newer methods research and years of user feedback.

The statement keeps a checklist of items covering how a trial was designed, run, analyzed, and funded, plus a diagram tracking every participant. Changes clarify items that users found confusing and add points that experience showed were often skipped. To spread the rules fast, journals across medicine published the statement at the same time and made it free to read.
europmc-pmc2941839:
Krone and co-authors argued in 2010 that an older lab method, gas chromatography with mass spectrometry, still leads in discovering steroid disorders. A newer liquid-based method was taking over routine hormone testing thanks to small samples and sharper targeting.

The newer approach excels at measuring single known steroids but misses the wider picture. A gas-based scan captures every steroid in a urine sample at once, revealing whole patterns of hormone output. Nearly all inherited steroid faults, from early discoveries to recent ones involving oxidoreductase faults, were first defined this way. Presenting the flood of data remains the method's weak point.
europmc-pmc2943439:
Bastian, Glasziou, and Chalmers examined the flood of clinical trial reports in a 2010 essay and asked how anyone can keep pace. Trial publication had grown from a trickle decades earlier to a daily torrent.

By their count, seventy-five trial reports and eleven systematic reviews appear each day, with no slowdown in sight. Only a minority of trials feed into current systematic reviews, and most literature summaries stay unsystematic stories. They urge fewer needless trials, priority for proper reviews, faster review methods, and open access so patients and clinicians can actually use the evidence.
europmc-pmc2991639:
Boutcher reviewed high-intensity intermittent exercise and fat loss in a 2011 article, arguing that short hard bursts may trim fat where steady jogging barely does. Regular moderate aerobic work, studies show, changes body fat very little.

Trials of repeated intense intervals found notable drops in under-skin and belly fat, alongside gains in both aerobic and anaerobic fitness. The training also eased insulin resistance and reshaped muscle toward burning fat and handling sugar better. How exactly the fat comes off remains unsettled, and the review weighs candidate mechanisms plus use against obesity.
europmc-pmc3018439:
Viergever, Olifson, Ghaffar, and Terry offered a checklist for setting health research priorities in a 2010 article, drawn from literature and World Health Organization exercises since 2005. Priority setting steers money toward research with the largest public benefit, yet no single best method fits every setting.

Their checklist walks planners through nine themes of good practice, from pinning down context and choosing an approach to gathering information, involving stakeholders, applying criteria, and planning follow-through. Transparency and later evaluation get explicit emphasis. The aim is informed local choices rather than one rigid recipe.
europmc-pmc3022639:
Gulliver, Griffiths, and Christensen reviewed in 2010 why young people with mental health problems so often avoid getting professional help. Their systematic review gathered survey and interview studies on what blocks help seeking in teens and young adults, and what makes it easier. The problem is large, since mental disorders are common in youth yet only a minority ever reach services.

Across the studies, shame about mental illness and a wish to handle problems alone stood out as major blocks. Not knowing where to go and doubting that treatment would help also mattered. Support from family and friends, past good care, and better knowledge of services made help more likely. The review gives clinics and schools a clear list of hurdles to lower first.
europmc-pmc3038139:
Rostkowski, Olsson, Søndergaard, and Jensen built in 2011 a visual tool for studying how acidity changes proteins. A program called PROPKA predicts how easily each part of a protein gains or loses protons, which shapes its charge, stability, and activity. Its output was a dense text file, hard to connect back to the protein's three dimensional shape.

The new interface plugs into a standard molecule viewer and paints predicted values directly onto the structure. Users can click a residue to see why its value shifted, including lost water contact and nearby charges. The tool also shows how each group adds to stability at any chosen acidity, and compares several structures side by side. That makes it handy for protein design and for guessing function from structure. It was released freely online.
europmc-pmc3057439:
Saper led the ONSTIM feasibility study in 2011, testing whether gentle electrical stimulation of nerves at the back of the head can ease chronic migraine that drugs cannot control. Chronic migraine means headache on at least half the days of each month. Patients who responded to a temporary nerve block were assigned by chance to adjustable stimulation, fixed weak stimulation, or standard medical care.

After three months, about two in five patients in the adjustable group met the response bar. That bar meant halving headache days or clearly cutting pain. Almost no one in the other groups reached it. No unexpected device harms appeared. The main problem was the wire shifting from its spot, which happened in about a quarter of implanted patients. As a feasibility study it was not meant to be definitive. The authors say the signal is promising enough to justify larger, stricter trials.
europmc-pmc3071839:
Ramonet and coauthors reported in 2011 that mice engineered to carry the most common Parkinson disease mutation slowly lose the very brain cells that die in patients. The mutation sits in a gene called LRRK2 in full. Earlier mouse models with this gene showed faulty signaling but no real cell loss, a major gap. This team built mice carrying two human mutant versions and followed their brains with age.

Mice with one mutation lost dopamine producing neurons in the key movement pathway as they aged, in step with the late onset pattern in families. Their remaining neurons grew simpler branches, and aged brains showed jammed recycling systems and faulty power stations inside cells. The other mutation did not produce the same loss. These mice finally give researchers a living model of the cell death itself, for testing protective drugs.
europmc-pmc3080339:
Boulos, Wheeler, Tavares, and Jones surveyed in 2011 how smartphones were rapidly becoming health tools for patients and clinicians alike. Modern phones act as small computers with big screens, sensors, and open app stores. The review tours the market across the major phone platforms of the day, from fitness and lifestyle coaching to chronic disease support and professional education.

One detailed example follows a European project for older people living with several chronic conditions. Its phone app gathers readings from a sensor filled smart garment and the phone's location tracker, then sends them to a server where clinicians monitor patients remotely. The authors also weigh barriers honestly: cost, battery life, network limits, ease of use, and privacy worries. Their verdict is that phones will reshape care delivery, but only where those barriers are handled well.
europmc-pmc3107939:
Lydia Alvarez-Erviti and colleagues reported a 2011 cell study in Neurobiology of Disease on how a brain protein linked to Parkinson disease may spread. Clumps of this protein build up in sick neurons, and earlier work hinted that healthy cells can take it in. The team tested tiny membrane sacs released by cells as a route.

Cells making extra protein released sacs that carried it, and normal cells picked the protein up from those sacs. When the team blocked the cell compartments that break down waste, sac release rose and transfer rose with it. The result points to sac-based spread as a process that faulty waste handling speeds up, and as a possible target for treatment.
europmc-pmc3164639:
Tung Phan and colleagues catalogued viruses in the droppings of wild rodents in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Rodents meet people often and seed many human infections, yet their gut virus world was unmapped. The team purified and randomly read viral DNA and RNA from just over a hundred mice, voles, and rats caught in California and Virginia.

Known mammal virus families appeared in force, alongside seventeen tiny circular genomes that may found whole new families. Two likely new genera turned up in one family, plus a close relative of a human gut pathogen, the first mouse astrovirus genome, and a mouse papillomavirus. Large shares of the catch were insect and plant viruses, mirroring the rodent diet. Several rodent viruses sit close to human ones, hinting at past species jumps.
europmc-pmc3322439:
Volkova and Russell reviewed heart damage caused by a powerful family of cancer drugs, in a 2011 article. The drugs, called anthracyclines, include doxorubicin and remain mainstays against leukemias, lymphomas, and many solid tumors. Their usefulness is capped by harm to the heart that grows with total dose and can end in irreversible heart failure.

The review explains how the drugs injure heart muscle, how often the damage occurs, and which patients face the highest risk. It surveys ways to catch injury early, including heart imaging and blood markers, before symptoms appear. Prevention options include limiting total dose, spreading doses out, using protective companion drugs, and choosing gentler drug versions. Treatment of established damage follows standard heart failure care, and the authors stress that cancer doctors and heart doctors must plan together.
europmc-pmc3346739:
Powell and a large team profiled single tumor cells circulating in the blood of breast cancer patients, reporting in 2012. These rare cells, shed by solid tumors, may seed the spread of cancer, and knowing what they are could sharpen treatment. Reading their gene activity is hard because blood cells contaminate samples. The team used a magnetic device to pull out live tumor cells, then read eighty seven genes in each cell alone.

Usable cells came from about seven in ten patients, and none from healthy subjects or patients with non epithelial cancers. Individual cells differed strikingly from each other, splitting into two broad groups by their gene patterns. Cells from standard breast cancer cell lines clustered tightly and looked quite different from patient cells, raising doubts about using those lines to test late stage treatments. The authors pitch single cell profiling as a step toward liquid biopsies.
europmc-pmc3349739:
Chen and collaborators asked why males and females differ in body fat, using a mouse model that separates the effects of sex chromosomes from those of gonadal hormones. In the four core genotypes system, animals can carry XX or XY chromosome complements regardless of whether they develop ovaries or testes.

The team found that chromosome complement itself shaped adiposity. Mice with two X chromosomes gained more fat than XY animals on the same diet, pointing to X-chromosome dosage as a driver of the difference. The result suggests that genes escaping X inactivation may contribute to sex differences in obesity and related metabolic risk.
europmc-pmc3429039:
Brown and Naidoo reviewed in 2012 how the cell's protein-folding workshop, the endoplasmic reticulum, copes with stress across aging. When folding falters, the workshop raises an alarm program, the unfolded protein response, which boosts helper proteins, clears bad folds, and slows new production. Brief stress is handled well; unrelenting stress can push the cell to die.

With age, key folding helpers fade, so the alarm responds weakly just as misfolded proteins pile up. The review ties that failure to diseases of late life, from Alzheimer's and Parkinson's to type 2 diabetes, plus several cancers and inflammatory conditions. Many feature proteins collapsing into insoluble clumps. Keeping the folding system young, they suggest, is a promising front against age-related disease.
europmc-pmc3431839:
Lokman, Elder, Ricciardelli, and Oehler developed a chick-egg assay in 2012 to watch ovarian cancer invade and spread without using mice. Most ovarian cancer patients arrive with advanced disease, and better targeted drugs are badly needed. Mouse testing is slow and costly, while the membrane inside a chick egg offers a living, blood-rich surface for tumor cells.

Three ovarian cancer cell lines behaved on the membrane just as their movement and invasion in dishes predicted. The assay proved sturdy and cheap, and because the system is closed, test molecules last longer than in animal bodies. That makes it well suited to screening scarce candidate drugs. The protocol gives ovarian researchers a practical middle step before animal work.
europmc-pmc3469539:
Pragman and colleagues described the community of bacteria living in the lungs of people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, in PLoS ONE in 2012. Even when patients feel stable, their lungs hold bacteria, and infection drives about half of sudden flare-ups. The team washed the lungs of patients with moderate or severe disease and of healthy controls, then read bacterial DNA.

Samples from patients held a richer mix of bacteria than control samples. The main groups were the same in all lungs, and many species matched mouth bacteria, hinting they arrive by tiny inhalations of saliva. Samples grouped by the inhaled medicines patients used, not by disease stage. Pragman's work maps a baseline for asking how lung bacteria drive this disease.

faraday-experimental-researches-vol1-183:
Michael Faraday published Volume 1 of Experimental Researches in Electricity in 1839, gathering his papers of the 1830s. Faraday, a bookbinder's lad turned the Royal Institution's leading worker, reported his trials in numbered series. Volume 1 holds Series 1 through 14.

The series announce a great find: electric current made by moving magnets. That find lies behind every dynamo and transformer since. Faraday also set out the laws of how currents split compounds, and coined terms such as electrode and ion. His style reports each trial so others can repeat it. The volume is a founding record of electrical science.
frus-1861-d139:
From Washington on 26 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton after the Bull Run defeat. The letter is document 139 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Five days after Bull Run, Seward's word to Paris had to admit loss without yielding ground. France must not read the defeat as a reason to back the South. The letter shows that hard balance being struck in real time. France's foreign chief, Thouvenel, heard the Union's case from Dayton in person. In person talks let Dayton press points that paper alone could not carry. Thouvenel heard the same balance in person.
frus-1861-d239:
On 14 June 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. It stands as Document 239 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d39:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 10 April 1861. Adams was about to sail as the new American minister to Great Britain. The letter is document 39 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

London was the post that mattered most. Britain's mills craved Southern cotton, and its fleet ruled the seas. Seward's letter sent Adams to that post two days before Fort Sumter, with the fate of the Union in part in his hands. Adams carried a famous name: his father and grandfather had both been Presidents of the United States.
frus-1862-d139:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 8 September 1862. It stands as Document 139 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d239:
On 18 September 1862, the day after Antietam, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart of the British legation. The letter stands as Document 239 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Antietam had checked Lee's invasion at terrible cost, and Lincoln would soon issue his emancipation plan. News of the battle was still fresh and partial when Seward wrote. A letter from this date sits at a hinge in the record. The military facts that foreign governments had been waiting for were changing, and with them the odds of outside action. Lyons also reported home on each note, so most of these papers exist in two archives.
frus-1862-d339:
Filed as Document 339 but dated 21 October 1862, this dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. The printers set it after a later Dayton report in the 1862 volume.

The letter belongs with the Seward mail of 20 and 21 October, when Washington was pressing its advantage as the truce plan faltered. Its late filing is a clerical accident of the printed volume. Read by date, it joins the effort to lock in Britain's refusal before France could reopen the question. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d39:
Word from Charles Francis Adams reached Washington on 21 March 1862, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 39 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d439:
Gabriel García Tassara wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 October 1862. The note is Document 439 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

By October 1862 the rush of foreign intervention talk had eased, and the Spanish correspondence in Washington settled back toward its standing subjects. Tassara, long posted in the capital, handled Madrid's interests with Seward directly. Those interests touched Cuba, the Gulf, and the French advance in Mexico, which Spain had quit but still watched. His autumn note is one more turn in a long, careful exchange that kept two wary governments on speaking terms through the war.
frus-1862-d539:
On 28 July 1862 Roest van Limburg sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 539 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

End of July 1862 found the Dutch exchange in its regular stride, one note answering another across a few days. Van Limburg wrote for a government whose colonial ports lay close to the war's sea lanes. Those ports stood in the West Indies. American practice there was therefore a standing Dutch concern. His letters are formal by design, which makes them good evidence: what a government puts in a signed note, it means. The document adds another careful layer to the Washington side of the Netherlands file.
frus-1862-d639:
Townsend Harris wrote from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 July 1861, now addressing the secretary by name. The dispatch is Document 639 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

By July, word of the change of administration had long since reached Edo. Harris's correspondence settled into its wartime form. It consisted of reports to Seward from a post the war could not reach. His health was failing after five years in Japan. His letters of this season carry the strain of the post. He was a man holding a difficult station alone. The dispatch belongs to the last year of the first American mission to Japan. That mission is a story of endurance. The volume preserves it at the edge of its Civil War record.
frus-1863p1-d139:
On 31 March 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 139 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a month-end letter often tied off the month's loose ends. Seward's second sheet of 31 March sits in that place in the file. With its twin, it closes a March in which Washington wrote to London by the dozen and the score. The pair is a fair end to the thickest month in the printed exchange.
frus-1863p1-d239:

The dispatch is document 239 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

After the Emancipation Proclamation took effect on New Year's Day 1863, the war stood openly as a fight over slavery. That change made British support for the South harder to defend in public. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d339:
The American answer to London on 16 December 1862 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 339 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.

frus-1863p1-d439:
The date 2 April 1863 heads a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d539:
On 27 May 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d639:
Among the day's business on 16 October 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London to Secretary William H. Seward. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Read in sequence, the London letters show how close the two countries came to open conflict, and how both sides kept stepping back. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d139: Secretary Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on November 18, 1943, and the letter is Document 139 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hull stayed in Washington while the president traveled, minding the home front of American diplomacy. His letters in the voyage week kept the traveling party tied to the department. The record names the two men and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d239:
From Washington on 20 November 1943, Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a short secret telegram, passing on two reports from Ankara dated 17 and 18 November. Both concern Turkey's slow move toward joining the war.

Ankara reports that Foreign Minister Numan won his party leaders' approval to tell Eden the Turks had decided in principle to enter the war. Military help for Turkey now came first, ahead of the political question of Soviet pledges. The British feared the decision would leak and draw an early Axis attack, and noted heavy losses off Leros. The second report has German ambassador von Papen telling Finland's minister that Turkey would stay out, which the minister read as a lie meant to calm Hitler.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d339:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy sent Harry Hopkins a memorandum at Cairo on 30 November 1943. Hopkins was then at Tehran. The memorandum sets out the civil affairs arrangement worked out with the British. He asks Hopkins to approve it, and to phone him.

Four points make up the deal. America will treat the European Advisory Commission seriously and give Ambassador Winant a strong staff. Britain will drop the plan to move the Combined Civil Affairs Committee to London, and its Washington members will be empowered to act. Commission recommendations will pass through the Combined Chiefs of Staff for comment before going to the three governments as final. The chiefs will then write the field directives. McCloy has Hull's and Stimson's approval, and his one worry is speed, since Winant does not strike him as a fast administrator.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d39: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on October 6, 1943, and his message is Document 39 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The letter came as the three powers prepared their first foreign ministers' meeting of the war, set for Moscow later that month. The catalog gives the date and the names only. In the published volume the message sits among the exchanges that turned a hoped-for summit into a dated plan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d439:
A second set of Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes survives from December 4, 1943, the first day of the Second Cairo Conference. The Combined Chiefs were the top American and British officers who directed the two nations' shared war. The State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume preserves this session next to the day's other meetings.

Formal minutes like these keep the shape of the discussion: the questions put to the chiefs, the views of each side, and the conclusions entered into the record. For students of the war, the value lies in that detail. Grand strategy at Cairo was not declared in speeches; it was argued out in rooms like this one and written down.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d539:
Heaton Stevens, second secretary at the American embassy in China, wrote to his own ambassador, Clarence Gauss, on January 5, 1944. Internal embassy letters carried the frank judgments that formal reports to Washington sometimes softened. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Gauss ran a hard-pressed embassy in Chungking, China's wartime capital, and his junior officers fed him reporting from inside the mission. A letter up the internal chain shows diplomacy's workshop rather than its shop window. For readers, it adds a staff-level Chinese view to a volume dominated by presidents and prime ministers, in the weeks after the Cairo Declaration.
frus-1944-quebec-d139:
George Elsey, assistant to the president's naval aide, prepared this background memorandum on occupying Austria and the Balkans before the Quebec Conference. It traces how a question that seemed settled in May 1944 became confused within weeks. The confusion turned on one word: whether American agreement covered Austria's occupation or only its control.

Roosevelt had approved a policy of no American occupation forces in southern or southeastern Europe, Austria included. Yet Ambassador Winant told the European Advisory Commission America accepted tripartite occupation of Austria. Winant explained he had the president's permission for tripartite control, without committing any force. The Joint Chiefs finally allowed a possible token force, while General Wilson planned to occupy Austria with four British divisions.
frus-1944-quebec-d239:
Alexander Kirk, the American representative on the Advisory Council for Italy, reported from Caserta on September 12, 1944. General Wilson had heard from London that the War Cabinet wanted data on how relief in Italy was being administered. The British Service of Supplies was to report existing arrangements and expenditures to date, and what steps were being taken to restart Italian production.

The War Office also wanted General O'Dwyer's report, which he had carried to Washington, sent back with Wilson's comments urgently for the War Cabinet's use. London knew the report would reach the British through Washington in due course. In the meantime, Wilson was asked for his copy plus any additional pertinent information he could supply.
frus-1944-quebec-d39:
August 31, 1944 brought another Churchill message to Roosevelt. It closed the month's exchange between the two leaders. The State Department placed it in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill spent late August preparing to sail for Canada. Roosevelt would receive him at Quebec. His letters that week stated the British case. The questions awaiting them included Germany's future. They also included the war against Japan. For readers, the message is his final word from London. It came before the conference opened. His written preparation in this file was always thorough and detailed. The conference itself opened days later in Quebec City.
frus-1945-50-intel-d139:
Minutes of the 184th meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee are dated 5 February 1946. The committee's numbered run continues into the new year in the volume's second printing of its records. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The 184th meeting sat as the central system was being born next door, and the State Department's own intelligence office faced its new neighbor. Committee minutes at such a moment record a department adjusting to a settled fact. Readers who followed the November meetings can complete the arc here. The committee went from fixing a position in a fight to living with the fight's result. The staff committee's paper trail gives the State side of 1946 its steady pulse.
frus-1945-50-intel-d239:
On 11 February 1949, Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter sent a letter to the Speaker of the House of Representatives (Rayburn). Readers meet it as document 239 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first Dulles Report season had begun: an outside team judged the CIA while the agency and its partners answered back.

A formal letter was a step above a memo: it put a request or a stance on record under the writer's signature. Letters like this one let a reader follow a debate between two offices in their own words. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d339:
A letter from Sherman Kent reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 9 February 1948. The State Department prints it as document 339 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Replies in the same file show the exchange from both sides. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d39:
McCormack, the State Department's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to Admiral Leahy, the president's chief of staff, on 31 October 1945. Leahy was the gatekeeper at Truman's door. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Writing to Leahy was a way of writing to the president by the staff door. McCormack, whose office held the old OSS analysts, had a plan for central intelligence centered on State. He needed the White House to hear it. His letter shows the State Department taking its case to the top as the Budget Bureau did the same. Readers can feel the contest tightening: by Halloween of 1945, every claimant had found a path to the president's desk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d139:
Assistant Secretary of War McCloy laid the Bremen problem before the Secretary of State on 23 January 1945. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume in excerpt, asks for help at the coming conference. The issue is American control of the Bremen area in the British zone.

Ever since Quebec, McCloy writes, Washington has tried to get its hold on Bremen clarified, after giving the northwest of Germany to the British. Halifax backed a proposal that seemed to solve it. London's reply, though, added reservations that go pretty deep. The staff still will not clear ratification of the zones protocol until the matter is straight. If the conference staffs can clear the big snags, local commanders can settle the details.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d239:
Stettinius sent the President a draft answer to Churchill on Iran on 17 January 1945. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, encloses the suggested reply to the prime minister's telegram 890 on the oil concession controversy. The Department's own view comes first.

Iran should be discussed at the coming meeting, Washington agrees. It should be taken up among the three leaders themselves, as signatories of the Tehran Declaration. But no advance notice should be given, since notice would lend the subject undue importance. The draft reply concurs fully in the discussion. It adds a measured judgment. The evidence does not yet prove that Russia means to force a concession now. But her open dissatisfaction with Iran's wartime law stirs apprehension that should be quieted.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d339: Three quick points fill this handwritten note from Harry Hopkins to President Roosevelt, passed during the second plenary meeting on February 5, 1945. France, Hopkins noted, already sat on the European Advisory Commission, the only body then studying German affairs. He advised promising France a zone of occupation. He also advised putting off any decision about the Control Commission for Germany. Together these slips show how the French-zone question was settled in practice: zone now, machinery later.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d39: Roosevelt replied to Churchill on 2 January 1945, keeping their exchange unbroken into the summit month. The message stands as document 39 in the Foreign Relations volume covering the Malta and Yalta conferences. By then the American and British staffs were packing for Malta, where the two Western delegations would meet first before flying on together to the Crimea in February.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d439:
So far agreed: this delegation paper of February 10, 1945, prints the Polish formula as the three foreign ministers had settled it. A new situation, it opens, has been created by the complete liberation of Poland by the Red Army. A broader provisional government is called for.

The government then functioning in Poland should be reorganized on a broader democratic basis. Democratic leaders from Poland itself and from abroad would be included. The new body would be called the Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. Molotov, Harriman, and Clark Kerr would consult in Moscow, first with the present government's members. The text is the Yalta settlement on Poland, caught before the leaders signed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d139:
Acting Secretary Grew answered the London embassy's press question on July 14, 1945. His telegram to Ambassador Winant is document 139 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Winant had said that London newsmen expected a meeting place with the President's party late in the talks.

Grew explains that one man each from the Associated Press, United Press, and the news wire and film pools is traveling with the President. They will not attend the talks. They will wait at a meeting place still to be chosen, which some Washington newsmen may also join. The plan is for American newsmen only, and details will come from the White House through press aide Ross. The press stayed near the story but outside the sealed grounds.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d239:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded the Spanish ambassador's probe about Franco's Spain in extracts of a memorandum dated July 9, 1945. The extracts form document 239 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador de Cárdenas called that afternoon, speaking, he said, friend to friend and not under instructions.

Cárdenas raised the San Francisco decision. Under it, states whose regimes were set up with Axis military help would be barred from the world organization. The bar would last while those regimes lasted. That formula was aimed at Franco's Spain. He asked whether Grew knew of a proposed move by Chile and Uruguay. The move would apply the provision openly to Spain. He also asked whether Ambassador Armour had spoken on the subject in Madrid. Grew said he had no information on either point. Spain's status did reach the Potsdam table, where the three leaders condemned the Franco regime.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d339:
Germany's ban on all political activity is weighed in Murphy's top secret airgram of June 28, 1945, to Matthews, the director of European affairs. Murphy, the political adviser at supreme headquarters, supplements his earlier report of June 2. He lists the risks on both sides of the ban.

Groups allowed to organize soon, he warns, would likely turn against the American military government, above all if hard times came. Yet the ban itself was negative and suppressive, and it left a political vacuum others would try to fill. Kept too long, it might discourage the faint democratic stirrings he could already see among Germans.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d39:
Churchill quoted his own telegram to Stalin in this message to Truman of May 29, 1945. He would be very glad, he had told the Marshal, to meet him and President Truman soon. The place would be what is left of Berlin. He hoped the meeting might take place about the middle of June. He had repeated the telegram to Truman, he added.

The point had been raised in Stalin's talks with Hopkins, Churchill noted to the Marshal. All good wishes closed the message; he was very anxious to meet soon. The quotation shows London pressing for June while Washington aimed at July — a small gap that shaped the summer.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d439:
Czechoslovakia's formal case for expulsion is made in a note from Under-Secretary Clementis to the American chargé, dated at Prague on July 3, 1945. Before the fighting stopped, he writes, the President and government of Czechoslovakia had sent the allied governments a detailed memorandum. It set out the political necessity of evacuating most of the German and Hungarian population.

In doing so, Clementis says, they spoke for the elemental and unanimous wishes of the Czech and Slovak nations. Those nations, anxious for the state's future, wished to exclude elements that had proved propagators of national hatred. They had been, he charges, willing instruments of hostile propaganda and instigators of dissension within the country.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d539:
Post-war financial talks with Britain cannot wait, a briefing book summary argues. It is important to come very soon to definite understandings with the British on post-war financial questions. There is serious danger, it warns, that otherwise Britain may not ultimately go along with the American program to restore world-wide multilateralism in finance and trade.

The summary suggests the Prime Minister be asked to designate representatives to meet American representatives this summer. They would discuss lend-lease settlement policy, post-lend-lease credits, and post-V-J Day monetary and exchange policies. The talks would join the conversations already under way on foreign trade policy, toward comprehensive post-war arrangements under Article VII of the British master lend-lease agreement.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d639:
Minister Wadsworth reported a French peace feeler in the Levant from Beirut on July 1, 1945. His confidential wire is document 639 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It recounts a proposal passed quietly by the French envoy Ostrorog two days before.

Ostrorog proposed that the Troupes Speciales pass to Syria and Lebanon at once. French troops would then leave the Levant at the same time as British troops. That, he argued, would end the tension and let all sides settle their shared problems in good will. Lebanon's foreign minister Pharaon gave a careful answer. Transfer and withdrawal were main Syrian and Lebanese aims, he said. But the basic shape of future ties with France could be settled only in international talks, not in a private deal.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1039: William Clayton and Emile Despres sent this one-line secret telegram from Babelsberg to Willard Thorp in Washington on July 18, 1945. Both men were working on German economic affairs at the Potsdam Conference. Their question is narrow and practical. They ask Thorp to advise them whether the Soviet Union has been informed of the American proposal for a directive on German coal production and exports. The answer follows in the next document in the volume. The brevity of the cable shows a delegation checking one fact before its next move.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1139:
Arthur Bliss Lane, named as the new American ambassador to Poland, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 24 July 1945. Lane had his posting but not yet his post. The Warsaw embassy was not open, since Poland's future was still being fought over at Potsdam.

An envoy in waiting worked his brief from afar. He studied the country, the parties, and the men he would soon deal with. His cable shows that work under way days before the summit settled Poland's fate. It is foreign service in a strange pause: full duties, no embassy. The record keeps few such glimpses.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1239:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to the President on 18 July 1945. The chiefs' direct channel to Truman was a fixture of the war's last year. Their messages joined military judgment to the summit's bargaining while Germany's peace was drafted.

At Potsdam the chiefs' concerns ran from the forces in Europe to the invasion plans for Japan. A note sent on the talks' second day fed that judgment into the opening rounds.
