This message is one piece of the written record of the alliance at work. It shows the soldiers' house keeping its hand on the president's brief.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1339:
The acting secretary of state, Joseph Grew, wrote to Secretary of State James Byrnes on 19 July 1945. Byrnes was at Potsdam with President Truman, while Grew held the department in Washington. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

With the secretary abroad, the acting secretary's letters formed the spine of the department for weeks. They carried news, requests, and warnings across the Atlantic so the men at the summit stayed tied to their own government. This letter shows the home office at work during one of the busiest stretches of 1945. How much trust the system placed in the man left behind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-139:
The United States delegation circulated this memorandum at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. With two days left, staff papers carried urgent weight. A memo could lock a position before a plenary session began. This one was filed with the conference papers and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Final-week memoranda reward close reading. They often mark the last point where a view could still change. Writers stated their case in short, plain terms. For readers today, the memo is a dated marker of American thinking at the brink of the final deal. It adds grit to the smooth surface of the agreed texts.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-39:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes record the approval of their 196th meeting's conclusions, held July 19, 1945. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. It settles the rules for passing war information to the Russians, the dispute aired in volume one.

Two rules were written into the conclusions. On operational information and intelligence, each side may pass the Russians what it wishes, without bargaining. That covers the theaters for which each staff is responsible. On all other information, the two staffs must consult together first. Neither party may pass Moscow anything drawn wholly or partly from the other's sources without that party's consent. The chiefs then took up a draft directive to the Supreme Commander in Southeast Asia, proposed by the British chiefs.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d739:
Benjamin Gerig, the American alternate delegate to the United Nations Preparatory Commission, wrote to Leo Pasvolsky and Alger Hiss on July 26, 1945. Document 739 comes from the building of the new world body. The Commission, seated in London, was readying the first General Assembly. Gerig reported to two of the Department's top planners.

Letters like this one wired Potsdam to the United Nations' birth. The men addressed had shaped the charter at San Francisco. Readers see postwar planning as a single web: summit talks in Germany, organization work in London. The document shows staff keeping both efforts in step during a crowded week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d839:
Document 839 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 22, 1945. Staff drafted it as the conference closed its first week. Working papers at this stage answered points raised in the early sessions. The paper was kept in the delegation files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A week's-end draft shows learning in progress. The writers had heard the other sides and adjusted. Readers can track the change from the opening papers. The document also shows the staff's rhythm: sessions by day, drafting by night. That rhythm produced the mountain of paper from which the final protocol was cut.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d939:
Soviet Foreign Minister Molotov presented this second definition of war trophies at Potsdam on July 27, 1945. It restates the Soviet claim in two parts. War trophies mean all German military property. That includes gear meant for use by enemy military and paramilitary units, or by their members.

The second part reaches beyond the battlefield. It covers property the enemy used for military purposes. Such property counts even when it was removed from Germany during the war to serve Allied military needs. A later letter in the Pauley Files notes that no formal action was taken on either Soviet definition.
fundamental-orders-connecticut-1639:
Settlers from Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield adopted the Fundamental Orders in 1639 to govern their Connecticut towns. The document lays out a frame of government made by the settlers themselves. No royal charter stood behind it, which made the act bold for its time.

The orders provide for a general court, elected magistrates, and a governor chosen each year. They set rules for meetings, voting, and the duties of town deputies. Because the plan is written, general, and based on consent, many call it the first written constitution in America. It guided Connecticut until a royal charter arrived in 1662.
gao-gaoreports-b-296239: PPCSC/RAC Benning JV took its July 2005 contract fight to GAO as a joint venture, and this ruling is the verdict. The venture said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Joint ventures get the same full hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298239: PPG-CMS-PSI JV doubled its July 2006 protest — two case numbers, one joint-venture fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The venture challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299539: Moore's Cafeteria Services, doing business as MCS Management, took its June 2007 food-service fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call. The firm challenged the award; the ruling tests the claims. Chow-hall contracts get the full fair-play treatment too.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-139: The young homeland shop's merger needed staying power in 2005, and GAO's report says the long game was required. The review calls for the patient build. The young department deserved the integration. The build had to last. The haul was long.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-239: Germ-fight grant spending got a GAO accounting in 2005, and the report tracks what the locals spent and owed. The review follows the money trail. The ready crews deserved the count. The trail was followed. The money was followed. The count was complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-339: The nuclear cops needed to do more in 2005, and GAO's report says the NRC had to ensure plants controlled spent fuel effectively. The review demands the vigilance. The glowing rods deserved the guard. The commission had to act. The glowing rods deserved the guard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-539: Job training scorecards needed a rethink in 2005, and GAO's report says Labor should try fresh ways to grade the programs. The findings demand the rethink. The report warns that the trainees deserved workable rules. The trainees deserved workable rules. The rethink had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-639: The Global Fund's AIDS fight got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says the fund responded to challenges, though better information was needed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the dying deserved honest aid. The information had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-239: The SEC's 2005 financial statements got a GAO audit in 2005, and the report examines the books for fiscal years 2005 and 2004. The findings grade the accounting. The report shows the market cop's own money was checked. The statements had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-639: Oil spills in the St. Clair-Detroit waterway needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says better information and targeted prevention could help. The findings demand the data. The report warns that the shared waters deserved guarding. The management had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-839: Weapon buying needed better data rights in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon should strengthen policies for assessing technical data needs. The findings demand the rules. The report warns that the military's toys needed their blueprints secured. The policies had to be strong.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-139: FEMA's day-to-day money needed better tracking in 2007, and GAO's report says the agency needed adequate data, plans, and systems. The findings demand the tools. The report warns that the disaster agency should not be a disaster of bookkeeping. The books had to match the mission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-39: Guarding critical infrastructure was uneven in 2007, and GAO's report says progress in coordinating public and private efforts varied by sector. The findings map the gaps. The report warns that the power grid and water plants needed steadier guarding. The coordination had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-839: Iraq's oil money moved through Pentagon deals in 2007 — and GAO's report says the contracting rules got bent. Skipping key bidding principles on the oil contract put the government at risk. The findings read as a wartime cautionary tale: haste in contracting invites waste, or worse.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-39: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at stabilization and Reconstruction: Actions Are Needed to Develop a Planning and Coordination Framework and Establish the Civilian Reserve Corps. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-539: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at influenza Pandemic: Federal Agencies Should Continue to Assist States to Address Gaps in Pandemic Planning. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-939: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at federal Real Property: Progress Made in Reducing Unneeded Property, but VA Needs Better Information to Make Further Reductions. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
great-bible-1539:
Myles Coverdale prepared the Great Bible, printed in 1539 as the first English Bible authorized for public use. King Henry VIII ordered a copy placed in every parish church in England. Its huge page size gave it the name Great, and copies were chained to lecterns so anyone could hear or read them.

Coverdale built the text by revising Matthew's Bible, drawing on Latin and German sources where older English ran out. The volume holds the complete Old and New Testaments. It put one shared English Scripture in front of the whole country, and later translators, including the Geneva team, worked from it.
ioannis-aurelij-augurelli-p-ariminensis-: Ioannis Aurelii Augurelli Chrysopoeia et Vellus aureum, 1639. The gold-making poem. This book preserves that alchemy. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-millaud-moise-p:
Moïse Polydore Millaud, born at Bordeaux on August 27, 1813, was the French journalist and banker who built a press empire from almost nothing. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn tell his story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A poor Jewish tradesman's son with little schooling, he started as a bailiff's clerk and was publishing his own paper at twenty.

His early Paris ventures failed but taught him the trade, and his court-news paper L'Audience prospered from 1839 until 1845 against the official Gazette des Tribunaux. His La Liberté backed Louis Napoleon and was suppressed after the June rising of 1848. With Mirès he then launched the Journal des Chemins de Fer, which became a power in railway finance and speculation across France.
la-psychologie-et-la-phrenologie-compare: La psychologie et la phrénologie comparées, 1839. The French comparison. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
lakhovsky-secret-of-life-1939:
Georges Lakhovsky, a Russian-born engineer working in France, set out his theory of life and health in Le Secret de la Vie. Mark Clement's English version, The Secret of Life, came out in 1939. Its subject is cosmic rays and the unseen waves given off by living things.

Lakhovsky held that each cell works like a tiny radio set, tuned to waves from space. Sickness, in his view, is a cell out of tune. His Multiple Wave Oscillator was built to retune the body. Mainstream science never took the theory up, but the book led the fringe field of wave healing. His name still turns up wherever wave cures are sold.
laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-4:
Books eight to ten close Laplace's Mecanique Celeste, and Bowditch's fourth volume appeared in 1839. Satellites and comets take up much of this final part. Laplace also surveys the system of the world as a whole. A treatment of capillary attraction, the pull seen in narrow tubes, ends the work.

Bowditch's commentary runs alongside the text to the last page. With this volume the English set stands complete at four. The project took him a decade of spare hours. It carried the summit of French celestial mechanics to America. Readers who finish it have crossed the whole system. The feat still anchors his fame.
morton-crania-americana-1839:
Samuel George Morton, a Philadelphia physician, published Crania Americana in 1839. He measured hundreds of skulls from Indigenous peoples across North and South America. From those measurements he ranked human groups by supposed mental worth.

The plates and tables present his skull collection in careful detail. Later scholars, most famously Stephen Jay Gould, showed how bias warped the work. It became a founding text of American physical anthropology and of scientific racism. Readers today study it to see how prejudice can dress itself as measurement. Its large plates made it a reference work in American museums for decades.
openalex-w2009068239: Diarrhea still kills children — and vaccine makers need to know which germs. Lanata and colleagues' 2013 systematic review estimated global pathogen-specific causes of diarrheal deaths in children under five. The review of 1990–2011 studies ranked the 13 deadliest pathogens.
openalex-w2073832139: The universe's expansion is speeding up. A 1998 paper gave supernova proof for a speeding universe driven by dark energy. The 10 Type Ia supernovae rewrote cosmology — the discovery paper, later honored with a Nobel Prize.
openalex-w2105942939: Sick dogs have sick gut bugs. A 2012 study compared gut microbes in dogs with acute diarrhea and IBD. The work linked microbial shifts to canine gut disease and recovery over time — the first deep look at sick dog guts.
openalex-w2132089139: Unneeded C-sections carry real maternal risk. A 2010 analysis linked C-sections without medical need to severe maternal outcomes. The global debate over need got hard evidence — surgery's trade-off, measured at last for mothers now.
openalex-w2168608639: Rhizopus oryzae is a mold that can turn deadly, causing mucormycosis — a fast-spreading infection with a death rate above 50 percent. This 2009 PLoS Genetics paper decodes its genome and finds a surprise: the entire genome was duplicated at some point in its history. The analysis of this basal fungal lineage reveals how the doubling may have armed the fungus with extra genes for invasion and growth.
openalex-w2256016639: Reading a patient's genome means little without knowing what's normal. This 2016 Nature paper aggregates high-quality exome — protein-coding — DNA sequences from 60,706 people into a reference dataset. By cataloguing how genetic variation is distributed in the general population, the resource lets doctors and researchers tell harmless variants apart from ones that cause disease.
openalex-w2437571239: On December 26, 2015, LIGO's twin detectors caught a second chirp: GW151226, the merger of two stellar-mass black holes totaling about 22 suns. This 2016 Physical Review Letters paper reports the detection at 03:38:53 UTC, confirming the first signal was no fluke. Gravitational-wave astronomy had its second event — and a growing catalog of colliding black holes.
openalex-w2555590239: Who cleared eastern Bolivia's forests, where, when, and how much? This research article by Killeen and colleagues — published in Ecology and Society — reconstructs the total historical land-use change in the region. The accounting pins deforestation on its drivers across time, a baseline for understanding one of South America's great forest frontiers.
openalex-w2767215839: Cropland soils could be a giant carbon sponge — if managed right. This 2017 Scientific Reports paper assesses the global potential for sequestering organic carbon in agricultural soils. As both a possible emissions source under warming and a natural sink, soil carbon sits at the center of climate strategy.
openalex-w3025100939: COVID-19 was the century's great public-health emergency — and its psychological toll matched the physical. This 2020 Estudos de Psicologia paper (in Portuguese) examines mental health and psychological interventions amid the pandemic. The work addresses the suffering beyond the virus itself.
openalex-w4411441839: Ytterbium compounds hover between two electron counts. This experimental paper probed Yb3Si5 and Yb3Ge5 with X-ray spectroscopy across temperatures, tracking their intermediate-valence states. The authors mapped how the electronic structure shifts. A spectroscopy study of metals that cannot decide.
openalex-w7204235439: Hospitalized children need dental care too, and neglect can lead to serious complications. This integrative review studies the oral health of children in pediatric hospitals and the factors tied to it. The authors draw on observational research to map the problem. A quiet but important reminder that hospital dentistry protects vulnerable young patients.
openalex-w7205010439: Dengue never went away, but the pandemic scrambled its patterns. This article compares dengue incidence in Itabuna, Bahia, before, during, and after COVID-19, looking for shifts in the disease's epidemiological profile. The authors investigate what changed and what might explain it, from disrupted surveillance to altered mosquito ecology. A local case study with a bigger lesson about how pandemics ripple through other diseases.
openalex-w7206186239: Ear infections are usually minor, but in rare cases suppurative otitis media kills. This study counts those deaths across Brazil from 2016 to 2025, breaking them down by sex and age group using national health data. The time-series design reveals who is most at risk and whether the toll is rising or falling. A sober piece of epidemiology that turns a supposedly routine illness into a measurable public-health question.
phrenology-proved-illustrated-and-applie: Phrenology Proved, Illustrated, and Applied, 1839. The proved phrenology. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
plos-pbio-0020139:
Adam Amsterdam, Kirsten C. Sadler, Kevin Lai, and a large team screened zebrafish genes in PLOS Biology in 2004. They broke genes one by one to see which ones cause cancer when lost. To their surprise, many of the hits were genes for ribosomal proteins, the parts of the cell's protein-making machines.

A broken ribosomal protein gene can lead to tumors, a link also seen in some human syndromes. The screen found this class again and again, far more than chance would suggest. That breadth makes the claim strong. The work raised a fresh question for cancer biology: how does a fault in the basic protein factory push a cell toward uncontrolled growth?
plos-pbio-0020239:
Michael J. Galko and Mark A. Krasnow analyzed wound healing in fruit fly larvae in PLOS Biology in 2004. A cut in the larva's skin closes as cells around the wound stretch and move. The authors used genetics to find which genes that closing process needs.

Their study breaks healing into steps and names genes for each step, from first response to final seal. Fly larvae are simple enough to watch cell by cell, yet their healing shares parts with our own. A clean parts list lets other labs test single genes and single steps. Wound healing gone wrong causes chronic sores in people, so basic maps like this one have long term medical value.
plos-pone-0000039:
Mel Slater, Angus Antley, Adam Davison, and co-authors restaged one of psychology's most troubling experiments inside virtual reality in 2006. Stanley Milgram had shown in the 1960s that ordinary people would deliver what they believed were painful shocks when an authority figure ordered it. Repeating that with real people and real-seeming pain is no longer acceptable.

Their virtual reprise replaced the victim with a computer character, and participants knew it was not real. Even so, the setup let the team watch obedience, hesitation, and stress in a setting no ethics board would allow with a human victim. The study opened a way to study harmful obedience safely, and raised fresh questions about how real virtual people feel.
plos-pone-0000139:
Nitchakarn Noranate, Rémy Durand, Adama Tall, and colleagues published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tracks Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, and its growing resistance to antimalarial drugs. The worrying point, stated in the title, is that resistance spread fast even where drug use was strictly controlled.

Controlled use is supposed to slow resistance down. The authors document a case where it did not, at least not enough. That result warns malaria programs that careful prescribing alone may not save a failing drug. It also presses the case for monitoring resistance wherever these medicines are deployed.
plos-pone-0000239:
Ewan Thomas Macleod, Alistair Charles Darby, Ian Maudlin, and colleagues published this parasitology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Trypanosomes are the parasites behind sleeping sickness, carried by tsetse flies. The authors study factors affecting how the parasites mature inside the fly, a required stage before they can infect people.

Only mature parasites in the fly can pass to a human bite victim. Knowing what speeds or slows maturation helps predict transmission and may suggest ways to block it in the fly. The work is part of the long campaign against a disease that has shaped life across central Africa.
plos-pone-0000339:
Jeff Shrager, Richard Waldinger, Mark Stickel, and colleagues published this computing paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, introducing deductive biocomputing. The idea is to use formal deduction, step-by-step logical proof, as a computing method for biology. A system can then reason over biological knowledge and derive answers the way a theorem prover does.

Biology drowns in data but much of its knowledge sits in logical relationships. A deductive approach aims to chain those relationships automatically. The paper is a position and systems piece, arguing for logic-based tools alongside the statistics that dominate bioinformatics.
plos-pone-0000439:
Alberto Mazzoni and colleagues analyzed the chatter of neurons with no task at hand, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Even at rest, neuronal networks fire in spontaneous activity, patterns once dismissed as background noise. The team studied the dynamics of that activity, how the patterns form, spread, and change over time.

Spontaneous firing may rehearse the network's repertoire and keep its connections tuned. Its dynamics also reveal the network's built-in wiring rules, visible only when no stimulus is driving it. The study belongs to a shift in neuroscience toward treating rest activity as structured and meaningful rather than as static.
plos-pone-0000539:
Jordi Figuerola tracked how far shorebirds spread in dry versus wet years, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The birds are black-winged stilts, long-legged waders of shallow wetlands. Figuerola found that climate and dispersal are linked. Stilts disperse further in dry springs, when local wetlands shrink and young birds must travel on.

When local wetlands dry, young birds must travel farther to find breeding sites, spreading genes and colonizing new areas. Dispersal distance shapes how species respond to shifting climates. A clear year-to-year effect like this gives climate-change ecology a measured behavior, not just a projection, to build on.
plos-pone-0000639:
Craig R. White, Norman Day, Patrick J. Butler and colleagues asked how great cormorants actually find their food, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cormorants are pursuit-diving birds, widely seen as guided by vision while hunting underwater. They also post the highest known foraging yield of any marine predator. That success often puts them in conflict with human fishing interests.

The title poses the comparison sharply: more like herons than hawks? Herons strike from stillness, while hawks chase in open air. Testing what cormorant vision can and cannot do underwater reshapes which hunting style fits. Bird biologists and fisheries managers both have stakes in the answer.
plos-pone-0000739:
Tomas Knapen, Raymond van Ee and Randolph Blake watched the brain's visual tug-of-war move across the cortex, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In binocular rivalry, the two eyes see conflicting images, and perception alternates between them. One percept replaces the other not all at once but as a traveling wave sweeping across space. Such waves are a general way nervous systems switch states.

Their title adds a driver: stimulus motion propels those traveling waves. Moving the images sets the waves in motion and steers them. Vision scientists care because rivalry waves expose how the brain settles competition between signals, a process at work in everyday seeing.
plos-pone-0000839:
Bernardo V. Alvarez, Gregory S. Gilmour, Silvina C. Mema and colleagues showed that losing an acid-handling protein in the eye causes blindness. Vision begins with phototransduction in the outer retina, where photoreceptors' high metabolic rate generates large carbon dioxide loads. Inner retina cells then process both the visual signal and that CO2. The AE3 gene encodes a chloride/bicarbonate exchanger that moves acid equivalents out of cells.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE title states the consequence plainly: deficiency in the AE3 exchanger causes blindness. A waste-disposal failure in the retina is a surprising cause of vision loss. It points genetic screening for inherited blindness toward an ion transport gene.
plos-pone-0000939:
Christopher Beck and Daniel Promislow examined why females in some species prefer younger males, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. Older theory said females should pick older males, since survivors ought to be fitter than average. Yet in humans and lab species, males lose quality as they age, through damage built up over life.

That decline flips the prediction. Beck and Promislow set out the case for a female preference for younger males. Mate choice shapes how traits evolve, so getting its direction right matters. The paper also shows how a neat theory can fail once aging itself is priced in.
plos-pone-0001039:
Frans Walther, Alan Waring, Jose Hernandez-Juviel and colleagues tested a fully synthetic lung surfactant, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Surfactant is the slippery coating that keeps air sacs open in the lungs. Natural versions can be broken down by phospholipase enzymes during lung injury.

Their synthetic version pairs a new phospholipid built to resist that breakdown with a short peptide modeled on surfactant protein B. The team examined its surface activity and resistance to degradation. A synthetic surfactant could be made in steady supply, unlike animal derived versions. Premature infants and injured lungs are the patients who need it most.
plos-pone-0001139:
When a stream is broken into fragments by barriers, the fish inside each piece live apart. Benjamin Letcher and colleagues studied that situation in a 2007 PLOS ONE article on stream-dwelling brook trout. Fragmentation can strongly shape whether a population persists and how its life history plays out.

The team directly estimated dispersal, growth, and survival by fish size within a stream network containing connected and isolated stretches. Measuring all three at once gives a fuller picture than tracking movement alone. Their work shows how a population responds, in concrete numbers, when its habitat is chopped into pieces.
plos-pone-0001239:
Sex determination in fruit flies of the tephritid family, which includes major crop pests, is governed by a gene called transformer. María Fernanda Ruiz and colleagues traced that gene's evolution across insects, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. In the Mediterranean fruit fly and the olive fly, transformer acts as the memory device for sex determination. Working Tra protein is made only in females.

The authors investigate the Anastrepha fruit flies and compare the gene's history across insect groups. How a master sex switch evolves matters for pest control strategies that release sterile or all-male flies.
plos-pone-0001339:
Natural killer cells patrol the body for transformed cells, and receptors called NKp30 and NKp44 help switch on their attack. Andreina Byrd and colleagues analyzed expression of the ligands for these receptors, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Ligands are the surface molecules the receptors recognize; knowing which cells display them matters for rational design of NK-based therapies.

The authors map where the ligands for the natural cytotoxicity receptors appear, on normal and neoplastic cells. If tumor cells display them more than healthy cells do, the receptors can be exploited. Their expression analysis is groundwork for immunotherapy design.
plos-pone-0001439:
Brian Huntley and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how climate change may shift where European breeding birds live. As climate shifts, species ranges are set to move. Plans to guard wild life need hard counts of how far and how fast. The team modeled range shifts for the region's breeding birds.

Their models give the scale, course, and pace of likely shifts bird by bird. Some birds gain ground while others lose it sharply. Such counts are of most value when they can guide real choices. Park and reserve plans can use them to keep guarding birds as their ranges move north or uphill.
plos-pone-0001539:
Delphine Pages and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a soil germ that shrugs off metals. The germ lives widely in soil and water and resists many germ drugs by nature. One strain also bears high levels of toxic metals, from a tenth to fifty units in tests. The team asked how it holds up under that load.

They probed the genes and traits that let the germ bear metals that kill most kin. Such grit makes the germ a survivor in harsh, tainted sites. It could serve in clean up of metal waste. It also warns that drug grit and metal grit can travel as a pair.
plos-pone-0001639:
Ji-Yeon Lee and co-authors studied how signals in the brain and pituitary gland control body weight, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The signals pass through a protein pair called STAT5, which carries messages from cytokines, a group of immune and hormone-like messengers. STAT5 is switched on in nerve cells in the hypothalamus, a brain region that helps set hunger and energy use.

When the team removed this signaling in the central nervous system and pituitary gland of mice, the animals' energy balance shifted and they became obese. The full text gives the weight and feeding data and the hormone changes they recorded. The results point to a brain pathway that drug and diet research on obesity needs to take into account.
plos-pone-0001739:
Mikael Åkesson, Staffan Bensch, Dennis Hasselquist, and their co-authors compared two ways to estimate heredity in wild animals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Heritability and genetic correlations guide predictions of how traits evolve. The animal model, a statistical method using full pedigrees, had largely replaced parent-offspring regression, yet the two had rarely been tested on the same data.

Using data from a natural population, the team ran both methods on equivalent data sets and compared the estimates. The full text gives the trait values and where the methods agree or diverge. Field biologists stake evolutionary forecasts on these numbers, so knowing which method to trust, and when, is a practical result.
plos-pone-0001839:
Seyed M. Moghadas, Christopher S. Bowman, and Gergely Röst modeled antiviral resistance in a flu pandemic in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Resistance to the main flu drugs raised concerns about careful use of antiviral drugs in the next influenza pandemic. Resistant strains may start off weaker, but later mutations can restore much of that lost fitness.

The team modeled how resistance spreads during a pandemic under different drug use plans. The full text gives the scenarios and the timelines. Stockpiled antivirals are a central flu plan. If heavy use breeds resistance fast, planners must weigh treatment against prophylaxis with that risk included.
plos-pone-0001939:
Adam Wasserstrom and co-authors built family trees of cells inside mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Every cell in a body descends from the first cell, the zygote, by a long chain of divisions. That chain forms a lineage tree, which, if it could be read, would show how tissues are built.

A new method reads small mutations that pile up in cells over time and treats them like the marks used to build species trees. The team used it to rebuild parts of the cell tree in mice at fine detail. Such trees can reveal when lines split in growth, and where odd growth in disease begins.
plos-pone-0002039:
Benoit Smagghe, James Trent, and Mark Hargrove tested a chemical trick found across blood proteins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Genome work has turned up hundreds of new hemoglobins, found in nearly every kind of living thing. Lab tests of many of them show the same reactions, such as binding oxygen and a reaction that breaks down nitric oxide, called NO dioxygenation.

As the title states, that NO reaction is ubiquitous in the test tube. But in living cells it is limited by how fast the protein can be reset by reduction. A common talent, throttled in life: the gap warns against reading test-tube results as body truth.
plos-pone-0002139:
Seung-Chul Kim and co-authors traced how plant life spread and split into new species across Atlantic islands, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Macaronesia covers five island groups: the Azores, Canaries, Madeira, Cape Verde, and the Savage Islands. Its plant life is rich, with many species found nowhere else on Earth.

Island chains like these are natural labs for studying how new species arise. The team studied the timing and pace of adaptive radiations, bursts where one ancestor splits into many species fitted to local niches. Their timeline helps explain how a few arriving plants gave rise to whole floras across scattered islands.
plos-pone-0002239:
Sigal Rencus-Lazar, Yaniv Amir, Junetai Wu, and co-authors studied a cancer-linked gene in the fruit fly, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The gene Int6 is a proto-oncogene, a normal gene that can help drive cancer when it misbehaves. Its protein is part of the machine that starts protein building, and it also interacts with the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder.

How Int6 does its work was unclear. The team reports that Int6 is essential for neddylation, a tagging process that activates two proteins, Cul1 and Cul3, in Drosophila. Those proteins help choose which cell proteins get destroyed. The link places Int6 at a control point for protein turnover.
plos-pone-0002339:
Huiyi Chen, Bin Liu, Thomas Lukas, and co-authors profiled the aging tissue at the back of the eye, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Age is the greatest risk factor for age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of blindness in older people. Yet the cellular and molecular reasons why age matters so much are not generally known.

The team studied the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid, the layers that feed and support the light-sensing retina, as they age. Changes there may form the substratum, the ground in which macular degeneration takes root. Mapping the aging of this support tissue tells drug hunters where the disease truly begins.
plos-pone-0002439:
Miozzi joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Laura Miozzi, Rosario Michael Piro, Fabio Rosa, among others. Its subject is functional Annotation and Identification of Candidate Disease Genes by Computational Analysis of Normal Tissue Gene Expression Data. High-throughput gene expression data can predict gene function through the “guilt by association” principle: coexpressed genes are likely to be functionally linked.

We analyzed publicly available expression data on normal human tissues. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002539:
Esposito led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Irene Esposito, Diana Born, Frank Bergmann, among others. Its subject is autoimmune Pancreatocholangitis, Non-Autoimmune Pancreatitis and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis: A Comparative Morphological and Immunological Analysis. Autoimmune pancreatocholangitis (AIPC) is an emerging, not completely characterized disease.

Aim of this study was the comprehensive evaluation of a series of AIPC patients. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002639:
Y. Jeffrey Chiang and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was tankyrase 1 and tankyrase 2 are essential but redundant for mouse embryonic development. Authorship is credited in the record to Y. Jeffrey Chiang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Tankyrases are proteins with poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase activity. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002739:
David T. S. Hayman and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on evidence of henipavirus infection in west african fruit bats. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David T. S. Hayman, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Henipaviruses are emerging RNA viruses of fruit bat origin that can cause fatal encephalitis in man. It goes on to note a further point. Ghanaian fruit bats (megachiroptera) were tested for antibodies to henipaviruses. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002839:
A 2008 study by Sheila G. Crewther and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up potassium channel and NKCC cotransporter involvement in ocular refractive control mechanisms. The catalog record names Sheila G. Crewther first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Myopia affects well over 30% of adult humans globally. It goes on to note a further point. However, the underlying physiological mechanism is little understood. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002939:
Mbemba Jabbi, Jojanneke Bastiaansen and Christian Keysers scanned brains around disgust in 2008. Similar areas light up when we act, watch an act, or picture one, and the team asked whether feelings behave the same way. They focused on gustatory disgust, the revolting taste response.

The same subjects were scanned while they felt disgust, watched another person feel it, and imagined it. A shared area in the front insula took part in all three, while its connections diverged by condition. Published in PLOS ONE, the study refines how shared feeling is built in the brain.
plos-pone-0003039:
Nicholas Graham, Tim McClanahan, M. Aaron MacNeil and co-authors studied warming, protected areas, and coral reefs in 2008. Coral reefs are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate change. Warming's role in loss of live coral cover was well documented at large scales, while effects on reef fish were less settled.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team assesses ocean-scale integrity of reef ecosystems and what marine protected areas can preserve under warming. Protection cannot stop heat, but it may keep food webs intact. The study helps managers judge what reserves can and cannot do.
plos-pone-0003139:
Corrado Di Natale, Eugenio Martinelli, Roberto Paolesse and colleagues describe a test platform for artificial smell in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Artificial olfactory systems had been studied for two decades, mostly through the response patterns of smell receptors. Other basic traits of natural smell had only rarely been built into such systems, leaving current devices limited.

The team present an experimental platform that copies biology more closely, a biomimetic approach. Readers see an attempt to close the gap between machine sensors and a real nose. Such work matters for chemical sensing, food checks, and medical breath tests, where better smell tools are still needed.
plos-pone-0003239:
Vicente Sentandreu, Nuria Jiménez-Hernández, Manuela Torres-Puente and colleagues look for recombination in hepatitis C virus in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis C virus is a major cause of liver disease worldwide and a potential cause of substantial morbidity and mortality in the future. The virus is characterized by a high level of genetic heterogeneity. Homologous recombination had been demonstrated in many virus families.

The team present evidence of recombination in populations of the virus within a single patient. Readers see new viral variants arising not just by mutation but by mixing. Recombination can speed adaptation to drugs and immunity, which complicates treatment planning.
plos-pone-0003339:
Mai T. Q. Le, Heiman F. L. Wertheim, Hien D. Nguyen and colleagues report a virus shift in Vietnam in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Prior to 2007, highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 viruses isolated from poultry and humans in Vietnam were consistently reported to be clade 1 viruses, susceptible to oseltamivir but resistant to amantadine. The team describe re-emergence of human H5N1 virus with different traits.

Their title reports that clade 2.3.4 virus, with a different antiviral susceptibility profile, replaced clade 1 virus in humans in northern Vietnam. Readers see drug planning change with viral lineage. Surveillance of clades is essential for vaccine and stockpile decisions.
plos-pone-0003439:
Shih-Lei Lai and co-authors studied cell movement in early embryos in this 2008 paper. During gastrulation, embryo cells stream into new layers. That motion depends on actin, a protein that builds moving scaffolds inside cells. A regulator called Diaphanous helps direct actin assembly.

The team tested one formin, Diaphanous-related formin 2, plus profilin I. Both proved required for normal gastrulation cell movements. Without them, the embryo's early reshaping faltered. The work names key parts of the engine behind a basic step of life. Errors at this stage can end development before organs even form, which makes its machinery a basic research target.
plos-pone-0003539:
Matthew Heath, Anika Maraj, and Bryan Godbolt tested reaching without awareness in this 2008 study. Their title states the puzzle plainly: action without awareness. Volunteers reached for objects they did not remember seeing. Memory of the object and control of the hand came apart.

Accurate reaching showed the hand used visual data the mind forgot. Two visual streams may split knowing from doing. One stream serves conscious recognition, the other guides movement. The study catches that split in a simple lab task. Such tasks help map the split between seeing and doing in brain injury.
plos-pone-0003639:
Traci Mouw, Annemarie Koster, Margaret E. Wright, and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It asks whether the amount of schooling a person has relates to their risk of cancer. The authors used a large cohort of men and women in the United States.

They compared cancer rates across levels of education within that cohort. Education can stand in for income, work, habits, and access to care, all of which shape health. A study this size can show whether schooling tracks with cancer risk in the population as a whole.
plos-pone-0003739:
Jean N. Manirarora, Michele M. Kosiewicz, Sarah A. Parnell, and colleagues published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2008. NOD mice develop diabetes much like human type 1 diabetes. Their antigen-presenting cells fail to switch on regulatory T cells properly, and those peacekeeper cells keep the immune system from attacking the body.

The team found that activating the antigen-presenting cells restores working regulatory T cells. The revived cells, marked CD4 and CD25, could prevent diabetes from developing in the mice. The rescue points to immune retraining as a path against this autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0003839:
Xu Wang, Qi Sun, Sean D. McGrath, and colleagues published this genomics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Imprinted genes are active from only one parent's copy, depending on which parent passed them down. The strength of imprinting varies by tissue and stage, and it can go wrong in disease. The newborn mouse brain was unmapped territory.

The team scanned the whole transcriptome of neonatal mouse brain for imprinted genes. They identified novel imprinted genes beyond those already known. The brain-wide map expands the catalog of genes where a mother's and a father's copies are not treated as equal.
plos-pone-0003939:
Andrew Gallagher rechecked claims of tiny ancient humans from Palau in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Recent finds on the Pacific islands of Palau were said to be small-bodied humans. Some claimed the bones show island shrinking of body size. That claim had not yet faced a statistical test.

Gallagher assessed sixteen published limb bone specimens from Palau. He compared them with recent small-bodied human samples. Careful measurement can separate true island dwarfing from normal variation. The study urges caution before naming a new kind of small human. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004039:
Lynne A. Murray, Tillie L. Hackett, Stephanie M. Warner, and co-authors tested a growth factor against scarring in 2008. BMP-7 belongs to a family of growth factors in the TGF-beta superfamily. It had been reported to block kidney scarring. It also reportedly blocked a cell change that drives tissue fibrosis.

Their PLOS ONE article reports BMP-7 did not protect lung or skin. The damage agent was bleomycin, a drug that induces fibrosis. Negative findings matter where hopes for a therapy run high. They caution against assuming one organ's result transfers to others. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004139:
Sandeep Kumar, Aisha Farhana, and Seyed Hasnain published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the germ that causes tuberculosis, can sit quietly in the body for years in a low-activity state before waking to cause disease. To copy itself, the germ must first unwind its DNA at a start site called oriC.

Working with purified parts in the lab, the team shows that the DnaA protein opens the DNA helix at one precise spot in oriC. They also show that a protein resembling IciA blocks that opening. The result pinpoints a first step in how the germ starts copying its DNA, a step drugs might one day target.
plos-pone-0004239:
Peng Xu, Min Shi, and Xue-xin Chen published this bee study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Asiatic honey bee, Apis cerana, is an important honey bee across Asia. It still lives wild yet is also one of the few bee species people can domesticate, and it carries genetic advantages over its western cousin.

The authors traced the evolution of its antimicrobial peptides, small proteins that kill microbes and form a first line of immune defence. Comparing these peptides across bees shows how the weapons changed as the species adapted. The work adds an Asian chapter to the study of insect immunity.
plos-pone-0004339:
Suhail Asrar and colleagues published this synaptic study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Calcium enters through GluR2-lacking AMPA receptors, a calcium-permeable form of the main excitatory receptor. It can trigger long-lasting changes in synaptic strength in both interneurons and principal neurons. How it works remained unknown. Interneurons are the local circuit cells between main neurons.

Using genetically altered mice with weak or missing versions of these receptors, the team mapped the needed pathways. They report that this long-term potentiation requires PI3 and MAP kinases but not CaMKII. Separating which enzymes are needed maps the chemistry of a memory-like change.
plos-pone-0004439:
Harm caused by medicines given in hospital is the subject of a 2009 PLOS ONE study by Emma Davies, Christopher Green, Stephen Taylor, and co-authors. Bad drug reactions are a major reason people end up in hospital. Less was known about reactions that start after a patient is already admitted.

The team followed patients on twelve wards over six months in 2005, covering thousands of patient episodes. They recorded each bad reaction, its cause, and its effect on care. Fresh counts like these show how large the problem is inside hospital walls, not just at the door. They also help hospitals target the drugs and habits that put in-patients most at risk.
plos-pone-0004539:
Yeast can be used to hunt for the toxic form of amyloid, the protein clumps tied to several diseases. Julien Couthouis, Karine Rebora, Francoise Immel, and co-authors show how in PLOS ONE in 2009. Since amyloid structures were found in different diseases, the link between the clumps and the toxic species has been a central problem. Despite intense work, the harmful species is still unknown at the molecular level.

One reason may be the lack of a structure-based way to find it. The authors set up a screen in yeast that exemplifies an alternative pathway responsible for cytotoxicity. Yeast is cheap and fast to screen in bulk. If its toxic species mirrors the one in human disease, the screen could point to what actually kills cells.
plos-pone-0004639:
Chains of signals travel through cells at speeds set by the chain's design, show Christopher Govern and Arup Chakraborty in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells are not mixed bags of signaling molecules. A signal must travel from its origin to distant locations inside the cell. Much is understood about purely diffusive propagation, signals drifting like scent in still air.

Many signals, however, propagate via signaling cascades, relay chains of proteins that activate each other. The authors show cascades modulate the speed of signal propagation through space. A relay can move a message faster, or hold it back, compared with diffusion alone. For cell engineering and drug design, knowing the speed rules helps predict how a cell will answer a signal in time.
plos-pone-0004739:
Ravi Akundi and Scott Rivkees showed that low oxygen changes cell cycle proteins and rushes early brain cell growth, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Injury to white matter is a common brain harm in babies born too early. Low oxygen is a major factor that sets up that injury in the newborn period.

Cells that later wrap nerve fibers in insulation are at risk in this window. The team found low oxygen shifts their cycle controls and pushes them to mature too soon. Early forced growth may leave insulation thin or flawed. The work helps explain lasting harm after early birth.
plos-pone-0004839:
Jacqueline Schmuckli-Maurer and colleagues analyzed output of the Theileria parva subtelomere encoded variable secreted protein family, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The intracellular protozoan parasite transforms bovine lymphocytes, inducing uncontrolled growth. Proteins released from the parasite are assumed to help to host cell changes and parasite persistence. With eighty five members in genes encoding secreted proteins representing a large variable family.

Output patterns vary across family members and stages. Variable secretion may aid immune evasion. The parasite causes East Coast fever in cattle. Knowledge transformation could yield control methods. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004939:
Biologists would love to read a cell's chemical wiring from measurements. That task is called reverse engineering. Edgar Delgado-Eckert examined its feasibility in PLOS ONE in 2009. He focused on models called time-discrete finite dynamical systems. Interest in the approach had grown with high-throughput profiling.

He stress-tested a top-down algorithm by Laubenbacher and Stigler. The algorithm rebuilds biochemical networks from data. His analysis maps where the method works and where it breaks. The verdict helps researchers judge rebuilt networks. It shows what extra information a reliable reconstruction needs.
plos-pone-0005039:
Candida albicans is a yeast that lives in human mouths. It turns harmful when immunity drops. Mouth candidiasis is a warning sign of AIDS. Timothy Meiller and colleagues found a new evasion trick in PLOS ONE in 2009. Saliva carries antimicrobial peptides that kill germs. Candida cuts one of them apart.

The yeast uses its own enzymes for the cutting. This proteolytic cleavage destroys the peptide's protection. The sabotage disarms the mouth's first line of defense. It helps explain how the fungus colonizes mucosal surfaces. The work names a fresh target for antifungal thinking. Blocking the cutting enzymes could restore saliva's natural guard.
plos-pone-0005139:
A good TB vaccine must rally the right T cells. Helper CD4 cells are crucial for defense. Whether killer CD8 cells are also needed was unclear. Tara Elvang and colleagues compared vaccine strategies in PLOS ONE in 2009. All carried two TB antigens, Ag85B and TB10.4. The strategies differed: adjuvanted subunit, adenovector, or heterologous prime-boost.

The team measured both CD4 and CD8 responses to the antigens. The comparison shows which approach builds the strongest balanced response. A balanced army may protect best. The work guides the design of next-generation TB vaccines. TB still kills over a million people yearly. Small design choices in trials like this one shape the vaccines that reach clinics.
plos-pone-0005239:
Coral reefs worldwide are degrading under warming seas, overfishing, disease, and nutrient pollution. Diaz-Pulido and colleagues followed one reef through damage and recovery, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 under the apt frame of doom and boom.

Warming caused bleaching, algae then overgrew the reef, and yet corals later recovered. A reef that bounces back shows which conditions favor resilience. Tracking the full cycle gives conservationists concrete lessons about what helps reefs survive the next warming event. Most reefs do not get a second chance in this way, so the few that do are worth close study while the recovery is still fresh.
plos-pone-0005339:
Foods that pack many calories into each gram can promote overeating in lab studies. Whether dietary energy density predicts long-term weight change in free-living people was less clear. Du and colleagues followed European men and women prospectively, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study related the energy density of people's diets to later changes in weight and waist size. Waist change matters because belly fat carries the highest health risk. Evidence from daily life, not just labs, is what dietary guidelines are built on. Waist size tracks the fat that does most harm, so a link to waist gain, not just to weight, gives food advice a sharper aim for men and women alike.
plos-pone-0005439:
Pauline Leclerc, Alan Matthews, and Michel Garenne modelled the HIV epidemic in Zambia in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Earlier models of how HIV spreads in African countries often skipped the exact times when each person was at risk. That gap can blur who spreads the virus and when.

Their model follows single people, male and female, through their lives and risks. It was fitted to match the known course of the epidemic in Zambia. A model that tracks real risk periods can help planners judge which steps against HIV are most likely to work.
plos-pone-0005539:
Amy Murphy, Paul Guyre, and Charles Wira studied a hormone effect on immune cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Macrophages are front-line immune cells that release signals when they sense danger. The female hormone estradiol directly shapes how these cells behave.

The team studied how the hormone controls one form of its own receptor in human macrophages. That receptor form can change how strongly the hormone acts on immune responses. Knowing the control loop helps explain sex differences in infection and in diseases of inflammation. Sex differences in immunity are large and often unexplained, and hormone control loops like this one help explain them.
plos-pone-0005639:
Casey Greene, Nadia Penrod, and Scott Williams argued that failed replications in gene studies can still teach, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Genome-wide studies are judged by whether their findings repeat in new samples. That standard is strict, and real effects can be missed because of it.

The authors list the many reasons a true result may fail to repeat, from small samples to real differences between groups. They urge readers to mine failures for clues about how genes act. A failed repeat is data, not just disappointment. Their argument favours reporting failures openly, since hidden failures waste the next team's samples and funds.
plos-pone-0005739:
Ilana DeLuca and co-authors probed in 2009 why the immune system usually leaves a brain protein alone, until it suddenly does not. In the Hu syndrome, tumors trigger an immune attack on HuD, a protein found only in neurons. The attack can badly harm the nervous system.

Old experiments suggest the brain hides its proteins from immune patrols. The team tested how tolerance to HuD is kept, and how cancer breaks it. Their work uses the syndrome as a window on a broad question: how the body avoids attacking the brain. The answer bears on autoimmune disease and cancer care alike.
plos-pone-0005839:
Donald Anderson and Patrick Stover showed in 2009 that two related enzymes back each other up in making a DNA building block. Making thymidylate, the T of DNA, takes a three-enzyme pathway that moves into the nucleus during DNA copying. Two members of that team are near-twins, SHMT1 and SHMT2.

The team demonstrated the twins are functionally redundant for nuclear thymidylate synthesis. Losing one does not cripple DNA production because the other covers. Redundancy explains why single-gene faults here are rare in disease. It also tells drug designers that both enzymes may need blocking to starve fast-growing cells.
plos-pone-0005939:
About one ovarian cancer in ten is thought to run in families. Bamidele Tayo, Richard DiCioccio, Yulan Liang and colleagues asked how that risk passes down, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They used family records from the Gilda Radner registry, a collection built to study inherited ovarian cancer.

Their analysis of the family trees found a pattern that fits a dominant pattern of inheritance, as if one major gene copy can pass the risk on. That shape matters for how doctors counsel families and whom they watch most closely. The study gives the registry's rich records a clear use: sharper risk advice for the next generation.
plos-pone-0006039:
Clear cell cancer is the most common cancer of the adult kidney, yet its course varies wildly between patients. Hongjuan Zhao, Zongming Ma, Robert Tibshirani and colleagues hunted the gene patterns behind the worst cases in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper profiles gene activity in these tumors, building on a set of transcripts already known to predict survival after kidney removal.

In lethal tumors, two signature programs were altered: one for cortical differentiation, the kidney's mature identity, and one for wound response. A tumor that has lost its tissue identity and runs a wound program nonstop may be primed to kill. The patterns could guide prognosis and point treatment toward the programs that matter most.
plos-pone-0006139:
A pig pathogen must survive the lung's first wash of defenses to cause disease. Abdul Lone, Vincent Deslandes, John Nash and colleagues watched it adapt in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper exposes Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae, the cause of contagious pleuropneumonia in swine worldwide, to bronchoalveolar fluid, the liquid lining the lung, and measures how its gene expression shifts.

Genes that answer lung fluid are likely the tools of early infection. Reading that answer tells vets and vaccine makers where the germ is tender. Swine pneumonia costs farms heavily across the world, so a gene-level view of the first hours of infection has direct economic as well as scientific worth.
plos-pone-0006239:
Faces are hard to read, for people and machines alike, so psychologists use careful test tasks. Qi Zhu and colleagues put one such task under the microscope in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The part task, from the part-spacing paradigm, was meant to measure how much people use separate face parts.

The team shows the task is not a pure measure of part-based information. Other cues leak into the scores it gives. Impure measures can mislead theories of how faces are recognised. The paper helps labs choose and interpret face tests with more care.
plos-pone-0006339:
One enzyme both senses DNA damage and helps decide whether a stressed cell lives or dies. Ben Buelow and colleagues dissected PARP-1 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme responds to oxidative and nitrosative stress by building ADPR chains on proteins, and it also forms single ADPR units.

Their structure and function analysis maps which parts of PARP-1 produce the single-unit form under stress. Separating the two outputs clarifies the enzyme's fork-in-the-road role. PARP blockers are used in cancer care, so fine mechanism matters. The study guides how those drugs might be refined.
plos-pone-0006439:
Ruggero D'Anastasio and co-authors examined a very old skeleton from Sterkfontein, South Africa, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The partial skeleton, known as Stw 431, belongs to Australopithecus africanus, a late Pliocene early human relative. An earlier study had read marks on its spine bones as a wear condition called spondylosis deformans. The new team re-examined the bones for signs of disease.

Their title raises a striking possibility: the lesions may reflect brucellosis, an infection still known today. If so, disease shaped life long before modern humans. Reading illness in fossil bones is hard, and the claim is framed as possible. The study shows how much care such claims require.
plos-pone-0006539:
George Cerniglia and co-authors studied a cancer drug and the tissue around tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Drugs that block the EGFR growth signal have shown only modest effects when used alone against cancer. The team asked how EGFR blockade changes the tumor microenvironment, the mix of cells and vessels around a tumor. They focused on blood vessels.

Blocking EGFR can make tumor vessels more normal, a change called vascular normalization. More normal vessels may carry drugs and oxygen to the tumor in a better way. That in turn can help radiation and other drugs work. The study looks past the cancer cell to its whole setting.
plos-pone-0006639:
Hendrik Wilking, Mario Ziller, Christoph Staubach, and colleagues evaluated wild bird monitoring for bird flu in PLOS ONE in 2009. Highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5N1 proved remarkably mobile in migratory bird populations. It led to extensive outbreaks for which the true number of cases is unclear. Monitoring wild birds is a main surveillance strategy.

The authors assess chances and limitations of wild bird monitoring for H5N1. Detection of pathogens hides behind sampling biases: sick birds are easier to find than healthy carriers. Honest evaluation helps agencies spend surveillance money where it works. It also prevents false reassurance from weak monitoring.
plos-pone-0006739:
Gertjan S. Verhoeven and colleagues displayed short peptides on the surface of bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Displaying peptides on bacteria is a workhorse technique in biotechnology. Peptides sit inside a scaffold protein of the outer membrane. The scaffold here was OmpA, a common bacterial surface protein. The team inserted known antibody tags into its exposed loops.

They compared display using different parts of the OmpA membrane domain. The tags were the well-known 3xFLAG and 2xmyc epitopes. Some designs showed the peptides to antibodies better than others. Knowing which design displays best improves library screening. It also improves bacterial systems built to present antigens or bind targets.
plos-pone-0006839:
Polloneal Jymmiel R. Ocbina, Miquel Tuson, and Kathryn V. Anderson tested whether cilia are needed for a key embryo signal in PLOS ONE in 2009. Primary cilia are small antenna-like structures on cells. In mouse embryos, sonic hedgehog signaling requires the cilium. Cilia are built and maintained by intraflagellar transport proteins. Mutants lacking those proteins cannot answer hedgehog signals.

The authors asked whether canonical Wnt signaling also needs cilia. Their answer was no. Embryos without normal cilia still ran Wnt signaling properly. The negative result separates the two great developmental pathways. It tells researchers which signaling defects to expect in cilia disorders.
plos-pone-0006939:
Patrick Sénéchal, Geneviève Arseneault, Alexandre Leroux, and colleagues studied a yeast prion in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein chaperone Hsp104 helps yeast survive heat stress. Its disaggregase activity rescues misfolded proteins by pulling them apart. Hsp104 also helps propagate fungal prions, the self-copying protein states.

The team tested the fission yeast version of Hsp104 against a famous prion called [PSI+]. They found this Hsp104 unable to propagate that prion. The negative result is informative. It shows that prion propagation rules differ between yeast species, and it sharpens models of how chaperones handle misfolded proteins.
plos-pone-0007039:
M. Melissa Gilbert, Brian Robinson, and Kenneth Moberg studied tumor gene teamwork in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. The fly gene erupted is the counterpart of human TSG101. It helps run the ESCRT-1 complex, which routes proteins for disposal. Loss of such genes in fly tissues can grow into tumors of the imaginal discs.

The team tested how erupted interacts with two other genes, DaPKC and rbf1. Genetic teamwork can turn mild defects into strong growth. Their crosses map which combinations push discs toward tumors. Fly genetics like this often previews interactions later found in human cancer.
plos-pone-0007139:
Jeffrey Koehler, Michael Bolton, Amanda Rollins, and colleagues modelled dual infection in monkeys in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria and HIV overlap across sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. Co-infection is therefore a real risk for millions. Studies of HIV with the main human malaria parasite had shown strong interactions. The team built an animal model for relapsing malaria instead.

Rhesus macaques were co-infected with SIV and Plasmodium cynomolgi. Their immune responses differed from single infections. A relapsing malaria model mirrors much African disease better. It lets researchers test vaccines and treatments under realistic dual pressure.
plos-pone-0007239:
Sylvie Rodrigues-Ferreira, Anne Di Tommaso, Ariane Dimitrov, and colleagues reported a protective protein in breast cancer in 2009. Breast cancer is varied, and current therapies do not fully eradicate it. Sorting tumors into molecular subtypes helps doctors predict outcomes and likely treatment responses for patients.

The authors study ATIP3, a product of the MTUS1 gene on chromosome region 8p22. They describe ATIP3 as a new anti-mitotic protein, meaning it restrains cell division. They report it is underexpressed in invasive breast cancers with poor prognosis. Low levels may mark tumors needing closer attention.
plos-pone-0007339:
Melody Tsui, Tiao Xie, James D. Orth, and colleagues screened for genes that modify a cancer drug's effects in 2009. Kinesin-5 is a motor protein required to assemble the bipolar mitotic spindle. Its inhibitors, developed as potential anti-cancer drugs, arrest cells in mitosis and promote cancer cell death in dividing cells.

The authors perform a genome-wide siRNA screen with live cell imaging. Imaging is intermittent, balancing detail against cell health. They search for enhancers and suppressors of a kinesin-5 inhibitor. Hits from the screen point to combination treatments and resistance mechanisms for this drug class.
plos-pone-0007439:
Kara Johnson and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on BCR-ABL, the abnormal protein that defines chronic myeloid leukemia. BCR-ABL is an overactive enzyme, and its activity is required to start the disease. It was thought to work by gathering a team of adapter proteins into one complex. The team tested whether those direct partnerships are truly essential.

They built a mutant BCR-ABL that could no longer bind three adapters: GRB2, CBL, and CRKL. The altered protein kept its enzyme activity yet failed to cause leukemia in mice. That failure proves the direct connections are not decoration. They are required steps in how BCR-ABL triggers disease. The result points drug research toward the protein's binding surfaces as well as its enzyme pocket.
plos-pone-0007539:
Francesco Di Serio and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on viroids, the smallest known plant pathogens. A viroid is a naked loop of RNA with no protein coat and no genes for proteins. Infected plants fill with tiny RNAs copied from the viroid, signs of the plant's silencing defense. The team deep-sequenced those small RNAs from two disease-causing variants of a chloroplast viroid.

The sequences showed how the small RNAs arise from each variant. Their patterns also bear on how the viroids cause symptoms. Comparing a mild and a severe variant highlights which RNA pieces track with damage. Minimal pathogens leave few clues, so each pattern counts. The study uses the plant's own defense output as a window into viroid biology. It informs the broader question of how naked RNA can make a plant sick.
plos-pone-0007639:
Kelly Heim and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the rhythm of vitamin A signaling. Retinoic acid, the active form of vitamin A, works through nuclear receptors that switch genes on and off. Those receptors recruit helper complexes in rapid cycles. A coregulator called RIP140 represses receptor activity. The team examined how retinoic acid shapes receptor activity over longer stretches of time in their system.

They found evidence for long-paced oscillations in retinoid receptor activity. RIP140 appears to play a potential role in setting that slow rhythm. A timing layer in gene control means the same signal can mean different things at different hours. That matters for development, where retinoids pattern whole body regions. It also matters for drugs that mimic vitamin A. The study adds tempo to the usual picture of switches.
plos-pone-0007739:
Kevin Miller and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It follows how the pancreas builds its hormone-making clusters in newborn mice. Each cluster, an islet of Langerhans, mixes several cell types. Beta cells make insulin, while alpha cells make glucagon, among others.

How these mixed clusters assemble after birth was poorly mapped. The team traced islet formation through the neonatal period. Their account shows when and where the different cell types come together. Understanding normal islet growth matters for diabetes research, where working beta cells are lost or never form properly.
plos-pone-0007839:
Chin-Hsing Lin and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines how the protein c-Myc reshapes mouse embryonic stem cells. Myc is a transcription regulator tied to many tumor types. It also plays an important role inside stem cells.

Whether Myc has unique targets in stem cells was unclear. The authors mapped its gene regulation there. They also tracked epigenetic remodeling, the chemical changes that open or close DNA. The picture shows Myc steering both gene activity and chromatin state. That dual grip may explain why Myc is so central to growth and cancer.
plos-pone-0007939:
Kouki Fujioka and colleagues tried a new way to sniff out yeast, writing in PLOS ONE in 2009. Wine tasters name smells with rich comparisons, while machines that mimic the nose give plain numbers. The team joined the two styles, pairing true smell values with word pictures.

Blending the two kinds of data helped the system spot yeast more surely than either style alone. The trick borrows from human skill: a good metaphor can carry fine shades of scent that raw numbers miss. The method may help food and drink makers catch spoilage early with cheaper tools.
plos-pone-0008039:
Ragnvi Hagman and colleagues read gene activity in infected dog wombs for PLOS ONE in 2009. Severe womb infection is a common, dangerous illness in female dogs, and it can tip into sepsis, a whole-body crisis. The team compared sick tissue with healthy tissue.

Genes that chew up proteins ran hot in the sick wombs, while genes that pattern and regulate tissue ran cold. That tilt fits a tissue breaking down faster than it can hold form. The readout may help vets spot the worst cases early and may hint at new treatments.
plos-pone-0008139:
Maneesha Chhikara and colleagues showed how carbon monoxide quiets inflamed human blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The body makes small amounts of this gas itself, and it acts as a messenger that damps inflammation. The team exposed monocytes to a bacterial toxin that normally fires a storm of inflammatory genes.

With the gas present, the storm was cut short near its start. The break sat between the toxin sensor TLR4 and the command protein NF-kB. Genome-wide reads confirmed the cut. The precise break point may let drug makers copy the gas's calm without its poison risk.
plos-pone-0008239:
Géraldine Giraud and colleagues tested tumor samples for virus DNA in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Some polyomaviruses can cause cancer, and older types had been linked loosely to brain tumors. Three new polyomaviruses, named KI, WU, and Merkel cell, had recently been found. The team asked whether their DNA appears in childhood tumors. They checked central nervous system tumors and neuroblastomas.

No DNA from the three viruses was detected in those samples. A clear negative result still matters in a field full of hints. It narrows the search for viral causes of these childhood cancers. Future work can focus on other candidates.
plos-pone-0008339:
Stefano Farioli-Vecchioli and colleagues studied memory in knockout mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. New neurons are born in the dentate gyrus of the adult hippocampus. This neurogenesis has been implicated in plasticity and memory. The molecular controls on newborn neurons remain largely unknown. The team removed a gene called PC3/Tis21 in mice.

Without it, hippocampal granule neurons failed to finish differentiating. The mice also showed defective contextual memory. Linking one gene to both cell maturation and memory is a strong result. It helps explain how new neurons join memory circuits.
plos-pone-0008439:
Cristina Cigana and co-authors wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on lung infection in cystic fibrosis. A germ called Pseudomonas aeruginosa can live in the airways for life. Strains found late in the disease differ from strains found at first. The team study parts of the germ that the immune system senses. Those parts include lipid A and bits of the cell wall.

They find the late strains change those parts. The changes make the germ less apt to trigger innate defense. In short, the germ learns to hide from the host. That helps explain why the infection lasts so long in these lungs.
plos-pone-0008539:
Silke Raffegerst and co-authors report blood cancers in transgenic mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their mice carry a chimeric MHC class II gene called DR4. MHC molecules present antigen fragments to immune cells. The homozygous mouse line spontaneously develops diverse hematological malignancies. That happens at a high frequency of about seventy percent. Tumors split evenly between T cell and B cell types.

The malignancies include lymphoblastic T cell lymphomas and Hodgkin-like lymphomas. Such variety in one mouse line is unusual. The model may reveal how a single immune gene change unleashes many cancer types. It offers a system for testing treatments across blood cancers.
plos-pone-0008639:
Frances Mercer and co-authors study receptors on regulatory T cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Regulatory T cells suppress immune activation and prevent autoimmune diseases. Their ability to inhibit proliferation of other T cells is well established. It was not yet clear whether they also modulate inflammatory cytokines during responses. TNF and IL-1 are two major inflammatory cytokines. The team examine expression and function of their receptors on human regulatory T cells.

They find those receptors are expressed and functional on the cells. Through them, inflammatory signals can tune regulatory cell behavior. That tuning may decide if suppression holds during infection or flare. The receptors become potential levers for autoimmune therapy.
plos-pone-0008739:
Changrui Lu, Fang Ding, and Ailong Ke solved the shape of an ancient RNA-shredding machine. Their structural study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The exosome chews up RNA messages that cells no longer need. In archaea, simple microbes, it has a cutting ring and a binding ring. Earlier work suggested both rings were neatly threefold. A sharper portrait was needed.

Their crystal structure, from the archaeon Sulfolobus solfataricus, broke that neat picture. The binding ring sat in an uneven, flexible arrangement. Flexibility may help the machine grip many RNA shapes. The portrait informs models of RNA cleanup in all complex cells.
plos-pone-0008839:
Marinus van Batenburg, Hualing Li, J. Annelies Polman, and colleagues predicted a hormone target gene from a DNA pattern. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glucocorticoids are stress hormones with wide medical use. They act when their receptor binds response elements near genes. Most direct target genes in the body were still unknown. The team proposed that paired elements close together mark real targets.

That rule pointed to caveolin-1, a membrane protein gene. Tests supported it as a true glucocorticoid target. A predictive rule speeds the hunt for hormone-controlled genes. Such genes explain both benefits and side effects of steroid drugs.
