plos-pone-0008939:
Marie Benoit and colleagues read the gene activity of infected human heart valves for PLOS ONE in 2010. Infective endocarditis is an infection of the heart's inner lining and valves. Bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus cause most cases. The infection grows crusty deposits on valves and can destroy them.

The team measured which genes were turned up or down in diseased valve tissue. The pattern traced how the disease unfolds, step by step, inside the valve. Genes tied to immune defence and blood clotting stood out in the picture. That map of the disease's course may point doctors toward better treatments.
plos-pone-0009039:
Andrew Crossett, Nick Lauter, and Tanzy Love built a better error bar for gene hunting, in PLOS ONE in 2010. QTL mapping finds chromosome stretches behind traits like yield or disease risk. Each find comes with a confidence interval, the range where the gene likely sits. Sequenced genomes now make chasing those genes realistic, so intervals must be honest.

Old support-interval methods can misstate the true uncertainty. The team derived intervals from the data themselves, tailored to composite interval mapping. Their empirical method was checked against known cases. Tighter, truer intervals save laboratories from hunting genes in the wrong stretch.
plos-pone-0009139:
Vidya Devi Negi and co-authors vaccinated pregnant mice against Salmonella, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pregnancy softens the mother's immune defences so the fetus is not rejected. That truce leaves pregnant mothers more open to invading germs. Salmonella infection during pregnancy can end in loss of the litter.

The vaccine strain, called DV-STM-07, was designed to be safe in pregnancy. Vaccinated mothers resisted Salmonella infection while carrying their young. Abortions were prevented, and the newborn mice carried protection too. A vaccine for mothers that shields two generations at once is a double gain.
plos-pone-0009239:
Ruhee Dere, Patricia Wilson, Richard Sandford, and co-authors published this kidney study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Polycystic kidney disease is a common inherited disorder that fills kidneys with cysts. It is a major cause of kidney failure, and treatment options are limited. The disease comes from faults in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes.

The study follows polycystin-1, the protein made by PKD1. Its tail end was found to guide another protein, TSC2, to the right place in the cell. Positioned there, TSC2 holds back mTOR, a growth signal that cysts seem to exploit. The finding links the cyst gene to a pathway doctors already hope to target.
plos-pone-0009339:
Young-Beob Yu and co-authors published this herbal medicine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cinnamon bark from Cinnamomum cassia appears in two traditional herbal formulas. Proving that such mixtures work, and how, is hard because they mix many herbs. The team used the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans to test the formulas cleanly.

Worms given the formulas lived longer than untreated worms. The gain ran through insulin signaling and stress response pathways, two known levers of aging. Showing a pathway gives herbal research a mechanism to test further, beyond simple claims. It also links a traditional remedy to the basic biology of lifespan.
plos-pone-0009439:
Leopoldo de Meis and co-authors wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about brown fat in rats. Brown fat burns fuel to make heat for the body. Its heat making is driven by its mitochondria, the cell's power units. The team looked at two compartments inside brown fat cells: the endoplasmic reticulum and the mitochondria.

They saw the outer coat of the mitochondria fuse with the reticulum. Calcium signals helped switch on heat making after that fusion. A calcium pump known as SERCA 1 was found at the site. The result shows that cell parts can join up in a direct way to turn on warmth.
plos-pone-0009539:
Savita Khanna and co-authors studied slow healing wounds in diabetic mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wounds in diabetes often stay open and inflamed for a long time. Healing needs inflammation to end once its job is done. A key step is the clearing of dead cells by macrophages, a clean up process called efferocytosis. The team tested that step at wound sites in diabetic animals.

Macrophages in the diabetic wounds cleared dead cells poorly. With dead cells left in place, inflammation dragged on. The work names a precise failure behind a common and serious problem. Fixing the clean up step could help wounds in diabetes finally close.
plos-pone-0009639:
Marisa King, Jeb Owen, and Hubert Schwabl questioned a cherished idea about baby birds in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mother birds pass antibodies to their chicks, supposedly giving vital early protection. House sparrow chicks are born helpless and grow up in the nest. The team tracked how the chicks' own immune systems developed. They measured whether maternal antibodies played the central role often assumed.

Their data test that assumption against real development patterns. Maternal antibodies mattered less, or for shorter times, than the standard story claims. Findings like these reshape how ecologists model disease in wild birds. They also show why field checks beat armchair claims about immunity.
plos-pone-0009839:
Deep-diving seabirds must fight their own buoyancy on the way down. Timothée Cook and colleagues measured how one such bird manages that fight underwater. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Buoyancy is the upward push water gives to air-filled bodies.

The team recorded underwater locomotor performance during deep dives. The pattern suggested respiratory strategies, ways of handling air, that cut foraging effort. Air carried down adds lift, so managing breath saves energy. Smarter breathing lets the bird spend its dive hunting, not fighting to sink. Foraging effort decides whether a dive pays off.
plos-pone-0009939:
Parents are having children later than in past generations, and autism rates have climbed too. Jean Golding, Colin Steer, and Marcus Pembrey tested whether those trends connect. Their birth cohort study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The study covered autistic spectrum disorders across a whole birth cohort. A birth cohort follows everyone born in a set time and place. It weighed parental ages and, unusually, grandparental ages as well. Grandparents' ages can matter through effects passed down generations. Cohort data let the team test age effects without cherry-picking cases.
plos-pone-0010039:
Ole Norgaard and Jeffrey Lazarus wrote about searching medical literature during a crisis in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic produced thousands of papers and news items very fast. Finding the right studies in that flood was hard. Poor searching can leave decision makers using old or weak evidence.

Their PLOS ONE article used PubMed, the main medical database, as its test case. It considered how searches perform when a health emergency is moving quickly. The lessons apply to any outbreak where officials must find sound science under time pressure. Speed and accuracy both counted in their tests.
plos-pone-0010139:
The authors were Márcio Baptista, Carlos Melo, Mário Armelão, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used cultured rat brain neurons. They studied an enzyme that makes GABA, the brain's main calming signal molecule. Under excitotoxic conditions, when overexcited neurons are damaged, that enzyme gets cut into pieces.

The team tested whether the proteasome, the cell's main protein shredding machine, does that cutting. They worked with neurons from the hippocampus, a memory center. Understanding the cut could reveal how seizures and strokes disturb the brain's balance of signals. The work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010339:
Kevin Doherty, David Naugle and Jeffrey Evans wrote about sage-grouse and energy building in PLOS ONE in 2010. As the United States builds more energy projects at home, wild land is lost. Offsets try to balance that harm by funding protection elsewhere. Fans call offsets a useful way to pay for conservation. Critics fear the trade lets real damage slide.

The authors propose treating sage-grouse habitat like a currency that can be traded openly. A market price, they argue, could show what saving habitat is worth. Energy firms would buy credits; landowners who protect birds would earn them. The idea tries to make conservation compete in dollars. Whether such trading truly helps the bird is the debate the study joins.
plos-pone-0010439:
H. Christina Fan and Stephen Quake measured the true limits of a blood test for unborn babies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fragments of a fetus's DNA float in the mother's blood. Counting them by rapid sequencing can reveal extra chromosomes, as in Down syndrome. A quirk of the sequencer, favoring some DNA types, had capped the test's sensitivity. The authors asked what limits remain once that bias is handled.

They argue the ceiling is set by simple counting statistics. More counted fragments mean surer answers, in a predictable way. That clarity helps labs design tests with known reliability. A blood draw is far safer than sampling the womb directly. This analysis helped turn a lab feat into a dependable screening tool.
plos-pone-0010539:
Soo Chan Lee and colleagues traced the sex-related region and shared genome features of microsporidia and fungi in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microsporidia are tiny parasites that live inside cells of many animals, including humans. Evidence increasingly ties them closely to fungi, either inside that kingdom or beside it. Their genomes are stripped down by parasitic life. The team compared their sex locus and other genome features with true fungi.

Shared features support the fungal kinship with fresh detail. The sex-related locus shows how even mating machinery survives extreme genome shrinkage. Origins of parasite groups matter for predicting their biology and weaknesses. This study uses genome comparison as an ancestry test. It places an odd group more firmly on the tree of life.
plos-pone-0010639:
Hiromi Sawai and colleagues traced the family history of the domestic chicken, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chickens were tamed from wild junglefowl in Southeast Asia thousands of years ago. Which wild species contributed most was still debated among researchers.

The team compared DNA from many chicken breeds and two junglefowl species. The red junglefowl emerged as the main ancestor. The green junglefowl left smaller traces in some breeds. Genetic family trees like this one help breeders protect rare traits. They also show how human choices reshaped one wild bird into the world's most common farm animal.
plos-pone-0010739:
Wees Love and colleagues tested which immune sensor guards mouse lungs against mycoplasma, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mycoplasma pulmonis is a natural lung pathogen of mice, akin to germs that cause walking pneumonia in people. Mycoplasma surface fats are sensed by toll-like receptors, the body's early warning set.

Mice lacking the sensor TLR2 fought the infection far worse than normal mice. Lab cells with added TLR2 reacted strongly to the germ's surface fats. TLR2 thus carries most of the early defense in the lung. Knowing the key sensor focuses vaccine and drug work on the pathway that actually matters.
plos-pone-0010839:
Linda Douw, Marjolein de Groot, Edwin van Dellen and co-authors published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Epilepsy affects about one in a hundred people, but a first seizure is hard to judge because a standard EEG often shows no clear warning signs. The authors tested whether functional connectivity, a measure of how brain regions fire in sync, could do better.

They drew on hundreds of EEG records from patients seen after a first suspected seizure, then compared people later confirmed to have epilepsy with matched people who did not. A sync measure averaged across frequency bands separated the groups more sharply than the usual search for abnormal spikes. Douw and colleagues suggest that reading the EEG as a network, not just a trace, could make early epilepsy diagnosis more reliable.
plos-pone-0010939:
Nickolai Titov, Gavin Andrews, Matthew Davies and co-authors ran this trial of internet therapy for depression, published in PLOS ONE in 2010. Online cognitive behavioral therapy works for depression when a clinician guides it, but clinician time is scarce and costly. The authors asked whether a trained technician, offering support without clinical advice, could guide patients just as well.

Community volunteers with major depression were assigned at random to clinician-guided treatment, technician-guided treatment, or a waiting group. Both guided groups worked through six online lessons with weekly homework and weekly contact over eight weeks. Titov and colleagues set the trial up as a fairness test: if technician support matches clinician support, effective therapy can reach far more people. Their question goes to the heart of scaling mental health care online.
plos-pone-0011039:
Caroline Kizilyaprak, Danièle Spehner, Didier Devys and co-authors published this retina chromatin study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rod photoreceptor nuclei are built inside-out compared with most cells: a dense central ball of silent chromatin wrapped in a thin rim of active chromatin. The authors used these natural extremes to correlate structure with chemical marks and gene activity in intact cells.

Using cryo-preserved tissue, electron tomography, and gold-tagged antibodies, they mapped where histone modifications and the gene-reading enzyme sit relative to the dense core. The central domain carried the marks of silenced chromatin, while the machinery of active reading occupied the rim. Kizilyaprak and colleagues turn an oddball nucleus into a clean test of how packing states relate to function, informing the wider effort to read the histone code.
plos-pone-0011139:
Marrazzo, Thomas, Fiedler and colleagues ran a cohort study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was a common vaginal infection caused by a shift in normal bacteria. They followed women who report sex with women and recorded who developed the condition and when.

The study mapped the risks tied to picking up the infection in this group. Such detail was lacking, since most past work focused on other groups. Clearer risk data leads to better advice in clinics and better care. It also corrects a gap in women's health research for a group often left out of studies.
plos-pone-0011239:
Yew, Zhao, Hong and colleagues treated obese mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. In obesity, the liver often stops responding well to insulin, a step toward diabetes. The team blocked an enzyme that builds a fatty molecule in cell membranes and measured insulin action in the liver.

Blocking that enzyme increased how well the liver responded to insulin in mice made obese by diet. The enzyme thus becomes a named drug target for insulin resistance. A treatment built on it would attack a root fault rather than manage blood sugar alone. The finding now needs study of safety and effects beyond the liver.
plos-pone-0011339:
Kelli Barr and colleagues asked in 2010 whether germs living inside a corn pest help the pest disarm the plant. The western corn rootworm is a beetle whose young chew corn roots across North America and Europe. Plants fight back by switching on defense genes, but the attack often still succeeds and harvests suffer.

The team found that microbes living with the rootworm lower the plant's defense response in roots. With those genes turned down, the plant mounts a weaker counterattack while feeding goes on. The result shifts how scientists think about crop pests. The real opponent may be a partnership of insect plus microbes, so protecting corn may require breaking up that partnership rather than targeting the beetle alone.
plos-pone-0011439:
Hye-Jung Kim and co-authors tested in 2010 whether two supposedly minor immune cell types do real cleanup work in the thymus. The thymus trains immune cells, and many trainee cells die there by design. Those dead cells must be cleared quietly, or their contents could trigger autoimmunity, an attack on the body's own tissue.

By selectively removing eosinophils or neutrophils in mice, the team showed that clearing dead cells in the thymus became less efficient. Cells often cast as allergy or infection players thus hold a housekeeping job where self-tolerance is learned. The finding widens the cast of cells that keep the thymus orderly. It also hints that when these cells are missing or faulty, leftover debris might help explain how tolerance breaks down.
plos-pone-0011539:
Carol Camlin, Victoria Hosegood, and Marie-Louise Newell examined in 2010 how gender and migration together shape HIV risk in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The province carries one of the world's heaviest HIV burdens, and its pattern is not random. Men often migrate for work, while women remain with limited power to negotiate safety in their relationships, and the team traced how those forces meet.

Their analysis grounds infection risk in lived structure: who moves, who decides, and who is left vulnerable by both. Prevention that ignores that structure, handing out identical messages to everyone, misses why risk concentrates where it does. The findings argue for programs that reach migrant men at work sites and strengthen women's bargaining power at home. Epidemiology that names the social machinery gives policy something it can actually change.
plos-pone-0011639:
Jörg Ritter and co-authors presented a new microscope method for watching single molecules in living tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Seeing individual molecules at work promises detailed views of how the body functions. In thick living tissue, though, most microscopes are too slow, too blurry or too damaging to follow them.

Their technique pairs light sheet illumination, which lights only a thin slice, with ultra-sensitive detection. It tracks lone molecules while keeping tissue alive and largely unharmed. Biologists gain a gentler window onto molecular movement in its natural setting, opening studies that were not feasible before.
plos-pone-0011739:
Ciara Greene, Pooja Bahri and David Soto separated two emotional influences on memory, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mood and bodily arousal are both known to affect how well people think and remember. How much each one contributes, and how they interact, was poorly understood.

After a study phase with abstract shapes, the team altered participants' feeling states and measured recognition memory. Their design teased apart the effect of emotional tone from the effect of arousal. Finding two separate levers on what people remember helps explain conflicting results in earlier emotion research.
plos-pone-0011839:
Angela Kamps and co-workers studied fruit flies in 2010 to find out what the Tre1 receptor needs in order to guide moving cells. Tre1 belongs to the large receptor family that lets cells sense signals around them. In a fly embryo it helps germ cells, the future egg and sperm cells, travel to the right place.

The team pinpointed one building block, an arginine kept nearly unchanged across species, and showed that Tre1 fails without it. A single altered piece can therefore break a whole migration route. The result shows how finely built these receptors are, and it gives cell movement research a precise point where guidance can be switched off for study.
plos-pone-0011939:
Satyendra Tripathi and co-workers reported in 2010 a protein sign that marks the most risky cancers of the head and neck. The team set tumor tissue side by side with normal mouth lining and tagged proteins to find which ones differ. One stood out: a protein called S100A7, found in the core of tumor cells.

That core form of the protein was tied to poor outcomes for patients with this cancer type. A sign that sorts patients by how their disease is likely to run helps doctors choose who needs the strongest care and the closest watch. Since the test uses tissue that is already taken for diagnosis, it could slot into the checks patients now get.
plos-pone-0012039:
Sujoy Das and co-workers isolated in 2010 a factor from goat reproductive fluid that stops sperm from swimming. Several mammals carry sperm motility inhibiting factors in male reproductive fluids, but these proteins had not been adequately purified or characterized. The team worked with plasma from the caprine epididymis, the duct where sperm mature.

They purified the novel factor, called MIF-II, and characterized its properties. A natural, specific brake on sperm movement is scientifically interesting for how fertility is timed, and it hints at contraceptive ideas based on stopping sperm rather than hormones. Careful purification is the unglamorous step that makes any of that testable.
plos-pone-0012139:
Han Yan, Kavitha Venkatesan, John Beaver, and co-authors built a resource for predicting gene functions in the fruit fly, published in PLOS ONE in 2010. The fruit fly is one of biology's main model animals, yet the jobs of many of its genes remain unknown. Guessing each gene's role from large mixed datasets is a standing challenge for systems biology.

The team trained separate prediction programs for different functions, letting each data type count where it helps most, then combined the results into one public resource. Other researchers can look up a fly gene and get a ranked guess at its job, ready to test in the lab. Resources like this speed up genetics far beyond a single lab's reach.
plos-pone-0012239:
Takashi Saito, Akinori Nakamura, Yoshitsugu Aoki, and co-authors carried a gene therapy from dystrophic dogs toward a human patient, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Duchenne muscular dystrophy destroys muscle because the dystrophin message is broken; skipping the broken section during message assembly can restore a shorter but working protein. The team had treated dogs with a synthetic snippet that forces such skipping.

They then tested that same snippet in cells taken from a patient whose deletion pattern differs, and found it still worked. Showing one drug design can serve more than one deletion type widens the pool of boys it might help. Exon skipping remains one of the few strategies that treats this disease's root cause.
plos-pone-0012339:
Pawandeep Dhami, Peter Saffrey, Alexander Bruce, and co-authors examined the marks that outline genes' working segments, in PLOS ONE in 2010. As a gene is read, the cell must know which segments, exons, to keep in the final message and which to cut. Recent work had shown the protein spools along genes are placed and tagged in patterns that mirror those segments, as if chromatin itself keeps the outline.

Their analysis shows the outline is not explained by spool placement alone; the chemical tags carry independent information. That distinction matters for understanding splicing errors, which underlie many diseases. It also refines the picture of the gene as a text whose punctuation is written in several inks.
plos-pone-0012439:
Yoel Lubell, Anne Mills, Christopher Whitty and colleagues priced a policy of treating malaria at home in Uganda, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Home management teaches community workers to treat feverish children fast, before malaria turns deadly. The approach is widely promoted in Africa, but its cost per benefit needed a careful check.

Using an interactive Markov model that follows children through sickness and recovery states, the team weighed program costs against lives and health gained. Their analysis helps ministries decide whether home treatment deserves scarce funds next to clinics and bed nets. Models of this kind make policy trade-offs explicit instead of guessed.
plos-pone-0012539:
Bob Uttl and Kelly Kisinger examined what missing information means in witness statements and accident records, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Eyewitness reports and crash records often omit the very conditions researchers need — lighting, speed, attention — leaving gaps called missing values. Analysts usually treat a gap as no information, but Uttl and Kisinger question that habit.

They argue silence in a record often carries meaning: witnesses mention what struck them as notable, so what is absent was likely ordinary. Reading absence correctly changes conclusions in court cases and safety studies. The paper gives researchers rules for handling gaps without inventing data — or wasting real clues.
plos-pone-0012639:
Rodriguez, Aburjania, Priedigkeit and co-authors mapped the parts of a protein that decide whether it fights or feeds cancer. The protein KLF6 normally suppresses tumours, but a shortened variant made by splicing, called KLF6-SV1, does the opposite. The variant lacks the tail that helps the full protein work.

Their 2010 study found that regions guiding the protein into and out of the nucleus also control how fast it is destroyed. Place and lifespan together set whether the guard or its rival wins. That logic may help design drugs for cancers driven by this gene.
plos-pone-0012739:
Factor, Seo, Ishikawa and co-authors cut out a growth receptor in mice and watched liver regrowth stall late. After part of the liver is removed, the HGF and c-Met signal starts DNA copying for regrowth. Their 2010 study used mice lacking c-Met to see what happens after that start.

Without c-Met, a whole gene program needed for the late division step failed to run. Regrowing livers therefore need this signal twice, not once. The detail matters for liver surgery and for diseases where regrowth is weak.  Gene activity was read across the whole regrowth period.
plos-pone-0012839:
Agam, Yalcin, Bhomra and co-authors hunted for stretches of DNA that mice gain or lose compared with a reference genome. Such copy number variants can shift gene dosage and traits. Their 2010 study used array hybridisation, a chip method that spots gains and losses across the genome.

They found this class of variation oddly elusive in the mouse genome, with fewer clear cases than expected. Elusive does not mean absent, and the study probes the limits of the tool itself. Honest limits matter, since mouse genetics underpins much medical research.
plos-pone-0340539:
Hugo Charoud and four colleagues evaluate two programs that paid Colombian farmers to keep Amazon forest standing, in PLOS ONE in 2026. One was a government scheme offering cash across a wide area of Guaviare; the other, a four year charity project, worked closely with frontier farms on sustainable land use. Together the two covered different ground, and the authors measured how much deforestation each actually prevented.

Combined, the programs spared roughly fourteen hundred hectares of forest, a real but modest dent in regional clearing. The government scheme guarded larger, less threatened patches, while the charity targeted smaller farms at the sharp edge of clearing and added technical help such as tree dotted pasture systems. The authors argue the designs complement each other, yet payments alone cannot stop clearing without stronger measures behind them.
plos-pone-0341539:
Wengang Gan and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on roadbed material made from cement-stabilized phosphogypsum, an industrial byproduct, and how its springiness under traffic loading survives wetting and drying. That property, the resilient modulus, steers pavement design, yet codes still use a static version. The team ran dynamic triaxial tests varying confinement, repeated load, cement content, and wet-dry cycles, then examined microstructure to explain the changes.

The modulus rose with confining pressure and cement dose and fell as load and wet-dry cycles increased, with nearly all cycle damage done in the first four rounds. Microscopy and mineral analysis accounted for the decay. Dynamic values ran above static ones by a stable ratio, and a simple strength test predicted the modulus closely. A prediction model including cement content and cycle count, verified against experiments, is supplied for engineers designing with this recycled material.
plos-pone-0342639:
Masaru Sakai and co-authors grow edible mushrooms in Fukushima in 2026. Two species were grown on forest floor beds. Fourteen broad leaf forest sites took part in the work. The aim was to measure radioactive caesium uptake. That uptake has blocked outdoor growing since the accident. Air dose rates were checked at each site.

Both species stayed well below the food safety limit. That supports a return to outdoor growing in wide areas. Uptake tracked soil contamination in species specific ways. One species tracked litter and deep soil layers. The other tracked top soil and leaf mould more. Clean soil fill may help the first species. Clean litter cover may help the second one.
plos-pone-0344039:
Mohamed M Hassona and co-authors ran two seasons of field trials to see whether buckwheat, a gluten-free grain crop new to Egypt, can thrive there, and under what conditions. Two species, common buckwheat and the hardier Tartary type, were grown at a Nile Delta site and a desert fringe site. Each was sown in late autumn, midwinter, and early spring. Growth and yield were measured plant by plant.

The three-way interplay of species, place, and sowing date drove nearly every trait. Tartary buckwheat outperformed the common type at both sites, peaking with early spring sowing in the Delta at nearly a tonne of grain per hectare, while common buckwheat preferred an autumn sowing. The authors give Egyptian growers their first concrete calendar for a crop that could diversify farms under dry conditions.
plos-pone-0347739:
Funmito Omolola Fehintola and colleagues check teen smoking with a breath test. Their study from Osun State, Nigeria, appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Teens often understate smoking on forms. So the team measured carbon monoxide in the breath of six hundred sixteen school students. A handheld meter did the reading. A standard WHO form was filled in as well.

Breath scores at or past the smoker line flagged current smokers. That gave an objective count to set against what students admitted. The team also hunted for factors linked to smoking. The gap between breath and self-report matters far beyond Nigeria. Health plans everywhere rest on surveys that may understate youth smoking.
plos-pone-0347839:
Jialing Zhang and colleagues compared a prized Chinese medicinal herb, Ligusticum chuanxiong, grown in its classic Sichuan home with a distinct variety cultivated in Gansu. Buyers prize origin, so the team measured everything: plant size and colour, scent through an electronic nose, and chemistry through chromatography and mass spectrometry, hunting for what separates the two.

The Gansu plants grew bigger and browner, with a different scent profile. Sichuan material carried more of several key active compounds, though one ran higher in Gansu stock. The volatile analysis found eighty-two scent compounds in Gansu plants against sixty-two in Sichuan, with altitude threading through the differences. The study maps a quality case for the Gansu variety.
plos-pone-0348139:
Frances Charlotte Butcher, Patricia Kingori, and Michael Parker sort the moral views hidden inside global health security, the field that handles disease outbreaks crossing borders. Experts disagree about whose safety the field serves. Their 2026 study interviews thirty-eight professionals and groups their views into four models of what the work is really for.

One model treats outbreaks as threats to stop, another as shared risks to manage together. A third tries to reframe the field's terms entirely, and a fourth puts relief of suffering first. Naming the models gives negotiators a map of why talks stall: partners often argue from different moral maps without knowing it. Clearer terms could make outbreak agreements faster and fairer.
plos-pone-0348239:
Yunbo Gao and co-workers build a forecasting method for rail freight volumes that admits uncertainty instead of hiding it. Freight data are fuzzy and nonlinear, and point forecasts often miss badly. Their 2026 study first compresses nine years of monthly records from a Chinese freight center into low, central, and high fuzzy bands, then trains a tuned support vector model on each band.

The hybrid method posted the smallest errors of the models compared, for every band. It also drew the narrowest honest forecast interval around future volumes. An improved swarm search kept the training from settling too early on weak settings. Rail planners gain not just a number but a believable range for staffing, wagons, and warehouse space.
plos-pone-0348339:
Rangsima Lolekha and a Thai team followed 149 young adults born with HIV, cared for at two Bangkok hospitals. They wanted to see how schooling and working lives turned out in the treatment era. Their 2026 report draws on a youth development program the participants joined as teenagers. Annual follow-up ran for five more years, into 2020.

The picture is largely encouraging. Nearly all stayed on antiretroviral therapy. Most had healthy immune counts and suppressed virus. More than eight in ten finished at least secondary school, and three quarters were employed. Marriage and frequent drinking predicted skipping university. Having no disability and attending individual program sessions predicted pursuing it. The cohort shows perinatal HIV is now a condition people build adult lives around.
plos-pone-0348439:
Koki Tsuda and colleagues cast a wide net over lifestyle and thinking skills in healthy Japanese adults aged forty and above. Their dataset held roughly eighteen hundred measurements per person, from body composition to daily habits, alongside a standardised cognitive test battery. Seven hundred ten participants fed the 2026 exploratory analysis, which used strict corrections to avoid false alarms among so many comparisons.

Twenty-eight factors passed the filter. Walking pattern, blood vessel function, grip strength, and oral health stood out, while ordinary blood markers did not. The authors stress these are candidates, not conclusions: the snapshot design cannot show cause, and long-term studies must check whether these factors truly track mental sharpness.
plos-pone-0349239:
Cirque Gammelin and Daniel Schindler reconstructed sixty years of habitat conditions for young sockeye salmon in Alaska's remote Chignik Lakes watershed. The local salmon fishery collapsed in 2018, and the team asked whether the nursery lakes themselves had deteriorated. Different parts of the watershed change on their own clocks, which can mask or mimic decline.

Overall rearing capacity had not fallen. A shallow lake grew warmer over the decades while a deep lake stayed stable, the deep lake's plankton food supply actually improved, and young fish production shifted between habitats. Variability, not collapse, was the story. For managers, the result redirects the search for the fishery crash away from the nursery habitat and toward other stages of the salmon's life.
plos-pone-0349339:
Marek Weis and Wojciech Dawid trained a machine learning model to pick good locations for bike-sharing stations, a planning problem with many tangled factors. The model learned from land cover and population data around existing successful stations, comparing several learning methods including neural networks. It reached very high accuracy in identifying suitable spots.

Predicted stations matched the real network's logic and suggested sensible expansion points, clustered near big intersections and transit stops. As a harder test, the model was turned loose on Rzeszów, a Polish city with no bike system yet, and proposed a coherent starter network. Cities weighing a launch could use such a model to argue site choices with evidence instead of hunches.
plos-pone-0349439:
Khalid Awad Al-Kubaisi and colleagues asked drug shop staff across Jordan what they know about gene-based drug choice, and how ready their shops are to use it. A person's genes change how drugs work in the body, so gene tests can make drug choice safer. The poll reached staff in all three parts of the land and scored their know-how next to world rules.

It also scored their views, their sense of what blocks the change, and how set their shops are in staff, funds, and gear. Most people in Jordan get their drugs from shops like these, so shop readiness will decide if gene-based choice stays a hospital extra or turns into day-to-day care. Each gap needs its own fix: more training, more trust, or more funds.
plos-pone-0349939:
André Hajek and Hans-Helmut König surveyed adults in Germany in early 2026 about wearable health devices. More than a third already used one, and the authors also asked non users what might persuade them to start.

Smartwatches dominated use, with fitness bands a distant second and rings, glasses, and smart clothing rare. Among non users, future medical need was the top reason that would move them, followed by lower prices and interest in watching their own health. Age, income, and health shaped answers in the modelling. The results help firms and health services time their offers to life events.
plos-pone-0350039:
Prachi Singh and colleagues ran a small pilot trial of an herbal drink for insomnia, testing it against a placebo in a crossover design. Ten healthy adults over fifty with significant insomnia drank either the supplement, built on chicory and green tea extracts, or a dummy drink for a week, then switched after a two-week break. Sleep was measured by questionnaires, wrist movement tracking, and one lab sleep study.

Herbal sleep aids are popular but rarely put through blinded trials, so even ten participants add real evidence. Subjective sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and fatigue were tracked alongside the objective recordings. Pilot results of this kind cannot prove a supplement works; they show whether a larger, definitive trial is worth running and how it should be designed.
plos-pone-0350639:
Caifang Qiu, Hui Wang, and Ran Liu compared dance students with other women students in China in 2026, looking at body makeup and gut microbes. Dance training shapes bodies intensely, and whether it also shapes the gut community was unknown.

Seventy students, half from dance majors, gave body scans and stool samples for gene based microbe profiling. Dance students carried less fat by many measures and more favourable muscle and water ratios, while gut communities differed across several microbe groups. Some microbes tracked fat and muscle in opposite directions. The links are correlations, but they sketch how training, body, and gut travel together.
plos-pone-0350739:
Young basketball players need both raw strength and springy power, and a simple ratio can show which one lags. Casado-Martínez P and colleagues built a four-week in-season training plan around that ratio for twenty-one players averaging about sixteen years old, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Players were grouped by their starting ratio and given different emphases: heavy strength work, a mix, or jumping drills. Everyone trained three times a week beside normal practice. Jump height, squat force, and estimated lifting maximum were measured before and after. The strongest-looking group gained notably in squat force, showing short tailored blocks can shift muscle profiles mid-season.
plos-pone-0350839:
Maja Hemberg and colleagues tested a key defence protein against flu in human airway tissue grown in the lab in 2026. The protein, MAVS, relays alarms from virus sensors inside cells, and animal work suggested it was vital, but human airway proof was missing.

Using gene editing, the team removed MAVS from primary airway cultures grown at an air surface. Infected with flu, the edited tissue made far less of the main antiviral signals and let the virus grow more freely. The result confirms MAVS as a non backup part of human airway defence, a fact that matters for judging risk in people born with faults in this pathway.
plos-pone-0350939:
Rasmi Abu-Helu and colleagues at a Jerusalem hospital compared two ways of finding bacteria in urine and spinal fluid samples. Standard lab culture is slow and can miss germs that grow poorly or are present in tiny amounts. Alongside culture, the team ran a sequencing test that reads a shared bacterial gene to name what is present.

In urine, both methods found common infection germs such as E. coli. Sequencing also picked up several kinds of bacteria in samples that culture had called negative or unimportant, and it did the same for spinal fluid, where missing an infection can be deadly. The authors conclude that sequencing catches more of what is really in a sample than culture alone.
plos-pone-0351139:
Curi-Quinto and colleagues set a cutoff for insulin resistance in Peruvian teenagers in a 2026 study. A common index based on fasting sugar and insulin lacks agreed cutoffs for teens, and values differ by population. Records for more than three hundred seventy teens from a long-running study supplied the data.

The team found the index value that best matched metabolic syndrome signs. They also weighed habits and body measures that families can change, plus early-life weight and family history. A local cutoff helps school and clinic screening flag risk earlier in this population. Borrowing cutoffs from other countries could mislabel many Peruvian teens.
plos-pone-0351439:
Sai and Aleithan improved a promising solar cell type with a two-part surface treatment in a 2026 study. Perovskite cells are cheap to make but lose power through surface defects. A blend of two protective salts formed a thin layered skin where the light-absorbing film meets the next layer.

Treated cells reached notably higher voltage and efficiency than single-salt versions. The skin was smoother and shed water better, which shields the fragile film. Cells also lasted longer under humid air and steady light. Dual surface care like this pushes perovskite cells closer to rooftops, where durability has lagged behind their strong lab efficiency.
plos-pone-0351539:
Shaoxing Chen and colleagues tracked cancers that affect women in China from 1990 to 2023 using a world disease burden database. Breast, cervix, womb, and ovarian cancers were counted for new cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost. Trend tools split change into ageing, population growth, and true risk shifts, with forecasts for the next fifteen years.

Adjusted rates fell for most of these cancers, a sign of better control. Breast cancer was the exception, with its adjusted rate rising and new cases nearing three hundred and forty three thousand in 2023. Total counts rose for all four cancers as China aged and grew. Planning must hold both truths: rates can fall while clinics still face many more patients.
plos-pone-0351639:
Zhang analyzed persuasion in a Chinese government short-video account in a 2026 study. The account, promoting a province on a popular video app, supplied three hundred sixty top-liked videos from one year plus their public comments. Texts were mined for word patterns and feelings, then read closely for rhetorical appeals.

Emotional appeal led, filling posts with family warmth, collective pride, and urgency. Appeals to credibility came second, built through official voice and achievement claims. Reasoned argument played a smaller role. Knowing which appeals dominate helps explain what audiences reward with likes, and how official accounts tune messages to local pride.
plos-pone-0351739:
After leg amputation, many people feel pain in the missing limb, and Sneha Vidyasagar and colleagues reviewed whether the hormone calcitonin, given as an add-on drug, eases it. Their 2026 PLOS One paper looked back at thirty-five patients treated for at least three days between 2017 and 2023.

Patients rated pain strength, distress, and how much pain blocked activity before and after treatment. All three ratings improved, and patients reported feeling meaningful relief. The pattern held for people with and without diabetes, whose foot problems caused many of the amputations. As a backward-looking review without a comparison group, the study can only suggest promise.
plos-pone-0351839:
Marika Mariano and colleagues tested whether a virtual body that copies your movements makes you feel, deep down, that you caused what happens in virtual reality. Seventy adults switched on a virtual light bulb with real or guided hand movements while wearing a headset. The team measured agency two ways: what people said, and a timing illusion, intentional binding, that betrays felt control without asking.

People always claimed more control when they moved actively, whether or not the avatar mirrored them. The timing illusion appeared only when the avatar's hands moved in sync with the real hands, and only at the shortest delay. So a responsive avatar feeds the gut sense of acting, not the spoken one. Designers of rehab in virtual reality, where patients must feel ownership of movement, should note the split.
plos-pone-0351939:
Siviero and colleagues examined bite marks on dinosaur bones from Wyoming in a 2026 study. The bones came from a crowded burial site holding the plant-eating dinosaur Edmontosaurus, in rock from near the end of the age of dinosaurs. Marks on fossil bone are often called tooth traces, even when other causes fit better.

Out of more than three thousand bones checked, only twelve held marks the team could link to teeth. Fine grooves in two kinds of traces matched the tooth edges of Tyrannosaurus rex found at the same site. One set of holes turned out to have a different cause, which shows why close context checks matter.
plos-pone-0352239:
Nicholas G Mellor and colleagues coaxed brain cancer cells taken directly from patients to grow in neat grid patterns. The cells sat on a coated silicon surface. Their 2026 laboratory study used the mesenchymal form of glioblastoma. This is the most common and deadly adult brain tumor. The team fine-tuned pattern size, cell density, and growth conditions. Five scoring measures of their own design guided the tuning.

Two patient cell lines patterned with high fidelity. The arranged cells still behaved like living tumor cells. They flashed calcium signals when stimulated. Patterned networks matter because glioblastoma cells communicate through calcium waves as they invade. A tidy, repeatable grid lets researchers watch that signaling cell by cell. The platform is a first step toward testing drugs that might jam the tumor's internal conversations.
plos-pone-0352339:
Mohammad Alipour-Vaezi and colleagues used a huge United States health records network to ask which comes first in people with back, neck, and spine pain: mental illness or fading cognition. The two often arrive together in older pain patients, and each could feed the other. Matched groups were followed for three years in each direction to test both paths.

Both directions held. Pain patients with mental health conditions faced a higher risk of later cognitive impairment, steepest for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, with depression, anxiety, and other conditions also raising risk. Patients with earlier cognitive problems likewise faced higher risk of new mental illness, again led by bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. The authors recommend joined-up screening in pain clinics, since catching one side early may be the best chance to slow the other.
plos-pone-0352439:
Cao and colleagues, in a 2026 study, improve concrete made from recycled rubble so it can resist the salt attack that rusts steel inside bridges and sea walls. Recycled lumps carry old paste and cracks, weakening the mix. A baked mineral additive was tested as the fix, at several doses and several rubble replacement rates.

Strength and salt resistance both rose with the right pairings. One mix gained about a tenth in strength over the plain reference, and another cut salt passage by about a fifth, reaching a low permeability grade. Under the microscope, the additive and rubble together grew denser gel, filled pores, and delayed cracking, so failed samples showed no through-cracks. A scoring model that blends two weighting schemes then ranked the mixes fairly. The authors say recycled concrete, long the weaker cousin, can be engineered up to demanding jobs.
plos-pone-0352639:
Nima Rezvani Kakhki and five co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of melanoma cell chemistry. They compare melanoma lines that spread aggressively with one that spreads little. Normal skin-support cells serve as a baseline. The team profiled the cells' small molecules with nuclear magnetic resonance. They hunted for chemical signatures tied to spreading ability. Melanoma's deadliness comes mainly from spread.

Melanoma cells differed from normal cells across several energy and amino acid pathways. They stockpiled energy carriers and the antioxidant glutathione. They held less glucose and glutamine. The highly spreading line leaned further into antioxidant defense and altered amino acid use. It had more glutathione and glutamate, but less of a key energy cofactor. The authors read this as a shift toward resisting oxidative stress. That shift may help traveling tumor cells survive.
plos-pone-0353139:
Christina Artemenko and Mine Avcil test in 2026 a long held claim that brain activity for mental arithmetic shifts from front to back areas as children grow into adults. Their registered report measured brain activity with light based sensors in children, younger adults, and older adults doing two digit sums with carrying or borrowing steps.

Harder sums raised activity across the front and back network in every age group. Behaviour signs of struggle eased with age, yet the brain pattern stayed broadly stable, and back area activity did not rise as front activity fell. The claimed shift may hold only for single digit sums, the authors conclude.
plos-pone-0353739:
Hassan Ugail and Newton Howard introduce a free software toolkit for checking whether quantum machine-learning circuits keep the symmetries they promise, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Such circuits are usually graded on expressiveness or entanglement, but those scores never ask whether the circuit actually respects the symmetry built into its design. Their toolkit audits a circuit before training, reporting how it spreads across symmetry sectors and whether it stays coherent between them.

Tested on five circuit families with repeated random trials, the tool caught circuits whose symmetry machinery was silently inactive and separated designs that standard measures judged identical. Catching such faults before expensive training could save quantum researchers substantial wasted computing time.
plos-pone-0353839:
Debora Hashiguchi, Ana Luiza Dias, and Rodrigo Neves Romcy-Pereira study stress responses in young rats used to model autism, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. The rats were exposed before birth to valproic acid, a treatment known to produce autism-like traits. The team measured bodily and behavioural stress signs — freezing, vocal calls, and defecation — during handling, mild electric touch, fear learning, and watching another rat in distress.

Exposed rats showed stronger and longer-lasting stress reactions across nearly every test. Their fear responses also fell out of their usual timing with bodily reactions, and distress at a companion's suffering lingered. The authors argue the model captures the stress vulnerability that often accompanies autism, making it useful for testing calming treatments.
plos-pone-0353939:
Dogbla and colleagues, in a 2026 study, count how many French workers leave occupational health visits with limits on their work, or ruled unfit altogether. Such verdicts shape lives and labor supply, yet they are rarely counted together on a large scale. The team analyzed more than seventy thousand visits in one department over two years.

About nine in ten workers were passed fully fit. A small share received temporary limits, a slightly larger share permanent limits, and about one in seventy-five was ruled unfit. Age over fifty-five roughly doubled the risk of both kinds of limits, and having a disability raised it similarly. Longer service and mid-sized companies also raised risk. Unfitness, by contrast, grew less likely the longer a worker had been with the company. The authors give employers and doctors a rare population picture of work capacity decisions.
plos-pone-0354139:
Msilikale Walter Manyiri led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of child brain development in Bagamoyo, Tanzania. Nearly six hundred children from six months to ten years old took age-appropriate development tests, and family wealth was scored from household assets. The team compared scores across wealth groups at each age band.

Rich and poor children started out alike, then a gap opened around age two and widened into a substantial preschool and school-age disadvantage for the poorest. Manyiri suggests programs aimed at the preschool years could blunt the divide.
plos-pone-0354239:
Canfield and Miller present a 2026 protocol for a trial that layers two early-childhood programs into regular pediatric visits for low-income families. Poverty in the first years of life is linked to lasting gaps in health and learning. Both programs coach warm, steady bonds between parents and babies; one adds a focus on play and reading talk.

About three hundred fifty parent and child pairs will be assigned at random to the combined program or the standard one alone. Support comes at each checkup from birth to age two, with measures at the start and at one and two years. Main outcomes are the parent-child bond, how much parents stimulate learning, and the child's social and emotional growth. A small early phase tests how well clinics can deliver the combined model.
plos-pone-0354339: Severe pneumonia treated with third-generation cephalosporins — often against guidelines. This French critical care cohort found frequent non-guideline-concordant use. The findings expose antibiotic misuse in ICUs — fueling resistance while adding little benefit.
plos-pone-0355339:
Wenyan Zhu, Xiaowei Wu, and Rongkui Hu published this 2026 genetics study of gestational diabetes, the blood sugar disorder that appears in pregnancy. Standard gene studies blend all tissues together, hiding which cells matter. Merging Finnish genome data with gene activity data from a dozen immune cell types, they searched for genes whose activity ties to the disease in specific cells.

Fourteen genes surfaced, strongest in helper T cells and monocytes, and several help present foreign material to the immune system. Whole-blood analysis found almost none of them. Zhu argues cell-level views reveal biology that bulk studies miss.
plos-pone-0355739:
Nabila Masud and co-authors blasted lab-grown brain precursor cells with shockwaves to model blast brain injury. Explosions can injure the brain without any blow to the head, and the cell-level mechanics stay poorly mapped. Their 2026 study applied single and double shockwaves from two directions and probed the cells with atomic force microscopy and staining.

Double shockwaves travelling one way softened the cells, roughened their surfaces, and tore up their internal scaffolding. The same double dose from the opposite direction cut the numbers of support-cell offspring and young neurons instead. Direction, not just dose, changed the damage pattern. Masud and colleagues argue injury models must account for wave direction when judging harm.
plos-pone-0355839:
Jessica Trico and colleagues track what happens across the whole balance system after one inner ear is chemically destroyed in rats. Balance loss is common in people, yet the brain and the surviving ear's joint response is poorly mapped. Over a month, the team measured posture and behavior, hearing, immune-style cell reactions in the brain's balance center, and the tiny sensory endings in both ears.

Posture problems began at once, while restlessness and anxiety-like behavior appeared later and lasted. Alarm cells in the balance center surged early, with one cell type staying raised all month. Sensory endings vanished on the treated side, dipped briefly on the untouched side, then recovered there, while hearing damage stayed one-sided. Trico and colleagues say recovery is a whole-system negotiation, not just brain compensation.
plos-pone-0355939:
Zainab Shirazi and co-authors used detailed three-dimensional scans to check a fine point of root canal work. How precisely do modern motors stop at the right depth inside a tooth? Their 2026 laboratory study shaped sixty extracted single-root teeth. Two motors with built-in length sensors were compared against a standalone sensor used before shaping. The team then measured the gap between the finished canal and its natural narrow point.

No motor drilled past the canal's end. All three approaches landed within the accepted tolerance about equally often. Still, the standalone sensor's canals ended closest to the ideal point. Both motor groups finished similarly to each other. For dentists, the message is reassuring but nuanced. Built-in sensors are safe, though a separate measurement may hold the endpoint slightly truer.
plos-pone-0356139: He and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on reading stock market reactions with large models. They paired large language or AI models with time series forecasting tools. The aim was to judge how markets respond to news or events. Blending text-savvy models with price history may sharpen market analysis, a task where timing and tone both move money.
plos-pone-0356239:

Stewardship programs track antibiotics to fight resistance, but the standard measures can disagree. One counts standardized daily doses set by the World Health Organization; the other simply counts each day a patient receives a drug. The team pulled a year of records for just over six hundred ICU patients who received antimicrobials.

The two measures tracked each other closely overall, yet differed meaningfully for individual drugs. Counting treatment days, the authors argue, gives clinicians a clearer picture of how long patients are actually exposed in intensive care, where doses are often adjusted. Standardized doses remain better for comparing hospitals. Their conclusion is that the measures complement each other and should not be treated as interchangeable.
plos-pone-0356539:

Interviews are known to disadvantage autistic candidates, so employers often turn to tests as the objective alternative. The researchers gave autistic and neurotypical adults three widely used selection tools, covering general mental ability, personality, and situational judgment, situations in which applicants choose what they would do at work.

All three tools produced real score gaps against autistic adults. That gap persisted even with ability held equal, personality, age, and gender. The authors caution this is early work, but the pattern suggests that tests billed as neutral can carry the same adverse impact as interviews. They call for hiring methods built to capture job-relevant strengths in neurodiverse applicants rather than quietly screening them out.
plos-pone-0356739:

Weights were tuned by optimization, and managers can adjust the thresholds that trigger action. The team validated the system against historical Brazilian yellow fever data from the health ministry. That is a fitting test, since the disease spills from wildlife to people. Sharper alerts help surveillance teams spend scarce investigation budgets where an outbreak is likeliest.
plos-pone-0358039:

The bacterium has been linked to metabolic troubles beyond the stomach, but earlier studies were small and often ignored body weight and kidney function. Drawing on a huge health examination database of close to sixty-eight thousand adults, they adjusted step by step for metabolic, kidney, and inflammation factors.

At first glance the link looked clear: infected people had more high uric acid. But each adjustment layer shrank it, until in the fullest model the association was tiny and statistically uncertain. A very small rise in uric acid levels remained, and patterns held for men and women separately. Most of the apparent connection, they conclude, reflects the company infection keeps, body size and metabolic health, rather than a strong effect of the bacterium.
plos-pone-0358239:

The authors instead measured the diversity of shapes the particle's surface ligands can adopt, an information based score. They scored one hundred five gold nanoparticles from a benchmark dataset. Then they watched the charge rule break at a threshold.

Below the threshold, more positive charge meant more uptake, as textbooks say. Above it, the relationship reversed: charge predicted less uptake, consistent with floppy ligands shielding the surface. Adding the entropy score improved prediction across several model types, with the gains concentrated in the floppy regime. A second dataset of over six hundred mixed particles supported the pattern. Drug designers gain a descriptor that tells them when their dial stops working.
plos-pone-0358439:

The Extended Effort Assessment Scale measures how hard people must strain to follow speech, a burden hearing tests miss. No checked version existed for Kannada, a major language of southern India. The team translated the scale both ways, reviewed it with experts, and tested it on one hundred native speaking adults.

Nine of the ten items behaved well in statistical checks; the telephone item misfitted, likely because phone listening mixes several demands at once. Overall consistency and repeat reliability were excellent, and scores tracked a simple effort rating scale as expected. Two items behaved differently by age or gender, so the authors advise care comparing those across groups. Clinicians now have a tested Kannada tool for a complaint patients voice often.
plos-pone-0358539:

Multi professional medication reviews bring doctors, pharmacists, and nurses around one table to prune drug lists, and psychiatry, where patients often carry heavy sedative loads, had little evidence. The French university hospital study compared stays before and after reviews began across four psychiatric wards, spanning 2017 to 2023.

After reviews started, patients left hospital with about one fewer prescribed drug on average, a small but statistically firm shift. The cuts concentrated where they matter most: psychotropic medicines fell furthest, led by benzodiazepines, with antipsychotics and anticholinergic drugs also down, and even laxatives, often prescribed to counter drug side effects, declined. No drug class rose to compensate. The authors read the pattern as reviews doing quiet, compounding good in a high risk prescribing environment.

plos-pone-0358839:

plos-pone-0359339: Sun and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on turning Chinese Braille documents into text. Their subject sits at the crossing of farming practice and climate policy, since soil carbon is one of the largest levers in the land carbon budget.
