Fidel Alfaro-Almagro, Mark Jenkinson, and colleagues described brain image processing for UK Biobank in 2018. UK Biobank is a huge health study that invited many past participants back for scans. The imaging covers the brain, heart, and body, plus ultrasound and bone scans.

Their pipeline cleans and checks the first large batch of brain scans in a uniform way. Automated quality checks flag bad scans so analysts can trust the rest. Uniform processing matters because small handling differences can fake results at this scale. The work set the pattern for imaging studies with tens of thousands of people.
pmc-6323939:
Huaiyu Mi, Anushya Muruganujan, Dustin Ebert, and coauthors reported PANTHER version 14 in 2018. PANTHER classifies genes by evolution and function across the tree of life. It groups genes into families and maps them to shared roles.

The update adds many more genomes and a leaner set of ontology terms for quick enrichment tests. Users can ask which functions appear more often than chance in a gene list. Cleaner term sets make those answers easier to read. The resource serves both deep evolution studies and everyday gene-list interpretation in one place.
pmc-8008539:
Matthew Page and colleagues issued the PRISMA 2020 statement in 2021, the updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. A systematic review is only as credible as its report is complete, since readers cannot check steps the authors never described. The 2020 statement modernizes the checklist first published in 2009.

It sets out the items a review should report, covering the question, the search, study selection, results, and the certainty of the evidence. This journal version of the statement carries the same guidance as its sister publications, widening its reach to another readership. Editors, peer reviewers, and authors use the checklist daily, making it one of the most influential short documents in health research.
schoolcraft-algic-researches-vol1-1839:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft saves the tales of the lakes in Vol. 1 of Algic Researches, out in 1839. Schoolcraft was the state's man midst the tribes round the Great Lakes. His wife's kin gave him tales at first hand. Here he prints them in English: tales of Manabozho, the trickster sire of lore, of beasts that speak, and of how the world was made and marred.

The Algic name is his word for those tribes' stock. The set founds the study of their lore in English. Longfellow drew his famed song from these pages. This tome starts the hoard.
schoolcraft-algic-researches-vol2-1839:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft ends his hoard of lake tales in Vol. 2 of Algic Researches, out in 1839. The first tome gave the trickster's deeds and the world's birth. Here come grander beasts: the great thunder bird whose wings beat out the storm, and the Weendigo, the gaunt ice giant who eats men in the depth of the cold north woods.

Schoolcraft prints the tales as he heard them, with brief notes. His pair of tomes is the root hoard of Great Lakes lore in English. Fans of myth still mine them. This tome holds their most famed beasts.
scotus-quaestiones-physicorum-de-anima-w:
This Latin volume comes from Luke Wadding's 1639 edition of Duns Scotus. It holds the master's questions on two works of Aristotle: the Physics, all eight books, and the De Anima, on the soul. It adds his logical questions on the Isagoge of Porphyry and on the Categories. Notes by Franciscus Pitigianus and supplements by Hugo Cavellus fill the margins.

Scotus tests Aristotle point by point: motion, place, time, the powers of the soul, and the intellect that thinks. His answers shaped Franciscan teaching for centuries. No English version in the public domain exists. The Wadding text is the form in which the early modern world read the Subtle Doctor on nature and mind.
scotus-quaestiones-quodlibetales-wadding:
John Duns Scotus, the Subtle Doctor of the Franciscans, taught at Oxford and Paris in the years around 1300. His Quodlibetal Questions take up twenty-one disputed points, argued in open session on any topic the crowd might raise. The text here is from Luke Wadding's great edition of the works of Scotus, printed in 1639, with the commentary of Franciscus Lychetus. It is in Latin.

The questions range over God, the will, knowledge, and the fine joints of metaphysics, each split and weighed in the sharp style of Scotus. No English version in the public domain exists. The volume stands as a record of scholastic debate at its most exact and most daring.
stendhal-charterhouse-parma-1839:
Stendhal published The Charterhouse of Parma in 1839, a French novel set in Italy after Napoleon. Fabrizio del Dongo, a young nobleman, rushes to fight at Waterloo but barely grasps what he sees. Back in Parma, he enters the church to gain favor at court. Court intrigue, love, and prison shape his fate.

His aunt Gina schemes brilliantly to protect and advance him. Fabrizio falls in love with Clelia while jailed in a tower. Stendhal wrote the book fast, and its pace feels free and joyful. Critics rank it among the greatest novels ever written. Its mix of war, politics, and love still feels fresh.
the-american-phrenological-journal-and-m: The American Phrenological Journal and Miscellany, 1839. The American journal. This book preserves that periodical. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
the-comedy-of-errors-pg2239: Ephesus runs mad in this edition of Shakespeare's farce: two sets of twins, two Dromios, and a chain of errors that tangles masters and servants. Beatings, arrests, and mistaken wives pile up until the Abbess sorts them out. The fastest farce ever written, breathless with confusion.
the-history-of-england-from-the-accessio: Volume two of Macaulay’s History of England: from James II’s accession through the Revolution. The Whig epic continues, brilliant and partisan, the most famous history in English. The Revolution of 1688 was history’s most gentlemanly upheaval.
the-new-lavater-or-and-improved-system-o: The New Lavater, 1839. The improved physiognomy. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
the-winter-s-tale-pg1539: A king's groundless jealousy shatters his family in this edition of Shakespeare's late romance: Leontes accuses his innocent queen, loses his son, and abandons his baby daughter. Sixteen years pass before time, a shepherd's feast, and a statue that seems to breathe bring forgiveness. From tragedy to miracle: his most magical late play.
tob-0039:
After the Cold War, the United States government faced its own record of human radiation research. The Advisory Committee on Human Radiation Experiments issued its final report in 1995. Investigators read secret files and heard testimony about studies run from the 1940s onward.

Patients were injected with plutonium, soldiers were marched near atomic blasts, and prisoners and the sick were exposed, often with no real consent. Thousands of Americans passed through such tests. The committee judged much of the work wrong even by the standards of its day. The report stands as an official apology and a warning about secret science.
tob-10039:
Al-Ghazali, the great eleventh-century Muslim thinker also written Abu Hamid Muhammad, tells his own story in The Confessions. At the height of fame as a teacher, doubt struck him so hard that he could no longer trust what he knew or taught. He left his post and took to wandering as a Sufi seeker.

His account follows that crisis step by step: skepticism, breakdown, travel, and a slow recovery of certainty through lived spiritual practice. Few documents in Islamic literature are so personal about faith and reason. Readers meet a brilliant mind describing, honestly and in his own voice, how it lost and remade itself.
tob-13139:
Paul Carus, an American writer on religion, shaped the Buddha's life into gospel form in 1894. Drawing on the Pali canon, he retells the story in chapters that echo the style of the Christian Gospels. Western readers with no background in Buddhism could thus meet the Buddha on familiar ground.

The narrative follows the prince who leaves his palace, gains enlightenment under the tree, and preaches a path out of suffering. Carus stresses the teaching on craving, compassion, and release from rebirth. Scholars now call the book dated, but it brought thousands of Western readers to Buddhist thought for the first time.
tob-4139:
Volume two of Waite's Paracelsus continues the hermetic and alchemical writings with the Archidoxes and treatises on metals and healing. Readers should note the evidence marks this as a second copy of Waite's edition held in the library. The system of Hohenheim stands entire in its pages.

Paracelsus divides the world among the elements and the three principles, salt, sulphur, and mercury, and builds his cures on that frame. His medicine mixes observation, astrology, and faith in nature's signatures. Verified from the 1919 edition, the volume completes Waite's service: the alchemist-physician's thought, whole, for English readers.
turke-and-gowin-madden-1839:
The Turke and Gowin is a rough northern romance of Sir Gawain, edited by Frederic Madden in 1839. It belongs to the alliterative tradition, the strong verse form of northern England. A strange visitor sets its plot in motion at Arthur's court.

A giant who calls himself the Turk lays a grim challenge before the king and his knights. Gawain takes it up and rides north into a land of odd tests and stranger hosts. The tale is wilder and less polished than the famous Gawain poem. That roughness is part of its charm. It shows the popular edge of the Gawain legend in the late Middle Ages.
un-ga-res-139: Catalogued as General Assembly Resolution 139 and dated by the catalog to 1970, this record gives the number alone, with no subject in its title or notes. That dating sits oddly. The Assembly's low sequential numbers belong to its first years, before the later session-based numbering. What can be stated with care is the form. It is a formal decision of the full Assembly, kept as official record text from the UN's own files. It should be read on its own terms, not through guesswork about its topic.
un-ga-res-39:
Franco's Spain drew the UN General Assembly's sharpest rebuke of its first year in Resolution 39, adopted on 12 December 1946. The text recalls that the peoples of the UN, at San Francisco, Potsdam, and London, had condemned the Franco regime and barred Spain from the UN while it lasted. A Security Council probe in mid-1946 had then weighed what more could be done.

That probe found, without dissent, that the regime was fascist in origin, shape, and conduct. It had been built with much help from Hitler's Germany and Mussolini's Italy. The Assembly assures the Spanish people of warm goodwill, and of a welcome once they can join. For now, the door stays shut.
un-ga-res-a-69-39:
Terror groups seeking mass-kill arms are the fear behind Resolution A/69/39, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the vote of the year before on the same risk. It names the will of states to fight terror, as shown in past Assembly and Security Council texts. The risk of links between terror and weapons of mass destruction, it warns, keeps growing.

Steps by states under the Security Council's 2004 anti-spread vote are noted with care. So is the 2007 start of the world pact against acts of nuclear terror. Tighter guards on atomic goods, agreed in 2005 to the pact on the safety of such goods in transit and store, are welcomed as well.
un-ga-res-a-72-239:
Family farms won a decade of their own under Resolution A/72/239 of the General Assembly. The text looks back with praise on the International Year of Family Farming, kept in 2014. That year raised the standing of family farms, herding, and small plots in the fight for food and good diets. Many lands had since built plans in favor of such farms, with farm teams at home and small loans for small holders.

A shared bank of facts on family farming had been built, and its worth for talks and plans is praised. Such farms, the text holds, lift diets, guard food, end want, and keep the wild world whole. The vote declares the years ahead a Decade of Family Farming, to keep that work in view.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 39, adopted on 12 December 1946, dealt with Spain under its fascist government. The Assembly recalled that the peoples of the United Nations had condemned that regime at San Francisco, Potsdam, and London. It cited a Security Council inquiry finding it was patterned on the Axis regimes. The inquiry found it had given the enemy much aid during the war.

The Assembly held that the regime did not speak for the Spanish people. It urged that it be barred from United Nations agencies and meetings. That bar was to last until a new and proper government formed. Members were urged to call home their ambassadors from Madrid at once. If no government resting on the people's consent came within a fair time, the Security Council was asked to weigh steps.

Resolution 69/39 of the General Assembly addresses the risk that terrorists might acquire weapons of mass destruction. The Assembly notes the steps states have taken under Security Council resolution 1540 (2004). It notes the entry into force of the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism. It calls on all member states to support international efforts against such acquisition. It calls on them to consider joining that convention. It calls on them to strengthen national controls over weapons, delivery systems, and related materials and technology.

Resolution 72/239 of the General Assembly, adopted at the seventy-second session, proclaims 2019 to 2028 as the United Nations Decade of Family Farming. It builds on the International Year of Family Farming held in 2014 and on the national committees and policies that year produced.

The text stresses that family farms produce more than 80 per cent of the world's food by value. Some 815 million people still suffer hunger. Most of the extreme poor live in rural areas. It encourages states to develop and share public policies that support family farmers, especially smallholders and women. It puts the Food and Agriculture Organization and the International Fund for Agricultural Development in charge of leading the Decade. Progress is reported to the Assembly every two years.
un-sc-res-1039:
Lebanon's interim force was renewed by the Security Council on 29 January 1996. The Secretary-General had reported on the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon on 22 January. Lebanon's permanent representative had written on 17 January, and the government asked for the extension. The force's terms of reference went back to resolutions 425 and 426 (1978).

The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate for six months, to 31 July 1996. It restated its strong support for Lebanon's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence within its recognized borders. All parties were told to cooperate fully so the force could carry out its mandate in full. The Council condemned all acts of violence, above all those aimed at the force, and urged the parties to end them. It welcomed the streamlining of the force due by May 1996 and pressed for more savings in support services, as long as its working capacity stayed intact.
un-sc-res-1239:
Kosovo's refugee catastrophe drew a humanitarian appeal on 14 May 1999. Hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians had fled into Albania, Macedonia, and Bosnia. More were displaced inside Kosovo and Montenegro. The refugee agency and relief groups strained to feed and shelter them. The Secretary-General planned a needs assessment mission to the region.

The Council praised the states and relief organizations already helping the refugees. It urged all who could to give more resources for the relief effort. It called for access for the United Nations and all humanitarian staff working in Kosovo and other parts of Yugoslavia. The right of every refugee and displaced person to return home in safety and dignity was reaffirmed. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was pressed to let aid reach the displaced and to work toward a political settlement. The text stopped short of the force questions the Council would face in June.
un-sc-res-1339:
Georgia's observer mission was kept on as the Abkhazia talks stalled on 31 January 2001. The Secretary-General's report of 18 January lay before the Council. The zone of conflict stayed mostly calm but volatile. The two sides had met in their coordinating council on 23 January. UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force worked closely together.

The Council extended UNOMIG's mandate for a period ending 31 July 2001. The extension could be reviewed if the CIS force changed. The Council backed the special representative's plan to table a draft paper on dividing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi. Work on a protocol for refugee returns to the Gali region had to speed up. The Abkhaz side in particular was called to end its refusal to negotiate the core issues. The Council restated that the population shifts caused by the conflict were unacceptable and that all refugees held the right to return home.
un-sc-res-139: The Federation of Mali sought a seat at the United Nations in 1960. On 28 June 1960 the Security Council examined its application. It recommended to the General Assembly that the federation be admitted to membership. The vote was unanimous, and the text is a single sentence long. The federation joined weeks later. It broke apart soon after, and Mali and Senegal entered as separate states.
un-sc-res-1439:
Angola's peace held while the Council finished the UNITA sanctions story on 24 October 2002. The government and UNITA were applying the peace accords and the April 2002 memorandum that ended the war. The Joint Commission had met again, and a United Nations Mission in Angola had been set up. The Council still voiced concern at the war's humanitarian toll on civilians.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the UNITA monitoring mechanism for two months, to 19 December 2002. Two experts would be named to serve on it. The mechanism owed the sanctions committee a report by 13 December, focused on sanctions breaches. All states were called to cooperate with it fully. The Council also ended parts of resolution 1127 (1997), the travel measures on UNITA, from 1 November 2002. The step marked the sanctions regime winding down as the peace took hold.
un-sc-res-1539:
Children forced into war stand at the center of Resolution 1539, adopted in April 2004. Armed groups in several conflicts were recruiting boys and girls as fighters and servants. The Council condemned the practice and demanded action plans from listed parties to end it.

Inside, the members threaten measures against groups that keep using child soldiers and ask for a worldwide monitoring system to name violators. The text built toward the UN's later formal watch list for child recruitment. For readers, it marks the point where protecting children in war became a standing Council duty, not a passing concern.
un-sc-res-1639: Security Council Resolution 1639 is held here as a Wikisource transcription of the United Nations official record. Its form is standard and deliberate: situation first, judgment second, action third. Because later disputes often turn on what exactly was decided, preserving the whole text, rather than a summary, is the service this entry performs.
un-sc-res-1739:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1739, adopted on 10 January 2007. The country stayed split after civil war, and the crisis kept getting worse. Civilians suffered and many fled their homes. Elections were planned by 31 October 2007 under a transition plan.

The text extends the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and the French forces backing it until 30 June 2007. It restates the mission's full task list in detail. The tasks cover watching the cease-fire, disarming fighters and militias, guarding voter registration, and policing the arms embargo. The mission may use all necessary means, and French forces may step in to protect civilians and support the operation.
un-sc-res-1939: Resolution 1939 is one of the Security Council's formal acts, preserved in official wording through a Wikisource transcription. The document was written for immediate use by governments and UN officials, in language tested for agreement among fifteen delegations. That tested language is the entry, kept whole so its precision can still do its work.
un-sc-res-239:
Foreign mercenaries were fighting in the Congo again in 1967. The Congolese government had sent the Council a message on the threat. On 10 July 1967 the Council debated the danger to the Congo's independence. It restated its 1966 rule against outside interference. Mercenary bands had seized towns in the east that month. Their presence drove the emergency tone of the text.

Any state that lets mercenaries be recruited for overthrowing governments stands condemned. Governments must keep their land and their nationals out of such plots. Training, transit, and planning for mercenaries all had to be blocked. The target was the overthrow of the Congo's government. The Council stayed seized of the question.
un-sc-res-339: United Nations record keeping gives this text the number 339, and the catalog dates it 1973. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-39:
Kashmir's war brought India and Pakistan before the Security Council within months of their freedom. Resolution 39, passed on 20 January 1948, holds that the state of affairs between the two new states needs study as a matter of haste. Left to run, the fight could put world peace and safety at risk. The Council acts under its power to probe any dispute of that kind.

A Commission of the Security Council is set up, of three members. India picks one, Pakistan picks one, and the two so picked name the third. The team must go to the spot as fast as it can. It acts under the Council's sway and must keep the Council told of its work in full. The team grew into the long UN watch over Kashmir.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1039, passed on 29 January 1996, keeps the UN force in south Lebanon for six more months. The force, UNIFIL, had been there since 1978. A UN report of 22 January set out its recent work. Lebanon's envoy had asked in a letter for more time, and the Council granted the request.

The term now ran to 31 July 1996. The Council restated its strong backing for Lebanon's unity and freedom, inside borders the world accepts. It set out the force's tasks once more, as first drawn in 1978. All sides were told to work with the force in full, so it could do its job. Calm in the south served no one if the force stood blocked.

Resolution 1239, adopted on 14 May 1999, addresses the refugee catastrophe produced by the Kosovo crisis. Enormous numbers of Kosovar Albanians had fled into Albania, Macedonia, Bosnia, and beyond, while displacement inside Kosovo and other parts of Yugoslavia kept climbing. The Council grounded its concern in human rights law, refugee law, and the Geneva Conventions.

It demanded that aid agencies and the UN refugee agency be given safe, unimpeded access to Kosovo and the rest of Yugoslavia so help could reach people in need. It stressed coordinating relief among states and relief organizations, and it backed the right of all refugees and displaced people to return home safely. A UN humanitarian assessment mission to the region was also welcomed.

Georgia's frozen conflict in Abkhazia fills Resolution 1339, adopted unanimously on 31 January 2001. The Council called the continued lack of progress on a comprehensive settlement unacceptable. The zone was mostly calm, it noted, but the general situation remained very volatile, and the two sides' coordinating council had met just days earlier.

The mandate of the UN observer mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, was extended for six months, to July 2001. The Council stressed how closely the observers and the Commonwealth of Independent States peacekeeping force worked together on the ground. It welcomed their stabilizing contribution while making clear that observation was no substitute for a political deal on Abkhazia's status.

A union that lived for weeks still left its trace at the UN. On 28 June 1960, the Council adopted Resolution 139 without dissent. The applicant was the Federation of Mali. Senegal and the Sudanese Republic had formed it as French West Africa broke up. France had just granted the union its freedom, days before.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the federation. The union broke apart that August, before the Assembly met. The story then ran on through two more texts in this series. One seated the Republic of Mali, the other Senegal. Each state entered on its own in the end.

Resolution 1439, adopted unanimously on 24 October 2002, manages the tail end of sanctions against Angola's UNITA movement. Angola's long civil war had ended that April, months after UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi was killed, and the government and UNITA were carrying out their peace accords. A joint commission had reconvened, and a new UN mission in Angola had been created to support the settlement.

With that progress noted, the Council kept the sanctions monitoring machinery in place for a short final stretch, judging that watching compliance still mattered while peace took hold. It also voiced concern for civilians suffering the war's humanitarian effects. Angola's sanctions regime, once a centerpiece of Council action, was being wound down.

Child soldiers and other abuses against children in war are tackled on 22 April 2004. Earlier resolutions had built a framework of rules and lists of offending parties. Yet parties to conflicts still violated children's rights with impunity, the Council says, and little had changed on the ground.

Listed parties are demanded to produce action plans to stop recruiting and using children, with a warning of measures against those who refuse. The Secretary-General is asked to design, within three months, a full monitoring and reporting system on child soldier recruitment and other grave abuses. That system would draw on United Nations agencies, governments, regional bodies, and civic groups for timely and reliable information.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's European Union stabilization force is renewed on 21 November 2005 for a further planned period. The force had taken over from NATO's SFOR the year before. Full support is again voiced for the High Representative and for completing the 1995 peace agreement.

Acting under Chapter VII, states working through the European Union are authorized to keep the force in place under unified command. They may take all necessary measures to carry out the military terms of the peace agreement and to defend the force and help it complete its mission. The parties are told to respect the force's safety and freedom of movement, and the authorization would be reviewed as the peace required.

UNOCI's mandate is restated in full by Resolution 1739, adopted on 10 January 2007. Côte d'Ivoire's crisis persisted, with grave humanitarian effects, and elections were due by 31 October 2007 under the transition plan in Resolution 1721 (2006). The UN Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and the French forces backing it were the core of the international presence.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends both mandates until 30 June 2007. UNOCI's tasks are to watch the ceasefire, help disarm and demobilize fighters, dismantle militias, and secure voter identification and registration. They also cover protecting civilians under imminent threat, monitoring the arms embargo, supporting humanitarian access, helping restore state authority nationwide, and backing free elections with logistics and security. The French forces are authorized to use all necessary means in support, including protecting civilians in their areas. A review of mandate length and troop levels is promised by June 2007.

Nepal was working through a peace process after its long civil war when the Council adopted Resolution 1939 in 2010. The former Maoist rebels had joined politics under the peace agreement of 2006. The United Nations Mission in Nepal, called UNMIN, watched the arms and fighters of both sides.

The Council renewed UNMIN's mandate until 15 January 2011. It decided that the mission would then leave Nepal for good. Both the government and the Maoists had asked for that end date. Nepal's parties were pressed to finish the peace process by then. The hardest question was what would happen to the Maoist fighters. They had to join the security forces or return to civilian life. Work on a new constitution was also still unfinished.

Mercenaries, not Cyprus, drive Resolution 239. Foreign soldiers of fortune were fighting in the Congo again in 1967. White mercenaries had seized towns in the east. The Congolese government sent the Council an urgent message. Resolution 239 was adopted unanimously on 10 July 1967.

Members reaffirmed their 1966 demand on the Congo. They condemned any state still letting mercenaries be recruited. Governments had to police their own soil and citizens. No planning, training, or transit of mercenaries aimed at Congo's government would be tolerated. The Secretary-General had to track compliance closely. The text is an early landmark in the UN's long campaign against mercenary warfare in Africa.

The October war of 1973 was still burning when the Council adopted Resolution 339 on 23 October. Resolution 338, passed the day before, had ordered a cease-fire between Israel and its Arab neighbors. The fighting had not stopped in time. More had to be done to make the order real.

The Council confirmed its decision of the day before. All firing and all military action had to stop at once. The forces of the two sides were urged to return to their earlier positions. Those were the positions they held when the cease-fire was due to take effect. The Secretary-General was asked to send United Nations observers at once. They would watch over the cease-fire between Israel and Egypt. The observers would come from United Nations personnel already in the Middle East, above all in the Suez Canal area.

India and Pakistan, two brand-new states, were already in conflict over Jammu and Kashmir at the start of 1948. The princely state's future was the core of the dispute. Resolution 39, adopted on 20 January 1948, set up a United Nations commission for the dispute.

The commission had three members. India would pick one, Pakistan would pick one, and those two would name the third. The commission was sent to the area with a double job. It had to investigate the facts, under Article 34 of the Charter. It also had to act as a mediator between the parties, without slowing down the investigation. It could travel wherever its work required. Decisions would be taken by majority vote, and the Council would supply staff and help.

A small state on Europe's edge won its freedom in August 1991. It had been a Soviet republic. Now it sought a seat of its own at the UN. War clouds hung over its eastern strip, where rebels rejected the new state. Resolution 739 was passed without a vote on 5 February 1992.

The Council backed the bid from the Republic of Moldova. It told the General Assembly to admit the country. The Assembly did so in March 1992. The seat confirmed Moldova's borders in the eyes of the world. That point gained weight weeks later. Fights in the east flared into a short war. The clash froze into a dispute that still lasts.
villa-rubein-and-other-stories-pg2639: John Galsworthy's Villa Rubein and other stories: early tales of love and society. The Forsyte author's apprentice work, sensitive and refined. A fine collection. Galsworthy's early stories show the master forming, the master forming, sensitive and refined.
weddynge-syr-gawen-dame-ragnell-madden-1:
The Weddynge of Syr Gawen and Dame Ragnell is a Middle English romance edited by Frederic Madden in 1839. It tells the famous loathly lady tale. A threatening knight spares King Arthur's life on one condition, and Gawain must pay the price.

Arthur must learn within a year what women most desire. The hideous Dame Ragnell knows the answer, and she will trade it for marriage to Gawain. He agrees, for the king's sake, and treats his bride with full courtesy. On the wedding night her ugliness falls away. The answer, that women want rule over their own lives, is the tale's lasting point.
